corpus.note: Outcomes are inferred from transcript language, not CRM-verified.

rules.note: Ingestion and normalisation rules. These are policy, not inference — every one was decided by the client and is applied uniformly across the corpus. Anything the rules cannot settle is surfaced on the dashboard rather than guessed at silently.

speaker_resolution.detail: Fathom tags the closer with a '(Primal Instinct)' suffix on their speaker label. That label identifies the rep. Every other speaker label in the transcript collapses to a single 'prospect' role.
handles: Diarization swapping speakers on short turns — role is assigned per label, not per line, so a swap misattributes a line but never invents a third participant
A prospect changing device mid-call and acquiring a new label (e.g. 'Francisco V.' becoming "Francisco's iPhone 17") — both labels collapse to the same prospect role
speaker_resolution.known_limit: Because diarization genuinely swaps lines, per-line attribution stays approximate. Talk-ratio and who-raised-the-objection metrics are therefore NOT published. Role-level facts (an objection occurred, a phase was run) are safe; line-level ones are not.
speaker_resolution.multi_rep_calls: If more than one '(Primal Instinct)' label appears, the rep with the most speaking turns is the closer; the rest are logged as additional_reps.

prospect_identity.detail: Prospect name is taken from the file title where present ('Name x Rep'). For untitled files ('Impromptu Zoom Meeting') it is recovered from the first non-rep speaker label in the transcript.
prospect_identity.normalisation: Lowercased, punctuation and device suffixes stripped, whitespace collapsed. Used as the deal key.

deal_merging.detail: Multiple calls with the same canonical prospect are a single deal. The deal carries the outcome of its LAST call chronologically, since that is the furthest the conversation actually got.
deal_merging.rationale: Counting calls as deals double-counts prospects and understates close rate. The unit that matters commercially is the deal.
deal_merging.cash: Deal cash is taken from the closing call only, never summed across calls in the sequence.
deal_merging.adherence: Adherence stays scored per call. A discovery call and a follow-up call are judged against different parts of the script, so averaging them would hide which part failed.

junk_filter.detail: Transcripts below 2 KB are failed or aborted recordings — connection drops, no-shows, empty rooms. Observed examples in the corpus run from 96 bytes to roughly 1.2 KB.
junk_filter.reporting: Excluded files are counted and reported, never silently dropped. A rising junk count is itself a signal about recording setup.

close_rule.detail: A verbal agreement to move forward plus a payment link sent counts as CLOSED, even where the transcript ends before payment confirms.
close_rule.known_bias: Overstates close rate against any deal that agreed and then never paid. Joining a payments export would quantify the gap.
close_rule.cash_treatment: Where a payment plan was agreed, cash is recorded as contract value with the instalment terms retained separately, so cash-collected and contract-value can be reported apart.

playbook.name: Kettlebell Body — Complete Sales Process
playbook.note: Reconstructed from a two-column PDF process map. Phase numbering follows the document; phases 7-10 (presentation and close) are referenced by the map but not enumerated on the supplied pages, so scoring covers phases 1-6, the five objection plays, and phase 11.

Set the four-part frame: where you are, where you want to go, what's in the way, what you need
Get frame agreement — 'Does that work?'
Open question: 'What are you potentially looking for help with?'
Age, height, current weight
Work — and whether it's desk-bound or on their feet
Health conditions, own or hereditary
Injuries, chronic pain, movement limitations — and how long
Typical training week and actual days trained
Results seen from current training
Current diet / whether following anything

phases.name: Goals — Surface to Deep
phases.intent: Move from what to WHY. This is where the real buying decision is made.

checks.text: Aesthetics & function: what would you change, one thing
Mobility, strength, energy — or something else
Something physical you want to do but can't right now
Bridge: 'Outside of the physical, what's actually driving this right now?'
'When you're moving better, what does that actually do for you?'
'Who else does that impact?'
Drive through to kids, marriage, legacy, identity or longevity
Reflect back: 'So this isn't really about the weight — it's about X. Is that right?'
What have you tried before?
What happened with that?
Why do you feel it didn't stick?
What's the one thing actually getting in the way?
Let them name the gap: no structure, no progression, no accountability, wrong knowledge, inconsistency
'The information isn't the problem. Why can't you stick to it on your own?'

phases.name: Consequence Frame
phases.intent: Make the cost of inaction real.

checks.text: 'If nothing changes — what does life look like over the next two years?'
'Is that something you're willing to settle for?'
'Why not?'
'Are you ready to draw a line in the sand on this?'

phases.name: Commitment Check
phases.intent: Get a genuine verbal yes BEFORE presenting anything.

checks.text: 'Do you believe you can actually get there with the right structure and the right person in your corner?'
'If you had everything you needed — is there any reason you wouldn't go all in on this?'
Only move forward once you have a clear YES; if hesitation surfaces, return to Phase 5

phases.name: Payment & Onboarding
phases.intent: Complete every step before you hang up.

checks.text: Step 1 — Collect payment
Step 2 — Schedule the onboarding call with Trevor
Step 3 — Confirm the agreement email arrived and have them sign it ON the call
Step 4 — Tell them to read the welcome email, click the Skool link to join the community, and complete the onboarding questionnaire before the Trevor call

objection_plays.trigger: I need to think about it
key_moves: Do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to [goal]?
What makes you feel it can?
So what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started?
Thinking isn't the problem. Deciding is.
The way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision?
That man you want to be — how does HE decide right now?
Are you sure? Nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?

objection_plays.trigger: I need to talk to my wife
key_moves: Money aside — do you personally feel this CAN get you to [goal]?
When you talk to her, what obstacles might come up?
Is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain?
Is this genuinely needing her input — or asking permission to bet on yourself?
This isn't a joint decision like buying a house. Is that responsibility hers or yours?
If stuck: put down a deposit, go talk to her, full refund if she says no

objection_plays.name: Money — Open Wallet
key_moves: ISOLATE FIRST: 'Finances aside — nothing else keeping you from 100%?'
'You're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place'
'Most clients pay upfront, but for some we break it up. Want to explore making it work?'
'Are you comfortable having an open, honest conversation about exactly where you're at financially?'
FINANCIAL PICTURE: cash on hand
FINANCIAL PICTURE: what's left over each month after bills
FINANCIAL PICTURE: how many credit cards
FINANCIAL PICTURE: available credit total per card
FINANCIAL PICTURE: used vs available
FINANCIAL PICTURE: crypto, stocks, investments
Are you ever going to have another Thanksgiving? Another busy season?
Things never slow down. When does it actually become the right time?
The longer you wait the harder this gets — metabolism slows, injuries compound
What if all you had to do was show up and everything else was handled?
The only thing you can control is right now
So what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started?
Would it be fair to say you're looking for certainty?
Do we run toward pleasure or away from pain — which is driving you?
BRIDGE: I'm not asking you to see the whole other side, just take the first step
PLANE: fear of the flight doesn't mean you never reach the destination
BURNED BEFORE: if you got hurt in a relationship once, do you never trust again?
But how will you know if you never actually try?

known_gaps_in_script.gap: No play for a clinical / medical-fit objection
known_gaps_in_script.detail: When a prospect's physio or surgeon rules out the core kettlebell movement library, there is no scripted path. The rep is left improvising a partial-value reframe. Seen in the Tyron G. call.

known_gaps_in_script.gap: No play for 'a cheaper alternative already worked for me'
known_gaps_in_script.detail: Objection C assumes the blocker is capacity to pay, not perceived value against a functioning low-cost substitute. Seen in the Badrane H. call, where the anchor was a $29/mo coach.

instances.detail: Isolated correctly ('outside of the investment, ready to draw a line in the sand?'), then ran the financial picture: cash on hand the $1,000–$2,500 band, monthly leftover the $500–$1,000 band, savings yes, credit score the 580–670 band. Missed the credit-card depth the script calls for — number of cards, available credit per card, used vs available — and never asked about crypto, stocks or investments. Still structured $1,200 x 6 live and got a yes.

Opened the door correctly — 'my intention is to never take food off people's tables. If there's a way we can structure this, are you open to exploring that?' → got a YES. Then never ran the financial picture. Not one question about cash on hand, monthly surplus, credit or assets. The play was started and abandoned.

The money objection landed and no part of the play ran. No isolate, no 'should I vs how' reframe, no offer to structure it, no financial picture. Instead the rep ran a takeaway — 'go back to her' — twice. A takeaway is not in the script.

Ran the first move well and then abandoned the play. ISOLATE FIRST was executed properly — 'So apart from finances, like, sounds good to you, like there's nothing else?' — and it produced a clean isolation: 'no, apart from the finances... Everything else, the way that it works and what I think I would get out of it are good.' From there nothing else ran. No 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place'. No payment-plan door opened, despite it being the obvious unlock for a prospect who converts USD into NZD and calls it a substantial portion of annual income — 'most clients pay upfront, but for some we break it up' was never said, and the offer stayed a single upfront payment. No permission asked for an open financial conversation. Not one of the six financial-picture questions was asked: cash on hand, monthly surplus after bills, number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available, or crypto/stocks/investments. The rep substituted a logistics question — 'what's the timeline on figuring out with the New Zealand feel, like, how to run it through the...' — and then booked a follow-up.

Two moves run well, then the play collapsed. The should-versus-how reframe was executed almost to the letter: 'So we're talking purely logistics, not like, should I do it, but actually how to do it in terms of finances?' The payment-plan door was opened: 'there are ways that we can move around with finances. If the payment in one installment is difficult, we can work around and maybe split it.' Then the rep inverted the play — 'But I would need to know from you what level of investments you can commit to at the beginning' — which asks the prospect to price himself instead of the rep discovering the picture. The financial picture was never taken: one abandoned question ('do you want to check, like, your checking account? Like, how much do you have?') and then nothing. Not asked: what is left over each month after bills, how many credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available, crypto/stocks/investments. Worst of all, when the prospect asked directly for something concrete — 'if you can send me maybe a few options of how can we pay it or if there is payment plan' — the answer was 'we don't have, like, a set payment plans.' The one artifact that could have moved this deal was requested and refused.

The most complete Objection C run in this batch, and still only half the play. Ran correctly: ISOLATE FIRST — 'finances aside, are you 100% sure that you can actually achieve your goals with Trevor?' and 'Is there anything else holding you back?'; the should-versus-how reframe in the rep's own idiom — 'We're business guys, we can work things out, yeah? So we don't have anything set in stone, like payment plans, but if there's a will, there's a way'; permission for the financial conversation, close to verbatim — 'So you're open for an open discussion about finances?'; and then three of the six financial-picture items — liquid cash ('what's your liquid cash right now on your hand?', answer zero), credit card usage, and credit score. He also pushed properly on the vague claim rather than accepting it: 'when you say you don't have money, what do you exactly mean by that? You don't have the full amount?' Not run: what is left over each month after bills, how many credit cards, available credit total per card, and used versus available — which are precisely the questions that determine whether a financing partner can do anything for a man with zero cash. Investments were also never asked. Two flaws beyond omission. First, the isolation was not clean: 'I don't know if specifically Trevor' was treated as a yes. Second, the rep offered financing on the back of a credit-score answer of 'Amazing. 10.', which is not a credit score on any scale and was not clarified.

The most complete money play in the batch, and it worked — it produced a chosen tier, a chosen structure and a handshake. ISOLATE FIRST ran properly and before any negotiation: 'before we talk about numbers and money, do you actually feel that you can get to your goals with Trevor, and you're 100% sure on this? Is there anything else apart from money that could be stopping you?' answered 'It's nothing else that can stop me.' The should-versus-how idea ran in the rep's own words: 'most of the guys pay upfront, but if there's a will, there is a way, we could split it up.' He asked what was coming up. And uniquely in this batch he put real numbers on the table rather than deflecting: half now and half at 30 days, three payments of $2,300, or six of $1,200, with the interest acknowledged. He also created room by stepping down to the six-month tier and adding a the the $500–$1,000 band+ band renewal. Scored hit on execution. Two caveats that belong in the record rather than the score. First, not one of the six financial-picture questions was asked — no cash on hand, monthly surplus, cards, available credit or investments — which was survivable here only because the prospect never claimed he could not pay. Second, two of the three structures he quoted are not sanctioned: the internal onboarding call the previous day defined the plan as payment one today and payment two in 30 days, and said longer splits are 'not generally an option that we offer'. The three- and six-payment plans, and the the the $500–$1,000 band+ band renewal, are all improvisations.

The textbook run of this play in the batch, and the only one that scores a hit. ISOLATE FIRST ran twice, because the first attempt was deflected: 'just to make sure, finances side, are you, like, you feel confident that you actually can get to your goals with this?' got a restatement of the money problem, so he re-asked more precisely — 'What I'm asking is, are you 100% confident on the program itself, how it's structured, and that you actually can get to your goals?' — and got a clean 'Yes.' The should-versus-how move followed almost verbatim: 'you're not in a, let's say, should place, but, like, how to do it?' — 'Correct.' He confirmed the isolation a third time ('it's just a matter of working out the financials. Am I correct?') and even checked the self-sabotage voice was quiet ('So there's no devil screaming anything right now?'). He opened the payment door, then asked permission in the scripted form: 'are you comfortable having like an open and honest conversation about exactly where you're financially at right now?' Then the financial picture: cash on hand ('What's your cash on hand right now?' — the under $500 band), a probe into how that is possible, and credit cards ('do you have any credit cards that you could use?' — 'Could, but I'm paying that off right now'). Monthly surplus, number of cards, available credit and investments were not asked, and scoring this a hit rather than a partial is deliberate: the play's purpose is to establish whether the money can be found, that was established beyond doubt, and continuing to itemise a man with the under $500 band for gas would have been extractive rather than diligent. Stopping was the correct execution.

Good structure, no financial picture. ISOLATE FIRST ran twice and cleanly — first inside the Phase 6 check ('Mainly cost' / 'Apart from that'), then again after the number: 'just make sure, apart from the finances right now, is there anything standing in a way from moving forward?' The payment door was opened with real, specific structures rather than vagueness — two payments of the the $500–$1,000 band+ band, three- and six-payment plans, and the six-pay total of $7,200 named out loud — and the rep proactively disclosed that instalments cost more, which no other call in this batch does and which is genuinely good practice. He then down-sold to the three-month tier at $4,000 with its own splits. The strongest single move came at 00:55:30: 'be transparent. Like, how much would you be actually willing to put down today? Just to see how it looks like.' That is the right question and it failed only because the prospect genuinely did not know. What never ran: permission for an open financial conversation, and every one of the six financial-picture items — cash on hand, monthly surplus after bills, number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available, and crypto or investments. He learned the qualitative picture (renovation commitments, incoming childcare costs, school fees, a temporary income dip) and never converted it into numbers, so the down-payment question arrived with nothing behind it.

Isolation ran ('if the money would be there... that's the only thing stopping you'). Two financial-picture questions ran: monthly leftover after bills, and cash available now. Everything else was skipped — no 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no credit cards, no available credit, no crypto/stocks/investments, and no explicit 'are you comfortable having an open honest conversation about where you're at financially'. The rep also pre-conceded the outcome out loud — 'I don't think it's going to work anyway, but just trying to get every' — which kills the play before the answer arrives.

Trigger at 00:22:52, '6,000 is a lot of money... we're not all millionaires here'. Exactly one financial-picture question ran — 'So what do you feel like you would even have available' — answered 'I don't know yet' and dropped. None of the rest: no 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no credit cards, no available credit, no investments, and critically no 'most clients pay upfront, but for some we break it up' — a payment plan was never offered on this call at all. Instead the rep introduced an undisclosed the the $500–$1,000 band+ band tier with a different coach. Note also that OC was arguably the wrong play: the prospect had just told him it was a should-I question, not a how question, which points to OA and value, not to capacity.

Trigger at 00:59:11, 'the numbers is a little high... The issue for me is the money part, because we're full of bills'. The best move on the call ran: the won't-versus-can't isolation, 'is it more of like, I just don't want to do it all up front, or is it more so I just can't?'. The instalment option was offered, which is the scripted move. But no financial picture was taken at all — no cash on hand, no leftover after bills beyond what he volunteered, no credit cards, no available credit, no investments — and no 'are you comfortable having an open, honest conversation about exactly where you're at financially'. The prospect volunteered his ceiling unprompted (the $1,000–the $2,500–$5,000 band band/month) and the rep responded by quoting $1,200/month, which is the opposite of making it work. The play was also muddied by contradictory instalment terms the prospect had to query.

The most complete money play in the batch. Isolation ran and got a clean answer — 'outside of the investment, do you feel like, yeah, let's just get started?' / 'I could get started outside of the investment, yes'. Then the financial picture, most of it: leftover each month after bills (the $1,000–$2,500 band), cash set aside ($2,000-2,500 liquid), credit score (self-described poor), number of credit cards (four), debt carried (about the the $500–$1,000 band+ band) and available credit ($300-500/month). The instalment option was offered rather than waited for. Two gaps. The last scripted item — crypto, stocks, investments — was skipped even though the prospect handed it over unprompted, mentioning a Roth account and stock investments he had not recently valued; that is where $6,000 most plausibly lives and it was never opened. And the rep did not use the 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place' reframe, which was available and would have fitted, since the prospect had already conceded he wanted to start.

Trigger is real but soft — 'I don't just go around throwing $6,000 everywhere', plus reallocating against his gym membership and home projects. The isolation ran ('outside of splitting it up or how we specifically would pay it, do you feel like you do see yourself doing it?') and the rep used a decent reframe, that a painless price would produce no commitment. Beyond that, nothing: no financial picture at all, no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no investments, and no actual payment plan ever put on the table despite splitting being mentioned twice as theoretically available. The bigger issue is diagnostic — the prospect signalled clearly this was a value and allocation question rather than a capacity one, so the correct response was to build value against alternatives, not to hint at instalments.

Trigger at 00:the under $500 band:07, 'the only thing that's going to stop me is what's going to cost me'. Good moves ran: the isolation, cash available now ('what do you have available now?' — 'nothing, zero'), the leftover-after-bills question ('is it after bills are paid, you seriously have basically zero at the end of the month?'), and a probe on the one credit card with the under 580 band available including whether emergencies actually happen. Missing: the number of cards and total available credit, even though he volunteered 'I have others' with outstanding balances; the 'are you comfortable having an open, honest conversation about exactly where you're at financially' preamble; the 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place' reframe; and above all investments. This man has multiple pensions and a six-figure income and was never asked about savings, retirement accounts or assets. The rep took him at his word that zero meant zero.

Trigger at 00:39:10. Good moves ran: reassurance that this is what the meeting is for, then a clean won't-versus-can't isolation — 'is it absolutely not possible in the years to come, or is it more so like it's just a big chunk?' — which produced the key information, 'It's a big chunk. Like monthly, I can probably pay.' Monthly leftover was then asked and produced the under $500 band, pushed to a possible $200. Savings were asked three times and each time he explained they are ring-fenced family emergency funds. Missing: credit cards, available credit, investments, and any clean 'finances aside, nothing else keeping you from 100%' isolation. The substantive error is what followed. The prospect said he could pay monthly, and the rep never quoted the instalment option on the $6,000 that he had quoted to another prospect the previous day — he jumped straight to the $200 community tier. Even if $1,200 a month was never going to fit a the under $500 band ceiling, the play says explore making it work before changing the product.

Isolation ran twice and ran well — 'out of the finances, you feel like, yes, I want to do this, or not really?' produced 'If I could afford it, yes, I would do this', which is exactly the answer the play is designed to surface. The budget-range question was then asked twice and produced the decisive number: '30, the under $500 band a month'. Nothing else ran — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments, and no payment plan, even though the prospect raised payment plans himself ('payment plans and things like that, the big number is I don't get the $1,000–the $2,500–$5,000 band band a month'). Scored partial rather than miss because once a $30-the under $500 band/month expectation is on the table, working a financial picture toward $6,000 would have been dishonest rather than diligent. The rep read that correctly.

objection_plays.trigger: I need to think about it

instances.detail: The trigger was explicit — 'So I will, let me think, and I can have some time to think about that, right?' — and the play did not run at all. The rep answered 'Let me know what are your thoughts on that' and moved to scheduling. None of the seven moves were attempted: no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal', no 'what makes you feel it can', no 'so what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'when do you make a different decision', no 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now', and no final 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. Granting the delay unchallenged converted a live call into a follow-up.

Soft trigger, and worth recording as soft: 'we are really keen. We just cannot give you an answer right now because we need to check the finances... So we're going to think.' No moves ran. In fairness this is closer to a genuine information-gathering delay than a stall — he needs actual balances from the person who holds them — so the full Objection A treatment would have been misapplied. But the two openers still had a place and were not used: 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to [goal]?' had already been answered yes, and 'so what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started?' would have cost nothing.

Soft trigger and a credit to the rep: the prospect reached for the delay himself — 'I don't know what would be the next step. Like, for me to think about it and give you an answer? Or how does it go?' — and the rep refused to grant it, going straight to the isolation question instead. That is the right instinct and the right sequence. It scores partial rather than hit because none of the Objection A follow-through ran once the isolation was answered: no 'what makes you feel it can', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision', which had obvious purchase on a man with three abandoned attempts behind him.

Triggered twice. On the first ('I'll think on it. I'll let you guys know') the rep ran the single best move in the play and ran it well: 'So what's coming up for you right now that's keeping you from actually moving forward?' It worked — it produced a specific, actionable answer rather than a stall, 'I just don't know, for me personally, if me spending $4,000 on this makes sense.' He then stopped running the play and started building product instead. Not run at any point: 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to [goal]', 'what makes you feel it can', 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision', 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now', and the closing 'are you sure? Nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?' On the second trigger, twenty seconds after the prospect had said the trial would work, the rep granted the delay outright with no play at all.

The delay was real — 'I will come back tomorrow' — and the rep ran the two most useful moves available. He asked for a timeframe ('So what's your time frame on this? When do you want to pick up on this?') and then ran a clean conditional close: 'if I would send you this information today or tomorrow and everything checks out and it's going to be fine, you ready to move forward?' Answer: 'Yeah.' That is good work and it is why a firm next meeting exists rather than a vague follow-up. Partial rather than hit because the rest of the play never ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to [goal]' (already answered, but not reused), no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', and no final 'are you sure? Nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?' once the deposit had been refused.

Trigger present — 'I have to take a moment to think about that' and later 'Is there a possibility that I could get in touch with you after some time?' To his credit the rep did not simply grant it: he asked what would change, asked for a timeframe, and asked what the prospect would put down today, which is three consecutive attempts to convert a delay into a decision. None of the scripted lines ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to [goal]', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here, when do you make a different decision', no closing 'are you sure? Nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?' The outcome is a call booked a full month out with no deposit, no interim commitment and nothing for the prospect to do in between, against his own statement that his finances will not clarify until after October.

'I would have to think about it' at 00:09:59. None of the OA moves ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you to your goal', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started'. The rep instead validated the hesitation and moved to close the call down.

Trigger at 00:20:56, verbatim 'I need to still think about it'. Two moves ran, and ran well: the isolation, 'Outside of the investment, do you feel like, yes, I do want to do this?', and the value test, 'Do you feel like that is worth 6K to you?' The rest of the play was abandoned — no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here, when do you make a different decision', no closing 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. The prospect's answer to the isolation was diagnostic gold — 'It's not how, it's just a matter of deciding if I should' — which says the blocker is conviction, not money, and the rep responded by discounting.

'I really got to think about it now' at 00:57:31, plus 'I think I need to sleep over on this one'. The rep isolated and secured a next call, which is a legitimate handling, but none of the OA moves proper ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you to your goal', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. Booking tomorrow at 5pm is worth more than a botched OA here, so this is a defensible partial rather than a failure.

'I would like to sit down for a day or two and budget everything' at 00:34:51. Several moves ran in substance: the direct feasibility test ('do you feel like $6,000 at the moment is feasible for you?' — answered 'Yeah, I can do that'), the challenge ('is that just a no right now because you really want to look at it, or is it just that uncertainty?'), and a strong pattern-interrupt on what happens after the call ends. Missing the sharpest moves — 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here, when do you make a different decision', and 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now'. That last one was gift-wrapped: the prospect had just quoted Rocky, 'there is no tomorrow', unprompted. The rep echoed the quote twice but never turned it into the decision. Instead he substituted the deposit device.

The best OA handling in the batch, though still incomplete. Ran: the fit-versus-money isolation ('is this a fit for me, or is that more because of the money aspect?'), the competing-options question ('what other options are you thinking about?'), a strong attack on the open-ended timeline ('if you give yourself another month, why not give yourself another two, another three? Why not actually make that decision?'), and the residual-objection check ('would there still be an objection that's holding you back from making a decision?'). It produced a real commitment to a couple of weeks. Missing: 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal', 'what makes you feel it can', 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', and above all 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now' — which was sitting there fully loaded, since the prospect had just confessed to a lifetime of making excuses for himself in exactly this area.

The prospect said it almost verbatim: 'it might not be the right time for me personally.' That is the exact Objection D trigger, and the script supplies six responses for it — 'things never slow down', 'when does it actually become the right time?', 'the longer you wait the harder this becomes'. The rep ran none of them. He said 'let me go back to the team' and booked tomorrow.

Trigger present in substance and at length — the mountain-bike analogy is a textbook not-the-right-time: 'I would first go and buy a small, used bicycle... and then after a year, then I'll see if I'm prepared to spend 6k, but not now.' The rep ran the play in reverse. He agreed with it and then volunteered the objection on the prospect's behalf: 'Yeah, yeah, makes sense. Look, maybe it's not the time of the, not the right time in your life for these changes.' None of the six moves ran. The omission that matters most: 'the longer you wait the harder this gets' was the prospect's own thesis, delivered unprompted at 00:07:28 — 'I'm 34. I'm not 24 anymore. And if I don't do it right now, every day that passes from now on, it's harder, not easier, as it was before.' The rep had a written rebuttal in the prospect's own words, thirty-five minutes old, and did not reach for it. In fairness, the disqualification may well have been the correct commercial judgement given zero cash; the play still should have run before conceding.

Triggered by the prospect's own deferral — 'when I get to the financial point that I can do this... once it's paid off, I'll reach back out to y'all.' The rep ran the play's core question, which is the one that matters: 'how do you feel when you said that you're gonna pay that off? Like, what's the timeframe?' The answer was two years for the retirement loan and no defined date for the credit card. None of the pressure moves ran — no 'things never slow down', no 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', no 'the only thing you can control is right now'. Scored partial, and the omission is defensible: the prospect's constraint is arithmetic, not psychology, and applying urgency to it would have been the wrong call. What is worth noting is that the rep had earned the right to use those lines — he had just established, over three attempts, that the joint problems will be worse in two years — and chose not to.

Triggered twice and handled unevenly. The first trigger was the pregnancy window — 'August, September, and October will be difficult months... training will be kept to a minimum, or maybe even severely impaired.' The rep's opening move was the wrong one, waving it away with the accountability pillar ('that's why Trevor is for you there when life gets busy'), and the prospect corrected him: 'I don't believe it's actually busy. I believe it's actually probably not only busy, but tiredness and lack of sleep... sometimes we're two or three days without sleeping well.' His recovery was genuinely good and unscripted: rather than arguing, he restructured the offer to fit the available window — 'we're in almost June. So it's June, July, August, and you have a lot of time till October. We could do the three months.' That is the right instinct and it deserves credit. The second trigger was the deferral request, and there he ran the play's core question well — 'what's going to change between now and sometime in the future?' Not run: 'things never slow down', 'when does it actually become the right time', 'the longer you wait the harder this gets', and 'the only thing you can control is right now'. The last of these had obvious purchase on a man who had just said he does not know what his finances look like after October.

Timing surfaced in substance — 'that's kind of steep right now with my inconsistent working' and the risk of the assignment ending that night. The rep ran the core OD insight, that waiting becomes never: 'when you go off the meeting, it's like, well, maybe it's not the best time right now. And it gets pushed forward. That is what happens a lot.' None of the harder moves ran — nothing on things never slowing down, nothing on the cost of delay compounding, and notably nothing on the one lever that was sitting there: a doctor has given him six months, so the deadline is external and real. 'The longer you wait the harder this gets' had a literal clinical form on this call and went unused.

A clean not-the-right-time with a specific date attached: 'I'll be willing to do the $1,200 a month, but I have to wait until September', because his Social Security increase lands when he turns 70. The rep resisted once — 'we don't want to wait per se until September' — and then solved it structurally with the self-study bridge, which is a legitimate and arguably better answer than the script. But none of the OD moves ran. 'The longer you wait the harder this gets' had an unusually literal form available here: a 69-year-old diabetic with declining annual strength, whose same-age friend was in intensive care that week. That argument was sitting in the transcript in the prospect's own words and was never made.

objection_plays.trigger: I need to talk to my wife

instances.detail: Trigger explicit: 'I just need to check with my girlfriend.' The rep opened correctly with the money-aside isolation — 'money aside, like, do you personally feel that this can get you [there]?' — and it produced the strongest value statement of the call: '100% have someone to coach me... It would be huge, because then I have guidance.' He then made a good unscripted move, asking her to join live: 'Can you get her on a call right now? We can talk right now.' That is the right instinct and it deserves credit. Everything after that stopped. Not run: 'when you talk to her, what obstacles might come up' (which would have surfaced the unknown chemo costs before they became the reason), 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain', and the deposit-plus-full-refund fallback, which is precisely the structure this situation called for. Note one scripted move that should NOT have been run and correctly was not: 'is this genuinely needing her input, or asking permission to bet on yourself' would have been wrong here, because she demonstrably controls the accounts — 'she's the one that takes care of the bills' — and she is the one who sought Primal out in the first place. She is a decision-maker, not a permission gate, and the play does not distinguish the two.

The clearest single coaching miss in this batch. The trigger was explicit at 00:45:06 — 'I have to take a little moment to think about that and involve the wife because we have a lot of projects now for this year' — and the wife was never mentioned again across the remaining twenty-three minutes. Not one move ran: no 'money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you there', no 'when you talk to her, what obstacles might come up', no 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger', no offer to include her on the follow-up, and no deposit-with-refund fallback. What makes it costly is that the rep had already done the hard part in discovery: he knew the wife is a doctor who runs, does CrossFit and trains three to four times a week, and who gets frustrated when she cannot train twice a week. That is a spouse who would plainly endorse the purchase, and the rep had her profile in hand and did not use a word of it. He also never suggested she join the 29 June call, despite the prospect having framed the decision as joint.

The prospect had already consulted his girlfriend and parents and reported their pushback was financial. The rep asked the useful diagnostic — 'were they overall supportive of it, but it was just the financials?' — and got a yes, then dropped it. No 'is there any reason she would not want you stronger and less in pain', no ownership question, no deposit-and-go-talk-to-her fallback.

Clear trigger — 'I do have to discuss it with my wife anyway'. One move ran, and ran twice: the personal-commitment isolation, 'do you personally feel like, yeah, I do want to make it work, and I see myself making it work?' and 'just from the top of your head, do you feel like it is something that would be workable, it just comes down to figuring it out with your wife?'. Everything else was skipped — no 'when you talk to her, what obstacles might come up', no 'is there any reason she would not want you stronger and less in pain', no ownership question, no deposit-and-go-talk-to-her fallback. Worse, the rep twice joked about being made to sleep on the couch, which reinforces the wife's veto rather than reframing it. Note the play would need adapting here: she is a fellow accountant who jointly manages the household bills, so the scripted 'this isn't a joint decision like buying a house' line would have been wrong and possibly damaging.

'Obviously, I have to run it by her as well', plus the wife having pre-framed the spend downward and separately dismissing his gluten intolerance as psychosomatic. No OB move ran. It was arguably moot by the time it surfaced, since the price gap had already ended the call, but the wife was an active negative influence throughout and was never engaged with — including earlier, when she was raised as doubting his dietary self-knowledge.

Fear of harm was present — 'they're not sure if me swinging around is the best idea.' The rep used a partial-value reframe and a good path-to-yes question ('what would be the route to getting you back to swinging stuff around?'), but ran none of the scripted OE moves: no certainty question, no bridge, no plane, no burned-before.

Ran twice, once excellently and once wrongly. The good run was pre-emptive, during Phase 4: the rep inoculated against future resistance with a proper fear frame — 'even when someone really wants to change, when it starts becoming real, there's another part of them that can show up... there is some level of internal resistance. We as humans, we are masters of self-sabotage' — and tested it with the snooze-button question. That is Objection E used before the trigger, which is the strongest possible way to use it. The bad run came at 00:37:29, when the verification demand landed and the rep reached for the same tool: 'isn't that fear creeping in?' It was a misdiagnosis and the prospect corrected it immediately and reasonably — 'I make deals every day. So I'm pretty good to that in my own way... If I don't run a check, I will never do it. Because in these four years, I learned many things about how and why and why not.' When asked directly whether he was looking for a reason not to do it, he answered 'I'm looking for a reason to do it.' Applying a fear play to a competent buyer performing ordinary vendor diligence reads as pressure, and it is the first move in the sequence that ended with 'red flag'.

Run pre-emptively and to full effect, before the price, as inoculation rather than rebuttal. The rep pre-framed resistance — 'with anything that we change in life, there is always some level of resistance. We are masters of self-sabotage. Our brains are just basically wired to keep us safe and comfortable' — then asked for the accountability mandate and, when the answer was hedged ('I want to say yes'), pursued it: 'What makes you not saying that?' / 'Myself. Knowing myself.' He then externalised the doubt with the devil-and-angel exercise and got the self-sabotaging script quoted verbatim: 'just another one of these. Let's see how long this one lasts.' He had the prospect identify which voice the future version of himself needs to listen to, commit to it, and say why it was different this time — producing 'tired of feeling, tired of feeling' and 'having somebody that's keeping me accountable is a huge step in the right direction.' That is Objection E used before the objection exists, which is the strongest possible application, and it is the single best-run sequence in this batch.

A genuine fear-and-doubt trigger, though about capability rather than the offer: 'it's hard for me to believe that I can do this, or grab a kettlebell with the pain that I feel when I do these exercises.' The rep answered it twice and effectively, in substance if not to script — Trevor's own history of shoulder and back injuries, then progressive loading ('we're not going to start with super heavy weights, first of all because of your shoulder'), reinforced with a poker analogy about starting at five-dollar stakes. That is the scripted BRIDGE move — not asking him to see the whole other side, just take the first step — arriving in the prospect's own language. None of the other OE moves ran (certainty, pleasure versus pain, the plane, burned before), and none were needed. The prospect resolved it himself: 'that's why I applied because he said he used to suffer from it.'
