items.evidence: Misread the filming commitment as frequency rather than duration — 'You said five to 10 times a week?' Rep corrected to 'five to 10 minutes per week'. Prospect repeated it back twice more before it landed. Separately asked mobility cadence: 'How long would that be? And how often is that?'
Rep gave a compressed 'simple pitch' after the price objection rather than the three-pillar structure.
'No, I don't think so' when asked for questions. Had already watched her partner run the program for weeks.
'Yes.' No questions when invited twice.
Physio ruled out the core movement library — swings, snatches, cleans, Turkish get-ups, overhead presses, push press, windmills, high pulls. 'That's the stuff I kind of wanted to be doing more of.'

Delivered first and tied to his own sports — 'you're not just building strength, you're building conditioning and mobility at the same time, and it doesn't require hours of training. It's 30, 40 minutes, three, four times a week', then 'in your specific case, that will definitely help you also in endurance racing, but... you mentioned surfing, right?' Andy did not merely accept it, he ran with it and supplied his own supporting case: 'that's the other thing I liked about kettlebells is that they combine both the metabolic... I've worn my watch and I'm up to 150, 160... it's interval training, right?' and then connected it to surfing himself — 'that's the other time I felt that, trying to paddle out to the outside in big waves. It's constant, it's just brutal.' Caveat for the coach: the rep's mobility promise was generic ('wherever you have weak points, he will focus on that') and never touched the two hip replacements, which is the one place a specific answer would have landed.

Delivered first and tailored well to the medical context — the rep led with stiffness rather than strength ('what we're going to be focusing on is your mobility... you have those back stiffness, hips are stiff'), sized it against his fatigue ('you're coming back from radiotherapy, you're a little bit tired, you need to rest, but all you need is like 30 to 40 minutes, three to four times a week'), and promised bespoke mobility work for his weak points. He closed the pillar with a proper check: 'Does this sound like an approach that you've been looking for?' Bruno answered 'Yeah, 100%, yeah' and nothing further. Scored accepted rather than enthusiastic because the agreement was emphatic but bare — no elaboration, no question, no tie back to his own goal. The unaddressed gap: the pillar never touched whether ballistic loaded work is appropriate for someone eight weeks post-craniotomy and mid-radiotherapy, which is the one thing that would have made this pillar specific to him.

The rep led with the joints-versus-muscle argument for a beginner — 'if you haven't been working out, your joints and everything, they're gonna collapse at some point, because muscles are growing faster than joints can adapt' — and the prospect interrupted to agree and then extended the argument himself: 'Yeah, exactly that is the thing that I liked, and the reason why I'm here... the thing I saw in that video was like, it's not only, it's like the mixture of sport and workout. Like, it includes movement... it's something that attacks both angles, not only muscle building, but also flexibility.' He also volunteered his prior preference for calisthenics over gyms as a reason this fits. Unambiguously enthusiastic: he tied the pillar to his own goal without being asked, and the sit-to-stand longevity point landed on top of the father-versus-father-in-law thread he had raised earlier.

The recording ends at 00:18:24, inside the consequence frame and before the three-step presentation began. No pillar was delivered in the recorded portion. Worth noting for whoever re-pulls the file: the rep did use one fragment of the training-mobility argument early, during discovery rather than as a pillar — 'the muscles grow faster than your joints can adapt to it', offered in response to the prospect's steroid history — and the prospect agreed with it.

Delivered first and correctly prioritised to what the prospect had just named — 'for you, probably the mobility is going to be the main thing that we're going to start from because that's the foundation for all the movements' — with a decent tie to his sport: 'whenever an idea pops up to your head, hey, let's do a high rocks tomorrow in some distance, you're going to be ready.' The response was a flat 'Yeah' and, at the check, 'Makes sense? Yeah.' Accepted rather than enthusiastic: no elaboration, no question, nothing volunteered. The tailoring promise stayed generic ('any stiffness that you have, could have, and potentially like in hips, shoulders, whatever') and never named the two things the rep had just spent five minutes uncovering — four labral tears held together by stem cell injections and a rodded right leg with eight screws. Specific would have landed; generic did not.

Delivered with genuine specificity for once — the rep tied it directly to the prospect's own pathology rather than describing it generically: 'in your particular case, mobility is going to be the foundation of the whole training, because of the tight hips, because of the knee injuries, and the disc', and 'first month is going to be basically learning the basics of the movements, and also doing a lot of mobility work, for you to be more susceptible for more weights.' The prospect did not just accept it, he took it over and co-diagnosed: 'this will be the challenge. I know where is my problem. Not so much my knee, I think my hip, but it's like locked.' The rep met him — 'Believe me, everything comes from hips. This is the power of the whole body, core and hips' — and the prospect closed the loop, 'Yeah, so we're going to take care of that.' He then volunteered the Greece story unprompted when the rep mentioned travel, which is a prospect actively mapping the pillar onto his own failure history. Enthusiastic on both tests: volunteered reaction and tied to his own goal.

The most specifically targeted pillar delivery in the batch — the rep named the prospect's own pathology back to him before making any claim: 'remember when you said that you had the elbow surgery, the EDS, the shoulder dislocation, tightness with your hip flexors, which also is connected to lower back pain, knee pain, everything is connected, and that's why kettlebell workouts are way different, because in every session you work as a unit.' He then tied the benefit to the prospect's actual life rather than a generic outcome: 'when you get stronger, you're going to be showing up to work better. You can hold up the frame on the door and not being injured after that.' Reaction was minimal — 'Yes, sir' and 'Right' — hence accepted rather than enthusiastic. Recorded alongside it, because it matters more than the reaction: the pillar was presented as the remedy for symptoms caused by a genetic connective tissue disorder, and no one asked whether the prospect's chiropractor or physical therapist would sanction loaded ballistic work for hypermobility.

The most engaged pillar reaction in the batch. The rep opened it correctly for this prospect — mobility as the foundation that lets him add load to his existing calisthenics, 'if you are mobile, you're getting stronger, your joints are getting more adapted to the more weight that you can actually push, or even in calisthenics, get more weight on the dips' — and then made the key promise, that kettlebell and calisthenics days 'complement each other naturally. So you don't have to replace anything that you've built.' The prospect took the pillar over: he described in full detail the 30-minute EMOM he had done that same day (five snatches per arm, fifteen push-ups, five thrusters per side, five pull-ups) and what it exposed — 'push-ups and pull-ups are easy. But thrusters, I'm not actually too used to using the core as the thruster needs to be used... I was absolutely torched when I finished it, but it was good.' He also volunteered the aspiration outright: 'that body, Trevor's body, it's the way I want to be built. It's a decent amount of muscle mass, very low fat, really capable. That kind of body is my goal body.' Unambiguously enthusiastic on both tests.

Rep described the Primal University structure at length — 'full programs... where you learn the whole foundations from how to actually do the exercises to eventually also give you the knowledge on how to actually create your own routines', two months of foundations then a new routine monthly, plus the Thursday weekly sessions beginner to advanced. Prospect responded 'Okay... It's something I would be interested in' with no questions on the mechanics.

He interrupted the presentation with mechanics questions rather than reacting to the value: 'And are there particular times when you guys recommend work?', then 'So you basically just show someone and then they can go off and do it on their own? Like Zoom trainings or anything like that?' The rep answered 'No, it's not going to be like, oh, we're going to jump on every week', and he accepted the delivery model with a flat 'Yeah' to the check. Understood the mechanics, showed no enthusiasm — and the specific thing he probed for, live instruction, is the thing he most wants given form safety is his stated priority one.

Presented in full — 3-4 sessions of 30-45 minutes, full-body, plus a daily 5-15 minute mobility routine slotted into his 12-hour desk day, with the 'if you don't use it, you lose it' frame. Asked 'do you feel like, yes, that's what I'm looking for and I see myself doing that?' he answered 'Yes' immediately, and when the rep pushed 'What makes you be so confident about that?' he escalated it himself into meaning: 'it's time to commit to something bigger than me... the overarching longevity idea is bigger than me' and 'I'm ready to take two or three steps bigger than that.' He tied the pillar to his own goal unprompted, which is the enthusiastic marker.

He interrupted to ask 'Does the workout include stretching or not?', then volunteered the strongest buying statement of the call and tied it directly to why this is worth paying for: 'Mobility is a must for me. This is the reason why, because there's a lot of workouts out there, and there's a lot of information right there right now that you could do for free these days. But between other things, based on motivation and having that professional trainer, mobility is something that you don't find much.' He then pictured himself doing it — 'I probably got to start with a five-pounder' — and the rep normalised that well.

Presented with specific reference to his own body — three to four sessions of 45 minutes, plus a daily 5-15 minute mobility routine 'specific to you, to those knees, the shoulders, the herniated disc that you have at the moment'. Asked the check, he answered 'Yes' and the rep noted 'Love the conviction'. Agreed without questions and without volunteering anything, which is notable given he had just described a 6-out-of-10 pain level in four joints — the pillar aimed directly at his problem and drew only a flat yes.

Presented against his own numbers — the 5-out-of-10 shape rating and the 7-rising-to-10 mobility pain — covering strength, mobility and endurance together, three to four sessions of 30-45 minutes plus a daily 5-10 minute mobility routine, with the joints-in-alignment and 'if you don't use it, you lose it' framing. Asked the check he answered with a single 'Yep.' No questions, no elaboration, and no engagement with the compensation chain he had just described so vividly. For the pillar aimed squarely at his worst problem, that is a flat reaction.

He interrupted the presentation with a direct mechanics question — 'I have a question. Even if I don't do three to four days, what's the other options?' — and then surfaced the real scheduling conflict, that his football officiating season runs Wednesday to Saturday from late August with educational trainings on top. The rep answered adequately (frequency can flex, communicate with Trevor). He engaged again on the mobility component, tying it to his own stake: 'I don't want to lose what I have. I'm not as fast as I was 25 years ago, but I'm able to run with no problems, and that's the key thing. Because if I couldn't run, sit your butt down.' Understood the mechanics and probed them rather than reacting to the value.

Presented as three to four sessions of 30-45 minutes plus daily mobility, with a specific promise aimed at his injury: 'your hip is going to get better, so you're going to be able to squat if you want to do that again.' He answered 'Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah' with no questions. Agreed without probing — though he had already sold himself on the modality before the call, having watched Trevor for two weeks and trained with kettlebells for a week and a half.

Presented against his own body — overhead swings starting light because of the shoulder, whole-body work for the back, and a daily five-to-fifteen-minute mobility routine that could sit between poker hands. His reaction was the most positive in the batch: 'Of course. Yeah. Yes. I know this is the program. Like, I'm 100% sure.' Volunteered, unqualified, and tied straight back to the problem he came with.

Presented as three to four sessions of 30-45 minutes plus a daily five-to-fifteen-minute mobility routine aimed specifically at his balance and tight hamstrings. He confirmed 'Yes' and then asked a precise structural question to check his understanding: 'So you say that the program is approximately 20 to 45 minutes a day. And out of that time, about five to 15 minutes is a mobility type exercise? I just want to make sure I'm understanding the way you're saying it.' Engaged with the mechanics rather than the value. Note his earlier unanswered question — 'I don't know that working with a kettlebell will help with balance, I really don't know' — was never explicitly resolved, only folded into the mobility claim.
Recapped it back to check understanding, then asked 'Are you saying there's no macro, micro, there's no counting calories?'
Same — folded into a one-line summary.
'No, I don't think so.' Already running intermittent fasting alongside her partner.
'Yes.' Agreed to the eating-window change without pushback.
Covered on the prior call; recapped without questions.

The rep pre-conceded the pillar before delivering it — 'second thing is nutrition, but, in your case, actually, nutrition is already good, yeah, it's dialed in, pretty solid' — then gave the three-variable version anyway (what you eat, when you eat, how much; clean food, a 10-to-8-hour eating window, quantity taking care of itself). Andy raised no questions and no objection, which is unsurprising given he already tracks macros at about 130g protein a day and has a sports-science student for a son. Accepted rather than enthusiastic: no positive reaction was volunteered and no tie to his own goal was made. Note the missed opening — Andy said he had just swapped from high-fat/low-carb to higher carb on his 17-year-old son's advice and was unsure, which was a live nutrition question the pillar could have answered and did not.

The rep pre-conceded it — 'you already have it dialed in because you're doing keto. And actually, it's very similar to what Trevor is coaching' — then delivered the standard three-variable structure (what, when, how much; clean whole foods; a 10-to-8-hour eating window). Bruno's response was flat agreement: 'It's good, yeah. It sounds good.' Scored accepted. The reaction is not the interesting part of this row; the content is. The rep then added the standard weekly balance day — 'once a week, you're going to have like a, quote unquote, like a day off... you can have a pizza or something like that, just for mind's sound' — to a man running strict ketosis for eight weeks as part of a cancer protocol, where a pizza breaks the diet outright. Bruno did not object, so nothing corrected it. Also note the live nutrition problem the pillar failed to pick up: 'sometimes I go play and I haven't ate enough. So I go and I feel like I need a little bit of a boost of energy' — a real peri-workout fuelling question on keto, raised in discovery and never answered.

Pre-conceded as with every other call in this batch — 'nutrition for you is, from what I'm hearing, already [good]... Trevor probably would mainly fine-tune it.' The standard three variables were delivered (what, when, how much; whole foods; a 10-to-8-hour window) with one sensible personalisation: 'For you, probably it's going to be fine-tuned to your specific needs, because as you said, it's difficult for you to gain muscle. So you can probably eat more and you don't have to keep this strict window.' The prospect gave no reaction at all. Scored accepted rather than clarifying because he asked nothing — which is itself notable, since he had walked in with an active nutrition problem he had self-diagnosed: a hard-gainer on a mostly vegetarian diet who believes he must 'double my protein intake', has just started whey, and has just bought creatine. The pillar as scripted is built around not overeating; this prospect's entire problem is the opposite, and the rep's adjustment was a single sentence.

Not reached before the recording stopped. The rep had gathered the nutrition baseline thoroughly (current diet, the two-week restriction on bread, sugar, sodas and fast food, and the favourite-food probe that produced 'if anything is sweet, it's my favorite food') but had not begun the pillar.

Pre-conceded as in every other call in this batch — 'It sounds like you have dialed in' — then the standard three variables with the weekly free day. One genuinely responsive touch: the rep tied it back to the travel problem he had surfaced, 'with a plan that he will prepare you, it will be probably easier for you to sustain it when you're traveling. Of course, you can have a dessert.' That is the pillar doing its job against a disclosed pain, and the prospect had just admitted 'one bite turns into 20' on the road. It still drew only 'Okay.' No questions, no pushback, no engagement — accepted. Worth noting the rapport detour immediately before it, where the rep spent about a minute on an Alex Hormozi 'never skip dessert' reference that the prospect did not recognise and that produced nothing.

The most engaged nutrition reaction anywhere in this batch, and it ran in an unusual direction — the prospect pushed back toward more restriction, not less. Offered the standard weekly free day, he declined it: 'I think I will keep myself away from that for a while. Then when I see results, then I can cheat a little bit. Until then, I don't want to cheat, to be honest.' The rep handled that well and coached him off it — 'it's easy to go, okay, I'm going 100% in, and then you will fall off because it's very difficult to be 100%. It's damaging mentally' — which is exactly right for a man whose documented pattern is all-or-nothing collapse. The prospect then volunteered a self-observation that had not come up on the first call: cutting bread had changed his mood, 'I was like a more anxious and more nervous, getting upset', which the rep connected to carbohydrate crashes. The pillar was also personalised to his life rather than recited: 'Trevor is going to build a nutrition approach around your schedule and your lifestyle... whenever you're going to be on a business meeting or a dinner, you're going to know what to pick and how to eat.'

Delivered with good personalisation on one axis and a blind spot on another. The rep addressed the sweet tooth directly and warmly ('Mr. Sweet Tooth'), pre-empted the objection that dieting is punishing ('it's not about making your life harder... no extreme dieting, no obsessive tracking, no weighing on a scale'), gave the standard three variables, and adapted it to a long working day: 'if you have longer days that you need to eat out or whatever, you're going to know what to do.' The prospect said 'Sounds good' and nothing more. The blind spot is the constraint he had already disclosed thirty-two minutes earlier: 'At the moment, money's a little tight, so there is more carbs than I should be, just because it's cheaper.' A prescription of whole foods, eggs, meat, chicken, vegetables and fruit is more expensive than what he currently eats, and the cost of it was never mentioned. For this prospect the nutrition pillar has a price attached that the offer never acknowledges.

Pre-conceded as usual — 'from what I understood, you basically have it almost dialed in' — but this time the pillar hit an existing conviction rather than dead air. When the rep mentioned the eating window, the prospect ran with it unprompted and at length: 'I can't stress enough fasting because I think it's something so incredible. In the day that I'm fasting, I don't have low energy. I work more. The mind works very clearly. The mind is sharp. I can read like 10 articles and absorb all of them.' He had already volunteered that Trevor's fasting protocol, not just the kettlebells, was what drew him to the channel, and that he fasts 24 to 36 hours every one to two weeks and treats it as 'a cleansing day, a spiritual thing.' The pillar required no selling because the prospect was already practising a stricter version of it, which is worth noting for the rollup: this is alignment, not persuasion.
Mentioned only in passing as part of the same package — 'and then on top of that, also with the nutrition aspect'. No detail delivered, no reaction from the prospect either way.

He asked for the nutrition approach before the rep ever presented it — 'in terms of nutrition, could you maybe talk to me about how you guys typically do it? Because I'm not sure what to expect' — which is the strongest curiosity signal on the call. The rep gave the no-calorie-counting, no-chicken-and-rice, protocol-you-can-follow-forever answer. On the second pass the rep checked whether he was still vegetarian and proposed bumping protein above 100 grams; he answered 'Okay' with no follow-up and no objection.

Presented as small tweaks rather than an overhaul — 'It's not like you're eating garbage at the moment', the what/when/how-much frame, whole foods, two or three meals a day, sustainable rather than chicken and rice forever, and explicitly addressed his complaint about volume: 'when we're going to gain some, we can switch up the foods, make it more easy to also hit a little bit higher of calories instead of really needing to constantly be eating to get there.' He raised no questions and no pushback. The direct check 'do you feel like, yeah, that is something I see myself doing?' falls in a diarization-scrambled block, but nothing in the following minutes shows resistance.

Presented as the what/when/how-much frame, cutting the sodas, whole foods, no chicken-and-rice, producing a small deficit while protein stays high so muscle is preserved. He had already conceded the sugar problem earlier and agreed to change it ('I tried. I used to do it every day. Now I'm only on weekends'). Response to the pillar check was a short affirmative with no questions and no pushback.

Framed around his actual constraint, eating on the road across rotating shifts — the what/when/how-much model, whole foods, no calorie counting, no chicken and rice. He responded with a commitment rather than a question: 'Yeah, I can stick to a protocol. I can actually work around that. I can make that work.' He had already diagnosed his own nutrition problem earlier (carbs, sandwiches, processed meats, hotels without kitchens), so the pillar was landing on ground he had prepared himself.

Aimed correctly at his stated worst area — he had already rated his nutrition 'Terrible' — using the when/what/how-much frame, whole foods, no calorie counting, no chicken and rice, and specifically addressing the client-dinner problem: 'a lot of the people that Trevor works with travel a lot for work... if they're able to figure out how to do the workouts even when they're traveling, why wouldn't you be able to?' He answered with a commitment rather than a question: 'I also want to commit to that. Absolutely.' Understood and agreed, no probing.

Presented as the when/what/how-much frame, whole foods, minimal processed, no chicken and rice, plus an eating window, with the rep noting he does not cook much and offering to keep it simple. He agreed — 'Yeah, it could work for me, yes' — and then added his own framing: 'in reduction of caloric intake, that's important. So I don't have as many calories now that I may have eaten when I was 20, 30 years ago.' Agreed without questions. Critically, neither party connected any of this to his diabetes, which he had disclosed twice.

Framed as small tweaks rather than change, and correctly so — he had already cut from three or four meals to two and skips breakfast. The rep tied it to Trevor's own intermittent fasting and confirmed the occasional brownie is fine. Response was 'Yeah, 100%.' No questions. Notably he had earlier connected food directly to his ADHD brain fog — 'if I eat bad, I'm going to be all foggy' — and that thread was not picked up when the nutrition pillar was delivered.

He co-built this pillar rather than receiving it. Told the when/what/how-much frame he immediately matched it to his own practice — 'I fast, I eat between one and two, and then between eight and nine at night. So that's my eight hour window' — and then went further than the rep, volunteering 'what I want to do is I want to eat one ingredient foods' and reasoning it out with the rice-versus-potato example. He also framed keto as a temporary detox before transitioning to whole foods, which is exactly the destination the rep was describing. The longest and most engaged nutrition exchange in the batch.

The most substantive nutrition exchange in the batch and the only place the prospect visibly engaged with content rather than concept. He volunteered his gluten intolerance and its evidential basis, then challenged the low-carb framing directly — 'I remember I was trying to eat more fruit and somebody was saying, oh no, those are full of carbs... well, they're healthy carbs, aren't they?' — and then connected the eating-window explanation to his own reading: 'I'm really been reading a lot about intermittent fasting... I try not to eat before 10am or after 6pm. Is that what you're talking about?' The rep answered all three well, and the gluten point landed as a genuine match. This pillar was working.
'So, sorry, so accountability is your, that's the third pillar you're saying, right?' then recapped the components back.
Same. Only 24/7 support was named, in passing.
Raised the pregnancy plan as a conflict — 'I realized that that is going to affect the program.' Resolved by the pause provision.
'Good, good.' Framed by the rep as lifelong-success rather than accountability.
'Is there you have to log your workouts or something like that? Is that the process?'

Fully delivered: direct access to Trevor including his phone number, an instruction to over-communicate, a bespoke written plan off a one-to-one call, weekly check-ins covering sleep and stress, video form review until movements are locked in, and everything organised in TrueCoach. Andy's reaction was neutral-positive and immediately practical — he redirected to portability rather than to the coaching relationship: 'having the skills to have a few kettlebells of the right weights and some routines that basically I can take my training on the road... and that's the biggest thing for me.' When the rep asked directly, the answer was flat: 'now I don't have any questions. That sounds pretty straightforward.' Scored accepted, not enthusiastic: for a prospect whose stated gap is knowing what weight to use, the video form-check and progression element was the strongest card in the deck and it drew no reaction, suggesting it was not landed against his specific problem.

The rep opened it on the prospect's own ground — 'you're a coach, so you probably understand how coaching important is' — and framed it against the treatment ahead: 'you're probably going to be going through difficult times, too, because of the treatment. But you have Trevor in your corner.' Delivered direct WhatsApp access, an instruction to over-communicate, and program adjustment when sleep or stress goes off. Bruno's in-pillar response was minimal ('Make sense? Yes'), but he volunteered the enthusiasm later, unprompted, when the money-aside question was put to him: '100% have someone to coach me, especially fitness-wise, which is gonna be something really important to me right now... It would be huge, because then I have guidance. I mean, well, work as a coach, so I know how easy... Having someone next to you to guide you through the movements and what I'm doing right, what I'm doing wrong, and have the training set up and everything, it makes it way easier. Way easier.' That is a positive reaction tied directly to his own situation and his own professional knowledge, which is the enthusiastic bar. Accountability is unmistakably the pillar that sold this prospect.

The rep positioned it correctly as the pillar that matters for this specific prospect — 'third part, I think for you, it's going to be crucial. Because you've been trying to start that and you gave up a few times' — and closed with 'when work gets crazy, and it probably will, or motivation dips, you don't fall off like before.' Immediate agreement: 'I agree.' The enthusiasm arrived properly later, unprompted, in the middle of the price objection, when he volunteered his own vivid case for it: 'I work out, I do a push-up, and I'm thinking, like, damn, I have no idea if I did this push-up the right way or not... and if there was somebody standing right next to me telling me like, hey, no, those legs aren't straight, I'd be correcting them, but I don't have it — and I don't have the money to pay it, so so be it.' He also endorsed the differentiation directly: 'Definitely. I definitely agree. And in programming everything.' This is the central finding of the call: full, articulate, volunteered agreement on the value of the accountability pillar, and zero willingness to pay for it. The pillar was not the problem.

Not delivered as a pillar. The rep did make an unstructured accountability argument at 00:16:14 in response to the prospect's self-reliance objection — 'He can coach you, he can keep you accountable, but you have to show up every day' — but this was a rebuttal during discovery, not the presented pillar, and the prospect neither endorsed nor pushed back on it; he changed the subject to his blood pressure.

The decisive row in this file. The rep opened the pillar by inviting the prospect to reject it: 'And the third part, you said that you don't need hand-holding. Is that correct?' The prospect obliged — 'No, I mean, like, I'm sure a lot of other clients, like, you got to get them to actually work out every day. I'm going to be doing that, so.' The rep then delivered the pillar anyway (direct number, over-communication, video form review, weekly check-ins, roughly a month to learn the movements) against a prospect who had just been handed permission to dismiss it. He objected in substance twice more once price was on the table: 'after month one, like you mentioned, like, I don't really need, I don't see myself needing the additional check-ins', and 'I'd rather just pay for a program is really where my head's at, more so than paying for an ongoing handholding.' He had actually pre-flagged it in discovery too, at 00:07:55 — 'for me, it's probably less of a one-on-one coaching... and more so, like, just getting a program, working on it, like, using you guys as a resource when I need to.' The objection was visible eight minutes before the pillar was delivered and the pillar was framed to concede it rather than to answer it.

Delivered against his own failure history rather than in the abstract — 'You told me that you tried many times before and didn't do it fully. And that's why the coaching layer matters, because a lot of people can start, but the problem is staying consistent when life gets busy' — closing with 'when work gets crazy, or motivation dips, or life gets in the way, you don't fall off like before.' The response was firm but short: 'No, I should not. I would not. No, I would not. I don't want to', then 'it sounds pretty good for me, yes.' Scored accepted on the pillar itself. The enthusiasm for accountability had already been spent earlier and more powerfully, in Phase 5, where the rep asked for a mandate and got one: 'do I have your permission to hold you accountable to all the things that you said that are important to you?' / 'Yes, you should hold me accountable for that. Because that's what I'm here for.' And in Phase 4: 'Yeah, but I need as well. I think that's why I'm here with you.' Of the three pillars this is the one he had already bought before it was presented.

Well positioned against his documented history — 'you told me that you've tried some things, but you didn't stick to it, with the chiropractor and the exercises that you got from the physiotherapist' — and explicitly tied back to the self-sabotage work done earlier: 'this is going to be very important, because we're going to cover the devil on your shoulder.' The in-pillar reaction was flat, an 'Okay'. Scored accepted on that basis. But this is the pillar the prospect had already bought, twelve minutes before it was presented and in his own words, when asked why this attempt would be different: 'having somebody that's keeping me accountable is a huge step in the right direction.' He had also granted the rep a personal accountability mandate — 'do I have your permission to hold you accountable, to hold you to the fire?' / 'Yeah.' Of the three pillars this is the one that had genuine, volunteered demand behind it, and it is the one he could not pay for.

Well positioned against the one thing this prospect could not solve himself — 'when your second child will appear in this world, you're probably going to have less time and less sleep... there probably may be times that you could fall off. And here's where the accountability comes in.' Delivered direct phone access, over-communication, weekly check-ins and schedule rebuilding around the newborn. The response was polite and brief: 'Okay... That makes sense? Okay. Yeah. A lot.' Scored accepted rather than enthusiastic on the pillar itself, though he endorsed its value explicitly later, while declining on price: 'for Trevor's work and for the accountability, I think actually that is pretty fair.' That is the most useful sentence on the call — the accountability layer was valued at the price asked, and the transaction still failed on currency.

Presented as peer accountability inside the community — 'there's a couple of guys in there that are actually doing that the whole time... they're keeping each other the whole time accountable, so Trevor doesn't even need to keep them accountable', plus form feedback on posted videos. Prospect acknowledged the value of Trevor helping people — 'I liked what he's helping to, he's like helping people' — but did not engage with the accountability mechanism specifically.

Presented as lifelong success — teach a man to fish, six months then independence, filmed workouts with feedback, Trevor's personal number, weekly check-ins, programme adjusted on communication, plus the Thursday live sessions and the one-on-one client group. Asked 'Any questions on the lifelong success part?' he said 'No', and later 'Fantastic. Great.' Agreed without engagement. Given that his actual failure mode over twenty years is inconsistency, this was the pillar that should have been sold hardest and it drew the least reaction.

Delivered as the most important of the three — teach a man to fish over six months, form videos reviewed, Trevor's personal cell, programme switched monthly, log-checking with 'hey, what are you doing, why are you not working out?', Thursday live sessions, and the client community. Asked 'do you feel like you have any questions on that?' he said 'Not at the moment, no, sir.' Understood and agreed, but no volunteered enthusiasm — which is mild counter-signal given he explicitly came looking for structure and outside perspective.

Delivered as the most important pillar and aimed squarely at his stated gap — Trevor plans around his life, personal number, schedules changed when tax season hits, filmed workouts with form feedback, teach-a-man-to-fish. He confirmed understanding rather than excitement: 'so far it's good, so far I understand how it works.' Asked what would be missing he re-listed his own criteria — 'It's usually nutrition, the right instruction, and the right motivation' — and then flagged a positive surprise: 'maybe that Thursday Live, it could probably help also, I wasn't thinking that there was any live.' Given accountability is precisely what he has been missing for six years, this drew less reaction than it should have.

The pillar he bought. He named accountability as his gap before it was presented — 'I know what to do. I just have no accountability' — and when asked what would help most he came back to it unprompted: 'just accountability will be the main... it'll give me the drive'. He then elaborated with his own metaphor, quoting Rocky: 'there is no tomorrow. So today, with accountability, you have that process.' He also pre-enacted the mechanism, imagining Trevor's chasing message: 'oh, I'm going to get a nasty email, text message, or a phone call. Like, what are you doing?' Volunteered, tied to his own goal, and expressed in his own language.

Delivered as the answer to the thing he had named three separate times before it was presented — the push, direction, structure. Teach-a-man-to-fish, six months then independence, personal cell number, video form feedback, programme changes on communication, and the chasing message: 'hey, Omar, what are you doing?' His response was 'No, that's, yeah, definitely. Definitely what I'm looking for.' Confirmed rather than enthused. Notably he then immediately reduced it to something he could plausibly do alone — 'it's pretty simple at that point, right? Like, working on it isn't hard' — which the rep countered well ('it's simple, but it's not easy'), but the seed of the DIY objection is visible right there.

Delivered as the teach-a-man-to-fish pillar with video form feedback, Trevor's number, Thursday lives and chasing messages. His response was agreement laced with a signal worth noting: 'No, no, no. I understand. Like I said, I've been exposed to training, you know, acronyms, so, no big.' Asked whether any part stood out he said 'No, not right now', and then explained he had been through a lot of comparable coach education through USA Track and Field. He accepted the pillar while quietly establishing that he already knows this material — which is the seed of why he ended the call buying a self-study course rather than coaching.

Unambiguously the pillar he bought, and the most emotionally loaded reaction in the batch. Asked which of the three would help most he chose it immediately: 'Probably just holding me accountable... not that I'm lazy, because I love going to the gym. It's just knowing that somebody's better than me is holding me accountable. I gotta make him happy. I want him to see me succeed.' Then he went further, unprompted: 'I'm gonna look at him like he's my dad. I can't make my dad sad. I gotta keep him happy... dad, I'm not gonna fail you, I promise.' He had also framed it earlier through his Army background — a drill sergeant telling him what to do, 'yes, sir, I'll do it'. This is precisely why the community downsell failed: the product he wanted was the person.

The pillar that closed him, because it landed directly on a scar. He had already described being injured by a generic online programme with no feedback — 'how could I know if my form was right or wrong if I'm just following a video? And I got hurt' — so the filmed-workout form review answered a specific, personal failure: 'if I can film myself and send it to Trevor, and then he'll say, hey, when you're squatting, your knee is going forward, you shouldn't do that.' He then pre-committed unprompted: 'my commitment with Trevor is I'll show up every day. No excuses. If it's a five-day program, I'll show up every single day.' And asked what mattered most of the three, he chose this one: 'I just want to feel that there's someone supporting me through this journey.'

Delivered as teach-a-man-to-fish over six months, video form feedback, chasing messages ('hey, what are you doing, Richard?') and progressive loading. He raised no questions about the mechanism at all; his only interjection during it was a different concern — 'I've never been interested in bulky muscles... I don't want to have a pair of guns' — which the rep handled well. Given that he had just spent ten minutes explaining that prescribed, externally imposed exercise kills his motivation, the accountability pillar was arguably the wrong pitch for him and drew no reaction either way.

anchors.raw: I have coaches, have mentors and all that kind of stuff... I've just never done it for fitness
anchors.note: Pays for coaching in business; primed to accept paid coaching.

anchors.raw: I'm actually even more interested in it because of the fact that it costs six grand

unmet_demand.why_unmet: The documented offer is 6 months at $6,000 and 12 months at $9,000, both framed as ongoing coaching. The rep improvised a three-month tier at $4,000 to meet this want, and asserted 'we have like three tiers', but a three-month product does not appear in the offer as documented. He asked when the surgeries were, then disclosed his own need for a replacement and asked the prospect for advice, and when the training-and-mobility pillar was delivered the hips were not mentioned once; the mobility promise stayed generic ('wherever you have weak points, he will focus on that'). unmet_demand.want: Guidance on becoming a kettlebell trainer himself — a side business in his small town. 'I do want to build a coaching business, and so then I want some more guidance there' and 'there'd probably be an opportunity to do training, you know, to become a trainer.'

unmet_demand.want: Help making the fee a legitimate business expense in New Zealand — an invoice, a receipt framing, or a professional-development justification his accountant could accept.

unmet_demand.want: Written payment options he could take to the person who controls the money — 'if you can send me maybe a few options of how can we pay it or if there is payment plan.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep confirmed the company has no productised plans: 'we don't have, like, a set payment plans. Nothing was sent and no numbers were named, so the prospect went into the finance conversation with his girlfriend holding a single undifferentiated figure of $6,000 USD. The capability plainly exists — the rep had already offered to 'maybe split it' — it simply is not packaged, priced or sendable.

unmet_demand.want: Assurance that loaded kettlebell training is medically safe for him — eight weeks post-craniotomy, at session 18 of 33 radiotherapy sessions, with twelve months of chemotherapy to follow.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Neither party raised it. Whether the offer can serve this prospect safely is genuinely unknown to everyone involved, including the rep, and that is the finding.

unmet_demand.want: A nutrition approach that holds his therapeutic ketogenic protocol fixed rather than overlaying the standard structure on it, including the weekly off-day.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The pillar as scripted prescribes a weekly balance day with foods that break ketosis ('you can have a pizza or something like that'). unmet_demand.want: A low-cost way to prove the commitment before committing capital — a cheap first rung between free YouTube content and $6,000. 'I would first go and buy a small, used bicycle... and then after a year, then I'll see if I'm prepared to spend 6k, but not now.'

The rep's entire adjustment was one sentence: 'you can probably eat more and you don't have to keep this strict window.' Whether the programme actually delivers vegetarian-constrained muscle-gain nutrition is genuinely unknown from this call and should be checked with a human rather than assumed either way.

unmet_demand.want: Live form correction for a complete beginner — 'if there was somebody standing right next to me telling me like, hey, no, those legs aren't straight, I'd be correcting them, but I don't have it.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Recorded as served, not as a gap, and included here only because it is the clearest positive signal in the call: the offer does exactly this via video submission and Trevor's feedback loop, the rep explained it, and the prospect agreed it was valuable. It failed on price alone. Logging it so the rollup does not mistake this loss for a product deficiency — the product matched the want and the wallet did not.

unmet_demand.want: Assurance that loaded kettlebell training is safe for his body — a spinal disc compression diagnosed three years ago, a right knee that subluxes ('it might be hopping out'), a hip that will not let him cross one leg, high blood pressure, and 105 kg of bodyweight.

unmet_demand.why_unmet: The prospect is forming a medical expectation about a diagnosed condition, and the offer contains no medical oversight, makes no clinical claims and involves no clinician. Whether the programme is designed to replace, supplement or conflict with his current training was never established, and that ambiguity is part of why he could only see it as 'a program' rather than a system.

unmet_demand.want: Loading that respects two stem-cell-treated shoulders with four labral tears and a right leg containing a metal bar and eight screws.

Same clinical blind spot recorded across this batch.

unmet_demand.want: Verification material about the company and the coach before releasing money — 'information about the company that you are working with, your company, Trevor's', plus independent evidence: 'I think you have also some people who are satisfied or not satisfied with your job... The proof almost certainly exists; it is simply not assembled or sendable, and in its place the rep offered a $100 deposit, which made the trust problem worse.

unmet_demand.want: A reason to choose Primal specifically rather than any competent coach — implied by 'Either with you, either with somebody else.'

He agreed to 'the six K' on a monthly schedule that totals $7,200. Nothing was sent in writing, no schedule was confirmed, and no agreement document was mentioned. The capability exists; the artifact does not.

unmet_demand.want: Confidence that loaded ballistic kettlebell training is safe for a compressed disc, a subluxing knee, a locked hip and two years of hypertension at 105 kg.

unmet_demand.why_unmet: There is no clinical screening step in the process and no mechanism to consult the clinicians already treating him. This is the one call in the batch where the rep did ask whether doctors were involved and whether prescribed exercises were being followed, which makes the omission sharper rather than softer: he had a chiropractor and a physical therapist named on the call and never asked whether either would sanction the training, then presented that training as the fix for exactly those symptoms. Whether the programme helps or harms someone with hypermobility is genuinely unknown to everyone who was on this call, and it should be answered by a human before any similar prospect is sold to.

unmet_demand.want: Something between the free follow-along guide and $6,000 for a prospect with real need, real intent and no money — he proposed the interim path himself and asked to come back when his debts clear.

The rep improvised the only available answer, promising to send further free materials and to stay in touch, which is the right instinct and is not a product. Third occurrence of this gap in this batch, after Jorge Fernández's used-bicycle analogy and Jared L.'s request to buy a programme rather than a relationship — three prospects in four sales calls asking for a rung on the ladder that does not exist, for three entirely different reasons.

unmet_demand.want: A way to train around an extreme schedule and genuine exhaustion — up at 3am, out by 5, physical work until 2.30pm, then a 30 to 50 minute drive home.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Recorded as served rather than as a gap, and included so the rollup does not misread this loss. The rep improvised the closest available answer, restructuring to a three-month tier to fit the June-to-August window, which was genuinely good thinking — but it still required full payment now against a budget that will not clarify until after the birth. A refundable deposit that locks today's price for a start date in November would have fitted this prospect exactly and does not exist.

Whether Trevor actually programmes weighted calisthenics progression alongside kettlebell work, or simply absorbs bodyweight movements into kettlebell complexes, is not established anywhere on this call and should be confirmed with a human before the follow-up.

Nobody established whether Trevor's work can be run alongside a physical-therapy protocol.

unmet_demand.why_unmet: Stated as a specific goal — 'I want to learn all kinds of techniques to be able to work on all different body parts, not just the basic kettlebell movements'. The presentation described full-body workouts and beginner-to-advanced Thursday sessions but never confirmed the curriculum breadth he asked about. Likely served; never explicitly answered.

unmet_demand.why_unmet: He raised the cardiac history twice, unprompted, and got no response either time. The programme has no screening step, no clearance requirement and no stated adaptation for cardiac patients, so the question was never answered and the sale proceeded past it. Whether the offer can serve him safely is genuinely unknown from this transcript.

unmet_demand.why_unmet: He disclosed the herniated disc plainly and the response folded it into the sales pitch — a daily mobility routine 'specific to you, to those knees, the shoulders, the herniated disc... to make sure it's only going to make it better'. Nobody asked whether his doctor has cleared him for resistance training, and he is currently under active medical supervision.

Plausibly served by a coach who plans around your life; never actually evidenced.

unmet_demand.why_unmet: This was his opening statement of what he wants and it was folded into a generic athletic-build benefit, then used once as a closing image. unmet_demand.why_unmet: He disclosed the diabetes twice and it was never acknowledged, so nothing was adapted, qualified or even discussed. unmet_demand.why_unmet: He named this explicitly and at length — 'this is going to be another piece that I can add to my coaching repertoire to show kids how they can develop their strength', tying it to explosive strength and coordination for track and field, and to Olympic lifting alternatives for athletes who cannot do them. unmet_demand.want: Training built around a chronic lumbar injury and active tendinitis in the foot and knee, in a 70-year-old
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The injuries were properly elicited, including their origin and severity, and then folded straight into the sales narrative — a daily mobility routine that will make the back 'stronger again'. unmet_demand.want: Direct one-to-one contact with Trevor at a price near $150-200 a month
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The ladder jumps from a $200/month peer community with no personal access to $6,000 for the one-to-one, with nothing in between. unmet_demand.want: Rehabilitation of a service-connected hip injury that currently prevents him squatting
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The injury was disclosed and lightly probed, then a direct therapeutic claim was made in the presentation — 'your hip is going to get better, so you're going to be able to squat if you want to do that again' — with no severity assessment, no duration question, no knowledge of what the injury actually is, and no awareness of what he is on disability for. He is a veteran with a documented accident injury and no clinician was mentioned by either side.

unmet_demand.want: Training and nutrition that account for ADHD and the brain fog he links to food
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He raised ADHD unprompted, connected it explicitly to diet, and said it is part of why he identifies with Trevor, who has spoken about having it. The rep acknowledged it in one garbled aside and never returned to it — not in the nutrition pillar, not in the accountability pillar, where structure and external prompting are precisely the ADHD-relevant selling points. A missed positioning opportunity rather than a product limitation.

unmet_demand.want: Form correction on the kettlebell movements he is currently self-teaching from video
unmet_demand.why_unmet: This is arguably served — video form review is in both tiers, and the rep confirmed the community tier includes it. It is listed because he named the need clearly and it was never used as the argument against the free substitute he is currently relying on, which is the one place it would have done real work.

unmet_demand.want: Confidence that he can perform overhead kettlebell work with a shoulder that currently cannot go through a full lateral or overhead range without pain
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He raised this as his central doubt — 'it's hard for me to believe that I can grab a kettlebell with the pain that I feel when I do these exercises' — and the answer was reassurance rather than assessment: Trevor has had shoulder injuries too, and we will start light. Nobody established what the shoulder actually is, whether it has been examined, or whether overhead loading is appropriate. The rep also asserted the training would fix it, which is a clinical claim about an undiagnosed restriction.

unmet_demand.want: A resolution to several years of chronic lower back pain, severe enough that he is flying to Dallas in September for chiropractic treatment
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The pain was well quantified in discovery and then folded into the sales narrative — the daily mobility routine 'directly going to help with suppressing the pain with, well, the mobility, because it actually fixes it'. That is a therapeutic claim about a multi-year condition under no assessment, made to a prospect who is simultaneously seeking medical intervention for it. Whether the two approaches conflict was never discussed.

unmet_demand.want: Help with daily smoking, which he identifies as the direct cause of the cravings that break his diet
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He volunteered it plainly — 'if I don't smoke, then I get no cravings at all... if I smoke, I'll get the munchies' — and the rep probed only the frequency, in the context of dietary discipline, then moved on. The nutrition protocol makes no mention of it, and it is the single behavioural lever he himself named as controlling his adherence.

unmet_demand.want: A programme he actively enjoys, since he abandons regimes that work but are not enjoyable
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He said it twice, including about carnivore — 'I feel great, but I'm not enjoying the process of feeling great' — and 'during this whole process with Trevor, I want to enjoy the process'. The rep addressed the nutrition half convincingly (whole foods, not chicken and rice, sustainable) but never addressed whether the training itself would be enjoyable. Probably served, since he chose kettlebells partly out of curiosity, but it is his documented failure mode and nobody closed it off.

unmet_demand.want: Guided, personalised coaching at anywhere near $30-100 a month
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Nothing in the range exists. The rep gestured at a community product with standard programmes but never named its price, and the reduced $3,000 tier he did mention was also refused. Even the $200/month self-study tier offered to other prospects in this batch is five times his stated ceiling. This is a genuine hole in the product ladder relative to what an inbound application can attract.

unmet_demand.want: A programme he finds intrinsically enjoyable rather than one that works by external accountability

The offer's central mechanism is accountability, check-ins and chasing messages, which is closer to the thing that failed him than to the thing that works. The programme may well suit him; nothing on the call demonstrated it.
