His problem is the inverse, and it is complicated by a household that is meat-free. The rep's entire adjustment was one sentence: 'you can probably eat more and you don't have to keep this strict window.' Whether the programme actually delivers vegetarian-constrained muscle-gain nutrition is genuinely unknown from this call and should be checked with a human rather than assumed either way.

unvalidated.want: Assurance that loaded kettlebell training is safe for his body — a spinal disc compression diagnosed three years ago, a right knee that subluxes ('it might be hopping out'), a hip that will not let him cross one leg, high blood pressure, and 105 kg of bodyweight.
unvalidated.why_unmet: No clinical clearance question exists anywhere in the process and none was asked in the recorded portion. The evidence that this matters is already on the table: two weeks of unsupervised kettlebell work has produced new back pain in a man with a known disc problem. Whether Trevor's programme can safely load this body, and whether it should be doing so before a physio or a doctor has looked at the knee and the disc, is unknown to everyone on the call.

unvalidated.want: Resolution of his high blood pressure through training and diet rather than medication — he stated the expectation directly: 'if I start to improve my health, and my body health, and how I eat, and what I eat, and when I eat, I think all this, it will go away by himself.'
unvalidated.why_unmet: The prospect is forming a medical expectation about a diagnosed condition, and the offer contains no medical oversight, makes no clinical claims and involves no clinician. The rep did not correct, qualify or engage the expectation — he had just begun the consequence frame when the recording stopped. This needs a human to decide policy: a prospect who buys expecting his hypertension to resolve is a refund and reputation risk regardless of whether the training would in fact help.

unvalidated.want: A short, low-commitment way to test the product before buying the full engagement — 'if there's a 30-day hybrid, I'd be open to that for sure.'
unvalidated.why_unmet: The rep invented one on the call, at $1,500 for 30 days, branded 'love it or leave it', with no refund mechanics, no written terms and no evidence of authorisation. The internal onboarding call recorded the previous day establishes that non-standard structures are 'not generally an option that we offer'. So the want was met by something that may not exist. Flagged for a human: either a 30-day trial is a real product and should be priced and documented, or a prospect has been quoted one that cannot be honoured.

unvalidated.want: Conditioning that complements Hyrox racing — he competes recreationally, intends to do more, and trains twice a day already.
unvalidated.why_unmet: The rep touched it once in passing ('let's do a high rocks tomorrow... you're going to be ready') and never addressed the actual question, which is how kettlebell work slots alongside an existing twice-daily programme without simply adding volume to a man with four repaired labra. Whether the programme is designed to replace, supplement or conflict with his current training was never established, and that ambiguity is part of why he could only see it as 'a program' rather than a system.

unvalidated.want: Loading that respects two stem-cell-treated shoulders with four labral tears and a right leg containing a metal bar and eight screws.
unvalidated.why_unmet: The rep drew the injuries out well and then never mentioned them again. The training and mobility pillar promised generic attention to 'any stiffness that you have, could have', with no reference to the specific structures involved and no question about clearance or load limits — despite the prospect volunteering that pain returns 'when I'm doing like a ton of volume and a ton of reps', which is a direct constraint on how a kettlebell programme should be written for him. Same clinical blind spot recorded across this batch.

unvalidated.want: Confidence that loaded ballistic kettlebell training is safe for a compressed disc, a subluxing knee, a locked hip and two years of hypertension at 105 kg.
unvalidated.why_unmet: Across two sessions and roughly 64 minutes, no clinician was mentioned by either party and no clearance question was asked. The mobility promise is real and well targeted, but it is a training promise, not a clinical one, and the prospect has already produced new back pain training unsupervised. There is no screening step anywhere in the process, so whether the programme can safely load this body remains unknown to everyone involved — including the rep who has now shaken hands on six months of it.

unvalidated.want: Confidence that loaded ballistic kettlebell training is appropriate for Ehlers-Danlos syndrome — a genetic connective tissue disorder producing recurrent joint subluxation, in a prospect who dislocated a shoulder catching a door and whose kneecap subluxes when he walks.
unvalidated.why_unmet: There is no clinical screening step in the process and no mechanism to consult the clinicians already treating him. This is the one call in the batch where the rep did ask whether doctors were involved and whether prescribed exercises were being followed, which makes the omission sharper rather than softer: he had a chiropractor and a physical therapist named on the call and never asked whether either would sanction the training, then presented that training as the fix for exactly those symptoms. Whether the programme helps or harms someone with hypermobility is genuinely unknown to everyone who was on this call, and it should be answered by a human before any similar prospect is sold to.

unvalidated.want: Programming that preserves and progresses weighted calisthenics alongside kettlebells — his stated primary condition, raised twice: 'that would be my primary will is to combine those things. To not lose the gains in strength in calisthenics.'
unvalidated.why_unmet: Recorded as answered-but-unverified rather than as a failure. The rep's response was good and the objection resolved, but the answer was a promise ('they complement each other naturally', 'this is tailored to your needs, whatever you will discuss with Trevor, he will build a program around that') rather than a specification, and the detail was deferred entirely to the onboarding call. Whether Trevor actually programmes weighted calisthenics progression alongside kettlebell work, or simply absorbs bodyweight movements into kettlebell complexes, is not established anywhere on this call and should be confirmed with a human before the follow-up.

unvalidated.want: Confirmation that intense kettlebell conditioning is safe given a history of AFib, hereditary heart disease and managed blood pressure — and how the programme handles that
unvalidated.why_unmet: He raised the cardiac history twice, unprompted, and got no response either time. The programme has no screening step, no clearance requirement and no stated adaptation for cardiac patients, so the question was never answered and the sale proceeded past it. Whether the offer can serve him safely is genuinely unknown from this transcript.

unvalidated.want: To add muscle while staying near 1,600-1,800 calories, because he dislikes the volume of eating that a real surplus requires
unvalidated.why_unmet: The rep's answer was to switch to more calorie-dense foods, which addresses the mechanics but not the arithmetic — he estimated he needs 2,200+ to gain, and the programme did not commit to a way around that. It is plausible the coaching can solve it with food selection, but nobody established it on the call.

unvalidated.want: Confirmation that kettlebell training can be programmed around a chronic lower back that rules out deadlifts
unvalidated.why_unmet: He named the constraint clearly and it was never addressed. The presentation instead promised a mobility routine tailored to his lower back, without anyone establishing whether the loaded hip-hinge movements at the core of kettlebell work are appropriate. Probably solvable by a competent coach, but unverified on the call and a genuine risk for a 56-year-old with a twenty-year back history.

unvalidated.want: A path back to recreational boxing once strength and agility return
unvalidated.why_unmet: He named it as a real goal and deferred it himself for fear of losing muscle mass at his age. Nobody said whether the programme supports or conflicts with that, so the motivational hook went unused and the question is unanswered.

unvalidated.want: Confirmation that loaded kettlebell training is safe with a herniated disc
unvalidated.why_unmet: He disclosed the herniated disc plainly and the response folded it into the sales pitch — a daily mobility routine 'specific to you, to those knees, the shoulders, the herniated disc... to make sure it's only going to make it better'. That is a therapeutic claim about a spinal condition, made without any clinical qualification, in a programme built on loaded hip hinges. Nobody asked whether his doctor has cleared him for resistance training, and he is currently under active medical supervision.

unvalidated.want: Programming that works around an elbow at 8-9 out of 10 on pushing and pulling movements
unvalidated.why_unmet: He described modifying or abandoning exercises mid-session because of this elbow, and it was never addressed. Kettlebell work is pressing and pulling heavy. Video form review plausibly catches it in practice, but nobody confirmed the programme can be built around a joint that currently limits him, and the mobility pillar was pitched as making everything better without qualification.

unvalidated.want: A training and nutrition protocol that is safe and appropriate for a 25-year diabetic with suspected kidney involvement
unvalidated.why_unmet: He disclosed the diabetes twice and it was never acknowledged, so nothing was adapted, qualified or even discussed. The nutrition pillar as sold — eating windows, a calorie deficit, 'your body's just going to tell you I'm full' — interacts directly with blood glucose management and medication timing, and no clinician was mentioned on either side. Whether the programme can serve him safely is genuinely unknown from this transcript, and it is the single most important open question in this batch.

unvalidated.want: Kettlebell instruction he can carry into his own coaching and teach to young athletes
unvalidated.why_unmet: He named this explicitly and at length — 'this is going to be another piece that I can add to my coaching repertoire to show kids how they can develop their strength', tying it to explosive strength and coordination for track and field, and to Olympic lifting alternatives for athletes who cannot do them. The rep gestured at it once ('you can also pass it on to other people') but nobody established whether the material is intended or permitted to be taught onward, or whether coach-facing content exists. This is arguably a different product than the one being sold.

unvalidated.want: Training built around a chronic lumbar injury and active tendinitis in the foot and knee, in a 70-year-old
unvalidated.why_unmet: The injuries were properly elicited, including their origin and severity, and then folded straight into the sales narrative — a daily mobility routine that will make the back 'stronger again'. That is a therapeutic claim made about an injury that currently requires chiropractic care, in a movement system built on loaded hip hinges, with no qualification and no clinical input.

unvalidated.want: Rehabilitation of a service-connected hip injury that currently prevents him squatting
unvalidated.why_unmet: The injury was disclosed and lightly probed, then a direct therapeutic claim was made in the presentation — 'your hip is going to get better, so you're going to be able to squat if you want to do that again' — with no severity assessment, no duration question, no knowledge of what the injury actually is, and no awareness of what he is on disability for. He is a veteran with a documented accident injury and no clinician was mentioned by either side.

unvalidated.want: Confidence that he can perform overhead kettlebell work with a shoulder that currently cannot go through a full lateral or overhead range without pain
unvalidated.why_unmet: He raised this as his central doubt — 'it's hard for me to believe that I can grab a kettlebell with the pain that I feel when I do these exercises' — and the answer was reassurance rather than assessment: Trevor has had shoulder injuries too, and we will start light. Nobody established what the shoulder actually is, whether it has been examined, or whether overhead loading is appropriate. The rep also asserted the training would fix it, which is a clinical claim about an undiagnosed restriction.

unvalidated.want: A resolution to several years of chronic lower back pain, severe enough that he is flying to Dallas in September for chiropractic treatment
unvalidated.why_unmet: The pain was well quantified in discovery and then folded into the sales narrative — the daily mobility routine 'directly going to help with suppressing the pain with, well, the mobility, because it actually fixes it'. That is a therapeutic claim about a multi-year condition under no assessment, made to a prospect who is simultaneously seeking medical intervention for it. Whether the two approaches conflict was never discussed.

unvalidated.want: Help with daily smoking, which he identifies as the direct cause of the cravings that break his diet
unvalidated.why_unmet: He volunteered it plainly — 'if I don't smoke, then I get no cravings at all... if I smoke, I'll get the munchies' — and the rep probed only the frequency, in the context of dietary discipline, then moved on. The nutrition protocol makes no mention of it, and it is the single behavioural lever he himself named as controlling his adherence.

unvalidated.want: Confirmation that kettlebell training addresses balance, which is the deficit that made him fall over
unvalidated.why_unmet: He asked outright and flagged his own uncertainty — 'I don't know that working with a kettlebell will help with balance as much as, I really don't, in all honesty, I don't really know' — and never received a direct answer. Balance was later swept into a general claim about the mobility routine. He had fallen and injured himself three weeks earlier, so this was the most concrete problem on the table.

unvalidated.want: Programming safe for a right shoulder with a repaired labrum and rotator cuff
unvalidated.why_unmet: Both surgeries were disclosed in response to a direct question and then never mentioned again, despite kettlebell training being heavily overhead and pressing. He is 67 and dismissed his own history as resolved, which is exactly when a screening step matters. Third instance in this batch of a disclosed musculoskeletal or medical issue that received no follow-up.

guarantees.guarantee: If you don't hit the goals set with Trevor in 6 months, we work with you for free until you do

A 30-day trial invented live on the call and named by the rep: 'Would you be down for, like, 30 days just checking how it works? And if you're satisfied with that, you would move on? If not?' ... 'We call it love it or leave it.' Explained as: 'you get a full month, you check it out, how it's, if it fits your needs or not, and afterwards, you can leave if you don't like it.' No refund mechanics, no terms and no written basis were given.

Stated for the first time in this corpus and attached only to the six-month tier: 'with six months, you have a guarantee that you will definitely gain at least 20, it's pounds, so it's going to be like around plus 10 kilos from the baseline that you start with on weight of kettlebells.' Explicitly not available on the shorter tier: 'with three months, we cannot guarantee that, because it's too short. I think it's too short for every fitness goal.'
Six months, full transformation guarantee; program can be paused for pregnancy or injury

stated.quote: The prospects we deal with are people who are already good in their life, they're successful, they own their own business, or they're a physician, something along those lines, they make good money, but health is the thing that has more so been neglected. They're still good, but they're kind of wanting to go from good to great. It's not like we have dudes who come here who are 50 pounds overweight, who are just like, I need to just lose weight and I hate working out.

criteria.label: Already successful — business owner, physician or equivalent
Health is the neglected area, not a crisis

assessments.note: Realtor, 40, married 16 years, 18% body fat training 5-6x/week, has business coaches. The textbook case — explicitly wants good to great.

Retail business owner and self-described salesman, highly active. Fits on profile but not on willingness to pay — anchored at $200/mo. The rep recognised this live and disqualified rather than discounted.

Not currently working; the purchase runs through her partner, an existing client. Falls outside the stated ICP on both occupation and income — and closed at full price. The clearest evidence that the stated ICP is narrower than the buying population.
47, 228 lb targeting 200, mid-thyroid-treatment, needed a payment plan and disclosed constrained finances. Closer to rescue than to good-to-great. Closed on instalments.

Ex-army, Tokyo, already funding a PT, chiro and physio. Fits commercially but the body does not fit the programme — the exclusion that matters here is clinical, and the stated ICP has no clinical criterion at all.

Fits the profile on everything except money and need. Successful: self-employed, runs his own expedition adventure race as event director, physics degree, published a book on endurance training — a business owner in the sense the ICP means. Good to great: about as pure a case as the corpus contains, in his own words 'there's nothing wrong right now' and he is 'looking to optimize'. Not deconditioned: 12% body fat at 50, climbing three or four nights a week, training eight to ten sessions a week — the opposite of the excluded profile, and the rep said so out loud, 'you're not our typical client because you're way ahead.' Misses income: a $4,000 fee is 'a substantial portion of my annual income', becomes roughly NZ$7,500 after exchange, and only works if his accountant lets him expense it — this is the same failure mode as the Badrane H. assessment, a good profile with no willingness or capacity to pay. Misses neglected_health: the criterion assumes health is the neglected area, and his health is the least neglected thing in his life; what he actually lacks is kettlebell technical knowledge, which is a narrower and cheaper want than the programme is priced for. Judged on the criteria, not the outcome — the call ended in a follow-up, and the edge rating reflects the income and need gaps that were visible well before price was quoted.

Outside the stated ICP on all three commercial criteria, and inside it on both physical ones — which is exactly the pattern that makes the stated definition look mis-specified. Misses successful: a pickleball coach, formerly a tennis coach, currently doing a few private lessons a week; not a business owner, physician or equivalent. Misses income: no meaningful income during treatment, and savings actively being consumed by privately funded oncology as an Australian non-resident — 'everything's coming out of my savings.' Misses neglected_health, decisively and in the opposite direction from the usual failure: the criterion asks for health as the neglected area rather than a crisis, and this is an unambiguous crisis — an aggressive brain cancer eight weeks post-surgery, mid-radiotherapy, with a year of chemotherapy ahead. Matches good_to_great in the narrow fitness sense the criterion tests: he is explicit that he is not seeking rescue — 'definitely not like get lift heavy weights or get extremely stronger, I just want to like build a bit of core, a bit of mobility.' Matches not_deconditioned emphatically: plays roughly 12 hours of pickleball across a weekend, strength trains three times a week, swings a 25 kg kettlebell. The finding worth escalating is that the stated ICP has no clinical criterion at all, so a prospect in active cancer treatment can pass two of its five tests and be sold six to twelve months of loaded training with nothing in the definition stopping it — the same structural blind spot already noted against the Tyron G. assessment, arriving here in a far more serious form. Judged on the criteria, not the outcome; the call ended in a follow-up, but the rating would be identical had it closed.

Outside the stated ICP, and the rep recognised it live and disqualified rather than discounted — the same commendable pattern recorded against Harry Edmonds on the Badrane H. call. Matches neglected_health cleanly: 34, no crisis, no medical history, and health is precisely the area of life he has left untended — 'I've never done any sort of exercise in my whole life.' Misses income decisively: zero liquid cash, credit lines already committed to flights, 'I don't have the budget to pay somebody', and '6k is like five and a half k more than I could ever think of' — with a stated reference price of $25 for a fitness purchase. Misses good_to_great outright and in the most literal way in the corpus: the criterion asks for good going to great, and his own words are 'I've never been in a good shape, ever.' There is no 'good' to start from. Misses not_deconditioned on the aversion half of the exclusion rather than the weight half — he is not fifty pounds overweight, he is the mirror image at 148 lb and 6'1", but the exclusion's operative pairing is untrained plus hates working out, and he stated the second part unambiguously: 'I'd rather watch a TV series than work out' and 'going to the gym, for me, it doesn't make sense... I don't like it.' The 'successful' criterion is deliberately recorded in neither list: he self-identifies as a business owner ('you're a businessman, I'm a business guy too', 'I do this for a living as well') and his Zoom label carries a company name, but the rep never asked what he does, so the occupation test is unverified rather than passed or failed — and the rep then built the entire money conversation on the businessman assumption, which is the finding. Judged on the criteria, not the outcome, and the two point the same way here: an ad-sourced lead who did not know what the call was, sitting three of five criteria outside the definition, should not have reached a closer at all.

Closest profile in this batch to the stated ICP, and it fails on the one criterion the ICP cares most about. Matches successful: a business owner, confirmed from the application by the rep — 'I saw in the application that you run your own company, correct?' — with management work, driving and site visits. Matches neglected_health on the same reading applied to the Francisco V. assessment: health is unambiguously the neglected area of an otherwise functioning life, degraded over a decade of 70% seated days rather than by any acute event. It is close to the edge of 'not a crisis' — a compressed disc, a subluxing knee and hypertension at 105 kg are real pathology — but the presentation is accumulated neglect, not emergency. Matches not_deconditioned, again by the V. precedent: he is roughly 15 kg above his own target rather than the 50 lb the exclusion names, and critically he is not gym-averse, which is the operative half of that criterion — he trained heavily last year, bought kettlebells on his own initiative and had already started before the call. Misses good_to_great, and decisively: he is not moving from good to great, he is trying to get back to where he was 14 to 16 years ago. 'Where I would like to land, to have like around 90 kilos... I can remember myself when I was having 90 kilos.' That is rescue, and his own framing confirms it — 'I want to just start with a new lifestyle, new mode.' The income criterion is deliberately in neither list: no financial discussion occurred anywhere in the recorded portion, so affordability is unverified rather than passed or failed. Edge rather than core on the good_to_great miss alone; if income later proves out, this is the profile the ICP was written for in every respect except starting point, which suggests the good_to_great criterion is the one doing the most work to exclude otherwise ideal buyers. Judged on criteria, not outcome — and the outcome is in any case unknown, since the recording is truncated at 00:18:24 before any offer.

Four of five, and the one miss is the reason he did not buy — which makes this the most instructive ICP row in the batch. Matches successful on overwhelming circumstantial evidence rather than a stated occupation: constant international travel with named stops in Mykonos, Ibiza, Saint-Tropez and Marbella, 'back-to-back meetings all day', a 15-hour flight to Barcelona for a race, and elective stem cell therapy in place of shoulder surgery. Recorded as a match with the caveat that the rep never asked what he does, so the occupation test passes on inference; that omission is itself a finding, since it is the single question the ICP is built on. Matches income unambiguously and by self-declaration — $1,500 to $2,000 a month on personal trainers, and 'it's not even like the $4,000. I spend way more on stupid [stuff] all the time.' Matches good_to_great almost verbatim: 'I'm not here to lose 10% of body fat or anything like that. I'm just looking to change it up', with a plateau as the presenting complaint. Matches not_deconditioned emphatically — training twice a day, Hyrox competitor, former competitive lacrosse player. Misses neglected_health, and this is not a technicality. The criterion assumes health is the under-tended area of an otherwise successful life; for Jared it is the most tended area of his life. He has no neglect to correct, which is precisely why he rejected the accountability pillar ('I'm sure a lot of other clients, you got to get them to actually work out every day. I'm going to be doing that') and why he could only value the offer as a programming product. Edge rather than core because that single miss removes a third of the offer's value proposition and drove the entire objection. The rep reached the same conclusion himself at 00:10:26, before pitching anything: 'you're not our typical client.' Judged on criteria, not outcome — the call ended in a follow-up, and the rating would be the same either way.

Same prospect as the 26 May call, re-assessed with the financial picture now visible. Matches successful: runs his own company, describes himself as a dealmaker who makes deals 'all day', provides for his family — though he resists the word himself, 'it's not like successful, but I think I'm in a good way.' Matches income, which was unresolved on the first call and is now answerable: he is in Denmark on what he calls a good salary and a good lifestyle, called $9,000 'a lot of money' rather than impossible, and agreed to $6,000 on a monthly schedule without any claim of inability to pay. That is a pass on affordability, and it is the difference between this prospect and the Badrane H. edge case, who was anchored at $200 a month. Matches neglected_health on the same reading applied to the Francisco V. assessment: health is the neglected area of an otherwise functioning life, degraded across a decade of 70% seated days rather than by an acute event — close to the crisis boundary given a compressed disc, a subluxing knee and two years of hypertension, but presenting as accumulated neglect. Matches not_deconditioned: roughly 15 kg above his own target rather than the 50 lb the exclusion names, and decisively not gym-averse in the sense the criterion means — he trained heavily last year, bought kettlebells unprompted, and planned to train immediately after this call. Misses good_to_great, and this remains the single material miss: he is not going from good to great, he is trying to return to a self he last inhabited fourteen years ago, and his own framing is a decline narrative — 'I think I'm heading downwards in this game at this point. And I will be more and more weak.' Edge rather than core on that one criterion. The wider finding, consistent across this batch: good_to_great is doing most of the exclusion work against prospects who otherwise fit the definition precisely and are willing to pay. This prospect passes four of five, shook hands on $6,000, and would be excluded on the criterion the ICP quote leans on hardest. Judged on criteria, not outcome — the call ended in a follow-up over vendor verification, not over fit.

The furthest outside the stated ICP of anyone in this batch, and the closest to the definition's own explicit exclusion. Misses successful: a municipal Parks and Recreation grounds manager, not a business owner, physician or equivalent. Misses income decisively and by the widest margin in the corpus — the under $500 band of cash on hand, earmarked for fuel, against a mortgage, a credit card being paid down and a retirement-account repayment with a two-year horizon. Misses good_to_great: this is rescue, not optimisation — 220 lb at 5'11", a 36-inch waist he wants down to 30, 'I would like to have core muscles', and 'Embarrassed of having this gut hanging out front.' Misses not_deconditioned, and this is the finding: the stated ICP excludes 'dudes who come here who are 50 pounds overweight, who are just like, I need to just lose weight and I hate working out', and this prospect describes his own weight as 'technically obese', is roughly 30 to the under $500 band lb above his own target, does not train, and avoids gyms both from shyness and from being filmed by other members. He is close to the literal negative example the ICP was written to exclude, and he still received a fifty-five minute closer call. Matches neglected_health, the one criterion that holds, and it holds awkwardly: health is unmistakably the neglected domain of his life, but the presentation is closer to the crisis end than the criterion contemplates — Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with recurrent shoulder and kneecap subluxation, daily pain, and ice packs after work. Recorded as a match on the same reading applied to the Francisco V. assessment, with the caveat noted. The broader observation this row supports: the stated ICP has no clinical criterion, and it also has no screening mechanism attached to any of its criteria, so a prospect who fails four of five can still consume a full closing slot. Judged on criteria, not outcome — and here the two agree, which is the exception in this batch rather than the rule.

The most consequential ICP row in the batch, because it tests the stated definition against its own example. The ICP quote says the prospects Primal deals with 'own their own business, or they're a physician, something along those lines' — and this is the corpus's first actual physician: private practice, hospital post, newly appointed professor of medicine, married to another doctor. Matches successful without qualification. Matches good_to_great as purely as anyone in the corpus: 'I got to a pretty decent strength level, an intermediate level for a calisthenic athlete, but I was neglecting a lot of stuff in terms of endurance, in terms of VO2 max... I'm not really satisfied with that', with a body-fat target of 10-12% from 13-14%. Matches not_deconditioned emphatically — eight to twelve clean pull-ups with 20 kg added, dips with 25 kg, training four to six sessions a week. Misses neglected_health outright and in the same benign direction as the Andy and Jared L. assessments: health is the most tended area of this man's life, not the neglected one, which means the criterion is excluding people who are fitter than the definition contemplates. Misses income, and this is the finding. He makes good money as a physician in Brazil, and the ICP's test for this criterion is affordability, which he failed — $6,000 converts to roughly R$25,000-28,000 and even the reduced $4,000 tier to about R$20,000, against a household mid-renovation with a second child due in October and a temporary income dip. He validated the price rather than disputing it: 'I don't think it's an absurd value... for Trevor's work and for the accountability, I think actually that is pretty fair.' So the ICP named his profession, he met the profile on every non-financial criterion, and he was excluded by an exchange rate. That is the same shape as the observation already recorded against the Badrane H. assessment — 'makes good money' doing work a payment plan should be doing — with geography added: 'makes good money' is not a property of an occupation, it is a property of an occupation in a currency, and the stated ICP has no currency or region dimension at all. Edge rather than outside because three of five criteria match and the two misses both point at the definition rather than at the prospect. Judged on criteria, not outcome.

He is a manager in a long-established family restaurant, which brushes the 'successful' criterion, but he is not currently working normal hours, is spending more than he takes in, and is being carried financially by his parents and siblings — so income clearly fails and 'successful' cannot be credited as stated. Health is not the neglected area here, it is an active crisis: he is in accident rehab with speech, mobility and shoulder impairment, multiple therapists and heavy medical bills, and he ranked brain recovery above training out loud. That makes this rescue, not good-to-great. He does clear the exclusion criterion — he is training with kettlebells and stretching daily, not deconditioned or gym-averse. High intent and high drive, but outside the stated ICP on the money and on the starting point.

He clears the starting-point criteria comfortably. Twenty years of lifting, currently 175 lb, already training kettlebells and visibly dropping body fat — plainly not deconditioned and not gym-averse. Health is not in crisis, and his own framing is textbook good-to-great: 'I'm not in terrible shape... I don't have a specific goal, I just wouldn't mind getting stronger, losing a bit more weight', with technique mastery rather than rescue as the aim. Income is the clear miss — '6,000 is a lot of money, right? Like, we're not all millionaires here', and his reference band for fitness spend is $100-200. The 'successful' criterion cannot be scored at all, and that is itself the finding: the rep never asked what he does for a living. The only occupational signal in 25 minutes is that he sits at a desk all day and got busier after college. Assessing the primary ICP criterion was impossible from this call, and it should not have been.

About as close to the stated ICP as the corpus gets. He is a PhD psychologist running his own practice and teaching graduate students — squarely the 'physician or equivalent' profile — and business is steady enough that he turns work down. Income is not in question: he ruled money out himself before price was ever mentioned. Health is the neglected area rather than a crisis; he is 160 lb at 5'8", cycles, does modified CrossFit and tracks his macros, and by his own account 'most 63 year olds I know don't do as well as I do'. The good-to-great framing is his own words — 'I'm ready to take two or three steps bigger than that'. He clearly clears the exclusion: not deconditioned, not gym-averse, already trains before work most days. Two things the stated criteria do not capture and a human should note: he is 63, older than the archetype the ICP describes, and he has a cardiac history (AFib, hereditary heart disease) that the stated ICP has no criterion for at all — the same clinical blind spot already flagged in the ICP observations, showing up here in a prospect who fits perfectly on paper and bought without hesitation.

Occupationally he fits: an accountant with his own office and a wife in the same profession, established enough that his hours have shrunk from 2am finishes to 9pm over the years. Health is plainly the neglected area rather than a crisis — two years without structured training while everything else got attention — and he is not deconditioned or gym-averse, at 185 lb and 5'10", playing soccer daily with his kids and already building a basement gym. Income is the clear miss: 'we're full of bills', multiple mortgages, two children, a self-declared ceiling of $1,000 a month and a purchase that needs joint sign-off from an equally cost-conscious spouse. Good-to-great is the closer call and I score it a miss — his own framing is comeback rather than optimisation ('I've been out of shape for a while', 'I let it go too much', 'this is kind of my last jump into it'), and the trigger was watching a younger wife get ahead of him rather than wanting to convert good into great. He pushes back on being seen as far gone ('I don't think I'm 240 pounds'), which is why this is edge and not outside. Same pattern as the Francisco V. assessment already in the ICP file: fits the profile, needs instalments, closer to rescue than to good-to-great.

Outside the stated ICP on almost every criterion, and a good test of whether the definition means anything. He is a travelling contract worker on rotating shifts whose current assignment may end within the week — not a business owner, physician or equivalent — and the income picture confirms it: a the $1,000–$2,500 band monthly surplus, the $2,500–$5,000 band liquid, four credit cards carrying the the $500–$1,000 band+ band of debt and a self-described poor credit score he is actively trying to rebuild. Health is not the neglected area but an active clinical situation: a doctor has given him six months before starting blood pressure medication, he gained the under $500 band lb in a year, and he has a herniated disc plus 6-out-of-10 joint pain. That is rescue, not good-to-great, and he frames it that way himself. The one criterion he clears is the exclusion — he is 30 to the under $500 band lb over his target rather than 50, and he is emphatically not gym-averse: ex-Marine Corps, five or six days a week of cardio kickboxing when his job allowed it, and he currently ships kettlebells to job sites. Worth flagging for the wider analysis: this is the third call in this batch where the prospect fits the programme's spirit and fails the income criterion, and the second where the stated ICP's lack of any clinical criterion leaves a diagnosed condition — here a herniated disc under active medical supervision — entirely unscreened.

The closest match to the stated ICP in this batch, and close enough that he nearly restates it himself. On neglected health his words track the ICP quote almost exactly: 'the rest of my life is going well, there's some extra success and all that stuff in my career, my personal life goes very well for me in a bunch of different areas. This is the one area where I've just accepted, I continue to make excuses for myself.' Successful and high-earning: a sales professional travelling internationally with client meetings booked across breakfast, lunch and dinner, who says 'I'm doing well' and places $6,000 as 'not a large amount of money'. Good-to-great is explicit — he rates his shape 5 out of 10, says 'I'm not like in terrible shape, thankfully I've aged well', and 'I don't want to be mediocre'. And plainly not deconditioned: a lifelong athlete who still boxes, spars and does mitt work at a private gym. The finding worth carrying forward is that this perfect-fit prospect did not buy, and not on price. He hesitated on proof and on method comparison — a stranger asking for thousands one day after he first saw a video, with no materials to evaluate. If the stated ICP is right about who the customer is, then the loss here is a sales-asset problem rather than a targeting problem, and it is the mirror image of the existing Robyn S. assessment where someone outside the ICP closed at full price.

He passes the two commercial criteria on their face and fails both starting-point criteria. Successful is comfortable: a retired-and-rehired school counsellor who is also a working football and basketball official, a track coach with USATF certifications, collecting pensions alongside a full salary. Income passes as stated — 'my income supersedes most retirees, it's well over six figures' — and that is exactly what makes this call diagnostically valuable, because he then disclosed zero dollars available today and a single the under 580 band credit line reserved for emergencies. The criterion tests earnings and this deal was blocked by liquidity, which reinforces the existing observation that 'makes good money' is doing work a payment plan already solves; here even the payment plan failed and only a $200 bridge tier kept it alive. Neglected health is a miss, and arguably backwards: he is the most health-attentive prospect in the batch, with a chiropractor, a podiatrist, annual stress tests, a rowing machine and a sauna blanket, and he has managed 25 years of diabetes without complications. Health is his most-attended area, not his neglected one, and there is a chronic disease in play rather than an absence of attention. Good to great is also a miss — at 69, 224 lb with a 42-inch waist, his own framing is preservation: 'I don't want to lose what I have' and 'I want to get to 78 standing and walking.' That is holding ground against decline, not converting good into great. He does clear the exclusion: active, running on the field as an official, and belonging to multiple gyms. Worth flagging for the wider analysis that the stated ICP has nothing to say about age or chronic disease, and this prospect is 69, turning 70, and diabetic.

A strong programme fit and a clear commercial misfit. He matches the two starting-point criteria emphatically: 164 lb, an Army veteran three years out who trains regularly, loves the gym and has been doing kettlebells for a week and a half — about as far from deconditioned or gym-averse as the corpus gets — and his framing is pure good-to-great, 'not that I'm overweight or anything, it's just I just like looking lean', wanting to lose about five pounds and get back to Army shape. Everything commercial fails. He is 27, not currently working, living on disability, about to start as a correctional officer specifically to bring in extra money, supporting a wife and five children, with a stated ceiling of $150 a month and savings ring-fenced as family emergency funds. Neglected health is also a miss and arguably inverted: health is the area he attends to most, alongside a wife who trains with him. Read against the internal call with Kim on this same date, where the setter described letting a 23-year-old through despite doubting financial qualification because he was 'such a good fit' and expecting to route him to the cheaper tier, this call looks like the same pattern playing out — profile fit passing the screen, income fit failing on the call, and a downsell that then fails because the prospect wants the one thing the cheap tier does not include.

A core fit, though on an unconventional profile. He is not a business owner or physician but he is self-employed and living off professional online poker, with a separate office and international travel — the 'or equivalent' clause covers him, and the rep read it correctly ('it sounds like you're doing quite well, if you're actually living off of that'). Income is not in doubt: $6,000 accepted in a single exchange with no plan requested and no financial conversation at all, alongside a planned trip to Dallas to see a specialist about his back. Neglected health is close to verbatim ICP — everything else in his life is working and 'I just wasn't taking care of myself'. Good to great is his own framing and it points past his former self rather than back to it: 'I just want to be in the best shape of my life.' And he plainly clears the exclusion: boxing three times a week, walking daily, already eight days into keto with an eight-hour eating window, roughly 11 kg above his normal weight rather than 50 lb overweight, and about as far from gym-averse as the corpus gets. The useful comparison is with the Omar call the previous day, the batch's other core fit, who did not buy. Both matched every criterion; one closed in seconds and one walked over proof and method comparison. That difference had nothing to do with ICP fit and everything to do with the prospect arriving pre-sold on the modality — Javier had watched Trevor's videos, understood why kettlebells, and had already been injured by the generic alternative.

Outside the stated ICP, and the clearest qualification failure in the batch. Successful is a miss on the criterion as written: a retired high school music teacher and former professional musician and lifeguard, now working 40-50 hours a week for a boss in a role nobody established, which is not a business owner, physician or equivalent. Income is an emphatic miss — 'there's no way I can afford 6,000', debts outstanding, a mortgage running another year, and an expectation of paying $30-40 a month. Good to great is a miss: he is 100 lb above his high school weight and 50 lb above his own target, and the whole framing is recovery of a former self after COVID knocked him down. Two criteria do land. Health genuinely is his neglected area rather than a crisis — career, house and family are all in order, and he has no acute condition. And he clears the exclusion comfortably: 10,000-20,000 steps a day, kayaking, swimming, a YMCA membership he actually uses, so not gym-averse by any reading, and 50 lb above an aspirational target rather than clinically far gone. The finding worth carrying forward is upstream of the ICP entirely. No setter is named on this call, the lead came through an inbound application, and no price framing occurred, so a prospect who expected a $30-a-month membership reached a $6,000 closing call and consumed fifty-three minutes. Whatever screening produced the Rudolph call, where the setter had already pre-framed cost, did not happen here.

observations.finding: The stated ICP has no clinical criterion
observations.detail: It screens on success, income and starting point, but not on whether the body can perform loaded overhead kettlebell work. That is the one thing the programme structurally requires, and it is the criterion that lost a well-qualified, well-funded prospect.

observations.finding: The buying population is wider than the stated ICP
observations.detail: Of the two deals that closed, one falls outside the stated ICP entirely on occupation and income. If that holds at scale, the ICP is describing the aspiration rather than the customer.

observations.finding: 'Makes good money' is doing the work that a payment plan already solves
observations.detail: One close needed instalments and was disclosed as financially constrained. Income screening may be filtering out deals the payment plan could have carried.

setter.name: Kim Forbes-Sobers
setter.evidence: I was talking to your, I guess, a gentleman, Kim

prospect.name: Tristian C.
prospect.occupation: Realtor (also does sales)
prospect.family_status: Married 16 years, one young son, wants more kids
prospect.training_background: Bodybuilding / bro split, did 75 Hard. Trains 5-6x/week, walks 45-60 min daily.

signals: Already fit and disciplined; wants good → great, not rescue
Turning 40 triggered a longevity/functionality reframe
Has business coaches and mentors already; understands and values paid coaching
Frames fitness as a ripple effect into business, fatherhood, marriage
Explicitly not price-skeptical: 'I'm actually more interested in it because of the fact that it costs six grand'

goals.text: Drop from 18% to 12% body fat and hold it consistently
Gain size while staying functional
Be able to play with his kid indefinitely; longevity
Improve mobility and athleticism, not just aesthetics
Escape the bulk/cut cycle
Inspire his wife to re-engage with her own fitness

pains.text: Fell off after peak condition; cannot sustain results
Training is aesthetics-focused, not functional
Body no longer responds the same at 40; slower injury recovery
Fitness apps don't align nutrition + mobility + training
Has never had accountability for fitness the way he does in business

objections.raw_quote: I'm prepping to sell this house, there's different things that I'm doing right now... for me to make this investment right now, it might not be the right time
objections.rep_response: Let me go back to the team. Maybe there's something that we can help you out with. Are you open to popping another call tomorrow?

objections.raw_quote: So I'll be honest, the investment is an investment... can you make that investment right now? That's the question
objections.rep_response: My intention is to never take food off people's tables. If there's a way we can structure this that works with your finances, are you open to exploring that?
objections.note: Prospect said yes to exploring, but the rep ran out of time and deferred instead of structuring it live.

objections.raw_quote: do you find that people stay with the program? Or is it just kind of like a, they tried out for a year or so
objections.rep_response: We have a philosophy of teaching you how to fish, as opposed to giving you the fish. Once you're done, you're done.

objections.raw_quote: I've never done kettlebells like this. And so this is kind of like more trusting the system
objections.rep_response: Shared own story: healed ACL/MCL injuries via Trevor's program, now only does kettlebells and Muay Thai

offer.guarantee_mentioned: If you don't hit the goals set with Trevor in 6 months, we work with you for free until you do

evidence: Rep: 'Are you open to popping another call tomorrow?' — prospect: 'Yeah'
Time confirmed for ~6 o'clock next day
No payment taken, no link sent
Prospect repeatedly affirms belief in the program; blocker is timing of cash, not conviction
outcome.next_step: Follow-up call booked for 2026-05-15, ~18:00

notable.note: Rep had to leave for his next call at the exact moment the prospect opened the door to payment structuring. High-intent prospect lost to a calendar collision, not to an objection.

quality.notes: Frequent short-turn swaps, especially in rapport sections. All quoted objections verified against surrounding context.

P1.evidence: 'Where are you today? Where do you want to be? If we can help, I can show you the options.' Three-part rather than four-part, but framed and agreed. Setter Kim's notes not read back despite a pre-qualified handoff.

P2.evidence: The weakest baseline in the pilot. Never asked height, weight, injuries, health conditions, diet, sleep or energy. Age 40 and 18% body fat were volunteered, not asked. For an offer whose first pillar is injury-aware programming, not asking about injuries is a structural miss.

P3.evidence: Excellent. Drove to potential, then ripple effect into business, fatherhood, leadership and marriage. Reflect-back landed: 'This is more than just swinging a few kettlebells around, isn't it?'

P4.evidence: 'What do you feel like has stopped you from already being there?' → named the gap himself: has coaches in business, never for fitness. Rep did not probe what he'd tried or why it failed.

P5.evidence: No consequence frame. Used a past-facing variant instead — 'if your 35-year-old self had this, where would you be today?' — which builds desire but never makes inaction cost anything.

P6.evidence: 'Do you actually feel like we can help you get to your goals?' → 'Yeah, I do.' Got belief, but never ran the 'any reason you wouldn't go all in' gate that surfaces hidden blockers before price.

P11.evidence: No close reached.

objection_plays.detail: Opened the door correctly — 'my intention is to never take food off people's tables. If there's a way we can structure this, are you open to exploring that?' → got a YES. Then never ran the financial picture. Not one question about cash on hand, monthly surplus, credit or assets. The play was started and abandoned.

The prospect said it almost verbatim: 'it might not be the right time for me personally.' That is the exact Objection D trigger, and the script supplies six responses for it — 'things never slow down', 'when does it actually become the right time?', 'the longer you wait the harder this becomes'. The rep ran none of them. He said 'let me go back to the team' and booked tomorrow.

adherence.notes: The most expensive miss in the pilot. A high-intent prospect who explicitly said the price made him MORE interested, met two scripted objections back to back, and neither play was run. The rep also hit a hard calendar stop mid-objection.

setter.evidence: No KFS/KL/DH suffix in the title and no setter is named on the call. The lead is inbound from an ad: "what did I see that the ad was for, hey, there's, we're taking a select number of, I can't remember what it was", plus a prior download of Trevor's Guide.

prospect.name: Andy
prospect.location: New Zealand (small town); originally from the USA
prospect.occupation: Self-employed event director — puts on his own expedition-length adventure race (one intense month a year, flexible the rest); previously a river-trip guide; recently started a new job
prospect.family_status: Going through a separation after a 25-year marriage, on good terms ('I'm really good friends with the woman I'm separating from'); two sons, one 17 and at university studying sports science; has a twin brother who is a professional adventure racer
prospect.training_background: Lifelong athlete. Expedition climbing when younger, then surfing and paddling, then endurance sport (Ironman-type racing), now expedition-level adventure racing (seven- and eight-day events; next one in India, at altitude). Wrote a book on using high-intensity interval training for endurance; physics degree. Currently trains roughly 8-10 sessions a week: 1-2 kettlebell days, 2 traditional lifting days, ~3 cycling days on a smart trainer, climbing 3-4 nights a week, plus three-minute bar hangs 4-5x/week and loaded carries (farmer, suitcase, racked, on a treadmill).
prospect.medical: Bilateral hip replacements — first about four to five years ago, second roughly 18 months later, clear of surgery about two to two and a half years. Cause described as a congenital condition ('not a genetic deformity, but I have a condition') compounded by extreme endurance volume; his twin brother needed the same. Residual limitation: 'the hip socket has changed because it's artificial now. So I don't have as much surface and it can pop out more easily, and that's bad.' Also arthritic shoulders and sore elbows from heavy lifting and weighted pull-ups, and a prior back injury from deadlifting that required four weeks of physio.

signals: Self-directed and highly capable: physics degree, wrote a book on endurance training, has taught himself most of the basic kettlebell movements from free content — 'I've taught myself most of the basic moves.'

Anchored to a cheap alternative that genuinely worked, and the alternative is Primal's own free content: 'one of the things I started doing of Trevor's that I really liked was the halo workout, he calls it 28s... made my shoulders better, and so I'm now surfing again, and without as much pain.'

Volunteered an explicit anti-premium-programme thesis: 'really it all works... what it takes is consistency... it's not like the kettlebell's a magical tool... all the other stuff is, to some extent, what flavor you want to use to get there.'
Has free expert coaching already: a twin brother who races professionally is programming his endurance block, and his sports-science-student son advises on nutrition.

COUNTER-SIGNAL toward the_optimizer: he is genuinely fit with nothing wrong ('there's nothing wrong right now'), wants good-to-great, and did not devalue the offer ('I'm not devaluing it at all'). The reason the_optimizer was not assigned is that for the_optimizer price is a quality signal rather than a barrier, and here price was the binding constraint — 'that's a substantial portion of my annual income.'

goals.text: Learn how to progress properly with kettlebells — load selection, programming and progression — instead of guessing
Progress without hurting himself; he currently picks weights that are too heavy for complexes and is wrecked the next day
Improve mobility, which he names as his single biggest weakness, around two artificial hips
Be able to train anywhere — from his van on surf trips and road trips — with a couple of kettlebells, instead of scheduling work around gym days
Stay strong and capable enough to keep climbing, surfing and adventure racing rather than becoming 'a cyclist that doesn't have any muscle'
Shift the balance of his training toward kettlebells because they are kinder to his joints than traditional lifting
Keep muscle and like how he looks, without chasing a sculpted physique
Reconnect with who he was and what he loves doing, after subordinating those things during a 25-year marriage that is now ending
Possibly become a trainer as a side business in his small town, using kettlebell knowledge as the credential
Be prepared for an expedition adventure race in India at altitude — but he explicitly parks this outside the programme, as his twin brother is already coaching him for it

pains.text: Joint damage from traditional lifting — arthritic shoulders and elbows that ache the morning after heavy work and weighted pull-ups: 'I wake up in the morning and I'm like, why am I so sore?'
Two hip replacements leave less socket surface, so the joint 'can pop out more easily' on some movements and he has to be careful with load and range
Does not know kettlebell progression, so he over-loads complexes and is excessively sore: 'sometimes I'll do complexes, and I choose way too heavy, and then I'm really sore the next day'

Too much conflicting kettlebell material online; self-programming would cost him a lot of time: 'there's so much stuff out there, I could spend a lot of time creating my own program, and then trying to optimize that'
Training is tethered to a gym, so he now fits work — course-setting for the races he runs — around his gym days: 'now I'm trying to fit it around my gym days, which is silly'

A hard emotional stretch around the separation; the gym has become his coping mechanism: 'it's been a bit of a coping mechanism, a positive one... it's kept me grounded. I've had a couple of tricky years.'
Earlier hip decline cost him work and his mood — he had to stop guiding and 'started just getting depressed because I couldn't go on run'; two years of failed conservative attempts before surgery

objections.raw_quote: There is a financial concern for me at the moment. I'm very time-free and my kids are out the house, which is good, but that is a significant, that would be a significant investment for me. So I'd have to think about ways to make that, yeah, make that, make that work.
objections.rep_response: Ran the isolation move correctly — 'So apart from finances, like, sounds good to you, like there's nothing else?' — got a clean yes on everything except money, and then stopped. No payment plan was floated, no permission was asked for an open financial conversation, and none of the financial-picture questions (cash on hand, monthly surplus, credit cards, available credit, investments) were asked. The rep pivoted straight to scheduling a follow-up.

objections.raw_quote: Well, I have to figure out if I can run it through my business, for one. That's my first step.
objections.rep_response: Asked a good clarifying question — 'When you say run it through your business, what do you mean exactly?' — and let Andy explain the New Zealand tax treatment, then asked for a timeline on getting an answer from the accountant. The rep did not help him build the professional-development case, offer an invoice or receipt framing, or explore whether the coaching-business angle would strengthen the deductibility argument.

objections.raw_quote: that's really looking at about 7,500 New Zealand dollars for me because of the exchange rate. So we're, if I still had money, because I'm from the U.S. originally, so if I still had my U.S. money, would be a lot different.
objections.rep_response: No response at all. The rep did not acknowledge the currency conversion or reframe the number, and moved directly to booking Friday.

objections.raw_quote: So I will, let me think, and I can have some time to think about that, right?
objections.rep_response: Granted it immediately — 'Let me know what are your thoughts on that, so we can...' — and booked a call for Friday at 6.30pm New Zealand time. None of the Objection A moves were run: no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you there', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'.

evidence: No payment, no verbal agreement, no payment link. Andy asked for time: 'let me think, and I can have some time to think about that, right?'

A concrete next call was set and confirmed: 'So how about on Friday if we schedule a call at 6.30 p.m., your time?' ... 'Okay, so 6.30pm, Friday, 29. Okay, so I will set up a meeting and you'll get the invite through your email.' Andy confirmed: 'Cool. Perfect.'

Two real, named blockers remain open: an accountant's answer on whether the fee is deductible as professional development in New Zealand, and whether he wants to spend what he calls a substantial portion of his annual income.

Positive signal — full needs agreement on everything but money: 'apart from the finances, the three months of, yeah, three months is good. Everything else, the way that it works and what I think I would get out of it are good.'

Counter-evidence against optimism: he twice framed the price as larger than expected ('probably I had thought that it would be quite that expensive'), converted it to ~NZ$7,500, and called it a substantial portion of annual income. The financial constraint is real, not a stall, and it was never worked.
outcome.next_step: Follow-up call booked for Friday 29 May, 6.30pm New Zealand time; rep to send the calendar invite by email. Andy to email his accountant this week about expensing the programme through his business as professional development, and to decide whether he wants to make the investment.

notable.note: Four things a manager should look at. (1) PRICING DEVIATION: the rep quoted a three-month tier at $4,000 USD. The documented offer is $6,000 / 6 months and $9,000 / 12 months; a three-month tier does not exist in it. He also volunteered 'we have like three tiers' and 'most of the guys go for the 12-month and six-month.' Someone needs to confirm whether a $4,000 / 3-month product is sanctioned. (2) PROACTIVE DOWN-SELL: the rep talked the prospect off the standard tiers unprompted and before any price was on the table — 'Most of the guys go for the 12-month and six-month, but that's not for you, in my opinion, because you're already in kettlebells... My advice would be go with the three-month program.' He then still lost the deal on price, so the discount bought nothing. (3) FRAME INVERSION: at 00:09:07 the rep disclosed that he personally needs a hip replacement and asked the prospect for advice — 'Would you advise someone to go for it? Because I have to do it too... That's me. I'm waiting at least five, 15 years.' The prospect then coached the rep for roughly three minutes. Discovery never recovered its authority after this. (4) The prospect's two artificial hips, with a stated dislocation risk, were never addressed in the training-and-mobility pillar despite being the one clinical fact that governs whether he can do the programme — the same clinical blind spot already logged as a known gap in the script. Also: the prospect's name is 'Andy' only; no surname was ever given, and the file title contains the rep's name plus a Polish Zoom string rather than the prospect's.

quality.notes: Extensive and sustained inversion; roles were resolved from content throughout. Whole passages sit under the wrong label — for example the block at 00:02:34 attributed to 'Andrew Jin (Primal Instinct)' ('I have two sons and they started getting into that age, like 14, 15... so I rejoined the gym with them') is unmistakably Andy, and the entire pillar presentation from roughly 00:35:31 to 00:39:32 ('Trevor probably could mainly fine-tune it', 'third piece, the accountability', 'you get his phone number') is attributed to Andy but is unmistakably the rep. The pricing exchange around 00:42:00-00:43:08 alternates incorrectly, with 'My advice would be go with the three-month program' landing under Andy's label and 'that sounds about the right amount of time' landing under the rep's. Prospect connection quality was also poor — he joined from a phone, dropped and froze several times, and the rep asked him to return to a room. Separately, the rep's display label reads 'Andrew Jin (Primal Instinct)' while the file title, the Drive folder and the stated location (Poland) all point to Andrew Musial; recorded as Andrew Musial, flagged for a human to confirm the two names are the same person.

P1.evidence: P1a N/A — no setter code in the title, no setter named, nothing to read back. P1b partial: the rep set three of the four parts, not four — 'I'm happy to walk you through the whole program, how it works, what's included, the investment side... But before I do that, I just want to get a quick picture of where you're actually at right now... what have you tried, and where you're trying to get to.' That covers where you are, where you want to go, and what you have tried; 'what you need' was never framed. P1c miss: the rep never asked for agreement; Andy volunteered 'Cool. Yeah, sounds good' unprompted, and the script credits asking. P1d hit: the frame itself functioned as the open invitation and Andy opened up at length off the back of it.

P2.evidence: P2a partial — height was asked directly ('And how tall you? 5\'7\"'), weight was volunteered ('I only weigh 64') and merely echoed back, and age was volunteered ('I'm 50') and never asked. P2b miss — the rep never asked what Andy does for work or whether it is desk-bound; the event-director and river-guiding history came out on its own. P2c partial — the rep asked one good follow-up, 'When did you do that surgery, the hip?', but never asked a general health-conditions or hereditary question; the twin brother's matching hips were volunteered. P2d partial — same reason: the hip replacements, arthritic shoulders, sore elbows and the four-week physio stint were all volunteered, with the rep only chasing duration on the hips. P2e hit — asked cleanly: 'And how many times a week do you work out?' P2f partial — 'Do you feel like there's anything, like, left on the table that could be more?' probes the outcome of current training, but the actual result that mattered ('made my shoulders better, and so I'm now surfing again') was volunteered rather than elicited. P2g hit — the rep pressed on diet twice and did not accept the first deflection: 'do you follow any kind of diet, or like, you eat all?' P2h and P2i miss — sleep and daily energy were never raised at all, which matters for a 50-year-old training eight to ten sessions a week.

P3.evidence: P3a hit — 'if you would have to say like in one sentence... what would be the like one thing that you want to work on?', which produced mobility. P3b partial — Andy named mobility himself; the rep never offered the strength/energy menu and instead used 'mobility, strength, that's one thing... second thing is nutrition' as a bridge into the pitch. P3c partial — the rep probed for a concrete physical target via the race ('you have this adventure race, so that's not your goal to be prepared for that?') but never asked the scripted 'something you want to do but can't right now'. P3d hit — the rep genuinely bridged outside the physical: 'In what way? You have a lot of time or what?', then 'To get back in the market, so to speak', then the strong one, 'Do you feel like you've lost that along the way?', which surfaced 'reconnecting to who I was and what I like doing.' P3e partial — the nearest move was 'what's the next level for you look like? Where do you want to get?', which is a goal question rather than a consequence-of-moving-better question. P3f partial — the rep supplied the answer rather than asking it: 'show your sons who's the man over here still.' P3g partial — identity and the marriage were live on the table and the rep dropped them, moving to training frequency instead of driving the thread; only the sons were touched, and only rhetorically. P4.evidence: The root-cause phase was effectively skipped, and that is why the close had no leverage. P5.evidence: Entirely absent. No version of 'if nothing changes, what does life look like over the next two years' was asked, no settling question, no 'why not', no line in the sand. This is the largest single gap in the call. The rep had two ready-made consequence levers handed to him — an artificial hip that 'can pop out more easily' and joints that already ache from traditional lifting at 50 — and used neither. Instead he actively removed the consequence: 'From what I'm hearing, it's not something that's wrong right now, you're just basically trying to, I don't know, optimize a little bit better,' and later 'you're not our typical client because you're way ahead.' Having told the prospect nothing is wrong, there was no cost of inaction left to sell against.

P6.evidence: P6a miss — the belief question was never asked in any form. P6c miss — the whole point of the phase is a clear yes before anything is presented, and the rep went from discovery straight into the three pillars, the delivery mechanics and a dollar figure without ever securing one. When hesitation surfaced he did not return to Phase 5, he booked Friday. The only post-presentation temperature check, 'So how do you actually feel about it? Because does this meet your needs?', is a needs question, not a commitment question, and Andy's answer ('Yeah, I think it would meet my needs') was immediately qualified into a shorter engagement.

P11.evidence: A price was quoted and the rep described the sequence in the abstract — 'we settled the payments, I get you on the onboarding call with Trevor, and you can start whenever you want' — but no verbal yes was obtained, so none of the four steps became reachable on this call. Scored N/A rather than miss so the phase does not double-penalise the P6 failure that caused it.

objection_plays.detail: Ran the first move well and then abandoned the play. ISOLATE FIRST was executed properly — 'So apart from finances, like, sounds good to you, like there's nothing else?' — and it produced a clean isolation: 'no, apart from the finances... Everything else, the way that it works and what I think I would get out of it are good.' From there nothing else ran. No 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place'. No payment-plan door opened, despite it being the obvious unlock for a prospect who converts USD into NZD and calls it a substantial portion of annual income — 'most clients pay upfront, but for some we break it up' was never said, and the offer stayed a single upfront payment. No permission asked for an open financial conversation. Not one of the six financial-picture questions was asked: cash on hand, monthly surplus after bills, number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available, or crypto/stocks/investments. The rep substituted a logistics question — 'what's the timeline on figuring out with the New Zealand feel, like, how to run it through the...' — and then booked a follow-up.

The trigger was explicit — 'So I will, let me think, and I can have some time to think about that, right?' — and the play did not run at all. The rep answered 'Let me know what are your thoughts on that' and moved to scheduling. None of the seven moves were attempted: no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal', no 'what makes you feel it can', no 'so what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'when do you make a different decision', no 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now', and no final 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. Granting the delay unchallenged converted a live call into a follow-up.

SCRIPT GAP, not a rep failure — a tax-deductibility and foreign-currency objection with no scripted play. Andy's first stated blocker was 'I have to figure out if I can run it through my business, for one,' and he laid out the arithmetic himself: 'the $4,000 US dollars becomes about $2,800 US dollars if I run the business.' He then added a second, larger currency problem: 'that's really looking at about 7,500 New Zealand dollars for me because of the exchange rate.' The playbook has nothing for either. Objection C assumes the blocker is capacity to pay, so it offers no path for a prospect who can pay but is trying to make the purchase tax-efficient, and no path for a non-US prospect whose real price is inflated ~87% by FX. The rep improvised a clarifying question and then deferred. Worth building a play here: this prospect had explicitly floated becoming a trainer, which is the professional-development case his accountant needs, and nobody helped him make it.

SECOND SCRIPT GAP — a free alternative, supplied by Primal itself, that genuinely worked. Andy is anchored on Trevor's free content and the downloadable Guide, and reported a real clinical result from them: 'one of the things I started doing of Trevor's that I really liked was the halo workout, he calls it 28s... made my shoulders better, and so I'm now surfing again, and without as much pain.' He then argued the general case against paying for structure: 'really it all works... what it takes is consistency, you have to show up consistently... it's not like the kettlebell's a magical tool.' This is the same shape as the known '$29/mo coach' gap, but harder, because the substitute is the company's own marketing. No play exists and none was improvised; the rep agreed with the framing rather than contesting it.

adherence.notes: Strong rapport and genuinely good diet questioning, undone by skipping the two phases that create urgency: root cause (P4) and the consequence frame (P5) were essentially not run, and no commitment was taken before presenting (P6). The rep then compounded it by removing his own leverage — telling a man with two artificial hips and arthritic shoulders that 'it's not something that's wrong right now' and that he is 'way ahead' of the typical client — and by down-selling to a three-month tier unprompted, before price was on the table, which still did not save the deal. Coach two things for Friday: build the cost-of-inaction case around the hip dislocation risk and the joint damage from traditional lifting, and run Objection C properly, starting with the payment-plan door that was never opened. Also flag for review: the $4,000 / 3-month tier is not in the documented offer, and at 00:09:07 the rep asked the prospect for medical advice about his own hip, inverting the frame for roughly three minutes.

notable.note: This call needs a human review, urgently, on duty-of-care grounds rather than sales grounds. The rep sold a six-to-twelve-month loaded kettlebell programme to a man eight weeks out from brain surgery, at session 18 of 33 radiotherapy sessions, facing twelve months of chemotherapy, and at no point asked whether an oncologist, surgeon or physio had cleared him for loaded overhead and ballistic kettlebell work. The word 'cleared' does not appear; no clinician is contacted; there is no medical-screening step anywhere in the process. This is the clinical blind spot already logged as a known script gap, at its most acute. Four further flags. (1) The diagnosis was used as the closing lever: 'I think you have the strongest why you need to do it out of all of the guys that I've ever spoke to over here', 'I cannot think of higher motivation than you have right now', and the close itself — 'are you sure you want to commit to this and become the version 2.0 of Bruno that kicks the [expletive] of the cancer'. Whether that is motivating or exploitative is a judgement call the company should make deliberately, not leave to a rep at 10.30pm. (2) The nutrition pillar directly contradicted the prospect's medical protocol. Bruno is on strict keto for eight weeks as part of his cancer strategy; the rep delivered the standard weekly balance day — 'you can have a pizza or something like that, just for mind's sound' — which breaks ketosis. Bruno agreed rather than objecting, which makes it worse, not better. (3) The prospect volunteered active distrust of his medical team — 'those doctors, when are you dead? So you've got to do a bit by yourself... They don't let me take anything' — and is self-administering unprescribed supplements. The rep endorsed the frame ('So we need to get you in the best position possible') rather than treating it as a risk. (4) Commercially: the prospect asked for written payment options and was told 'we don't have, like, a set payment plans', so the person who actually controls the money received nothing to evaluate. Pricing itself was correct on this call — $9,000 / 12 months and $6,000 / 6 months, matching the documented offer, which is notably not what the same rep quoted on the other call recorded the same day.

quality.notes: Severe, sustained inversion; roles were read from content throughout. The prospect joined from a phone and carries the device label 'Bruno's iPhone' rather than a name. Also note the app name is transcribed here as 'TrueCommerce' where the same rep's other call the same day says 'TrueCoach' — almost certainly ASR error, and TrueCoach is the real product. The rep's display label reads 'Andrew Jin (Primal Instinct)' while the title, folder and stated European location point to Andrew Musial; recorded as Andrew Musial and flagged for a human to confirm.
