He then pressed the commitment line, 'you said to me that you're 100% sure and positive about it', which the prospect deflected. The deposit request converted a warm handshake into a stated red flag and the rep did not recover the ground.

objections.raw_quote: You know, it's like, you know, I know the salespeople, you know, I'm also a sales guy, but here in Denmark, we don't do it in this way. We are, we give people time, you know... I know you're from USA, we are not, we are here, pretty cool. We give people time... Most salespeople, that's why they [mess] it up, because they want to do it right now, now, now, now.
objections.rep_response: No direct response. The rep moved to scheduling the next call. Proposed label for this objection type: sales_pace_cultural_mismatch — a prospect explicitly naming urgency tactics as the thing that loses his business, immediately after being subjected to one.

offer.payment_plan_terms: Quoted against the $6,000 six-month tier. Preferred: 'just to pay in half. So 3,000 now and 3,000 30 days later' — which matches the sanctioned structure described on the internal onboarding call. Also offered, with interest explicitly acknowledged ('that's gonna have like an additional interest on that'): a three-payment plan at 3 x $2,300 = $6,900, and a six-payment plan at 6 x $1,200 = $7,200. The prospect chose monthly — 'I pay a month, I use a month' — while describing it as 'the six K', and the rep never reconciled that monthly instalments total $7,200 rather than $6,000. The third tier row above is the renewal, not a standalone product: 'when you finish the six months and you feel like you would still need another six months, you can always top it up, but it won't be an additional 6K. It's going to be 3K.'

evidence: A verbal agreement was reached and then conditioned before any payment mechanism existed. The handshake was explicit: 'You want to shake hands on this?' / 'Let's shake hands on this, because I think it's more easier for everybody.' A tier and structure were chosen: six months, $6,000 headline, paid monthly.

The close rule does not apply: verbal agreement is present but no payment link was sent and no payment was taken, so this is not a close. The rep announced the sequence — 'We're going to go through the payment, and then I'm going to onboard you and book you a call with Trevor' — and the prospect immediately blocked it.
The block was unambiguous and pre-payment: 'Before I released money from my account... I need to check some things about you and Trevor. I will not pay before. I don't do that.'
A $100 refundable deposit was requested as a bridge and was refused, and the refusal escalated the position: 'it's like strange asking for it. So it's like, it's a red flag for me.'

A next call was agreed and pinned: the following day at 6pm on the same link, with the rep to send company and coach information beforehand. The prospect stated the decision point plainly: 'I will have enough time to check it and then in the afternoon we'll meet up and either I say yes or no.'

Counter-evidence in both directions. For: intent is extremely high and independently evidenced — kettlebells already bought, diet already changed, 'I'm looking for a reason to do it', and a yes to the conditional close, 'if everything checks out, you ready to move forward?'. Against: he also said he would proceed 'either with you, either with somebody else', so Primal is not yet differentiated from a competitor, and the deposit request has introduced active suspicion into a call that had been going extremely well.
outcome.next_step: Follow-up call the next day at 6pm on the same link. Rep to send details about Primal Instinct, the company entity and Trevor's background so the prospect can run his own verification, including looking for satisfied and dissatisfied customers. Prospect to complete his checks and give a yes or no at that meeting.

notable.note: By some distance the best-executed sales call in this batch — and it did not close, for a reason the playbook has no answer to. The rep opened with a full, accurate recap of the previous session that made the prospect feel genuinely heard, built a real consequence frame around how a bad knee reshapes a body over twenty years, ran the DIY challenge properly ('even the great football players all need coaches'), took commitment before the number and re-took it after, isolated the money objection before negotiating, and quoted concrete instalment options. He got a handshake. Then three things went wrong. (1) THE UNSCRIPTED OBJECTION: the prospect wanted to verify the company and the coach before releasing $6,000 to a foreign business — a completely reasonable request from a self-described dealmaker — and there was no collateral to send. The rep had to ask 'What kind of information would you need?', which is the wrong end of that conversation. (2) THE MISDIAGNOSIS: he classified due diligence as fear ('isn't that fear creeping in?') and the prospect corrected him flatly: 'I'm looking for a reason to do it' and 'If I don't run a check, I will never do it.' (3) THE DEPOSIT: asking for a $100 refundable deposit to hold a deal that had already been agreed converted the warmest moment of the call into a stated red flag, and immediately preceded the prospect delivering a short lecture on sales culture — 'here in Denmark, we don't do it in this way. We give people time... Most salespeople, that's why they [mess] it up, because they want to do it right now, now, now.' PRICING FINDINGS. The 12-month at $9,000 and 6-month at $6,000 are correct. Two things are not in the documented offer: a the the $500–$1,000 band+ band renewal for months seven to twelve, which halves the effective rate and invites the question of why the first six months cost double; and three- and six-payment instalment plans carrying interest ($6,900 and $7,200 respectively) when the internal onboarding call the previous day defined the sanctioned plan as 50% now and 50% at 30 days and nothing longer. MIS-SELLING RISK: the prospect agreed to 'the six K' paid monthly. Monthly is the six-payment plan at $7,200. Nobody said so. That $1,200 gap needs resolving before the next call. CLINICAL: across 64 minutes of conversation over two days, nobody asked whether a man with a compressed disc, a subluxing knee, a locked hip and two years of hypertension has been cleared by any clinician to do loaded ballistic kettlebell work — and he has already produced new back pain doing it unsupervised.

quality.notes: Extensive inversion; roles read from content throughout. Notable examples: the opening recap from 00:00:21 to 00:01:40 alternates so that the rep's summary items ('And you're running your own company') land under the prospect's label; at 00:03:25 'I believe it's quite stuck' sits under the rep but is plainly the prospect describing his own hip; at 00:26:27 the delivery walkthrough 'he will get on a call one-on-one with you to build your custom plan' sits under the prospect but is the rep; and at 00:35:21-00:35:49 the handshake exchange is split so that 'The most important thing today is that, Marian, you bet on yourself today' lands under the prospect's label. The single most consequential garble is the price at 00:27:50: 'The investment is 90' where the context, the prospect's reply ('9K is not a small amount') and the twelve-month framing make $9,000 unambiguous. Similarly '1995' at 00:01:40 is noise in a passage about being 90 kg fourteen years ago. Sound was clean this time; the audio problems were confined to the previous day's session. The rep's display label reads 'Andrew Jin (Primal Instinct)' throughout while the folder and the corpus identify him as Andrew Musial; the internal onboarding call in this batch supports Andrew Musial, and the prospect also addresses him once as 'Andy' at 00:40:26.

P1.evidence: P1a hit, and the strongest execution of this check in the batch. This is a continuation call, so the material to read back was the previous session rather than setter notes, and the rep read it back completely and accurately before doing anything else: 'let me just make a summary of what we did. So you're 39, around 105 kilos... you're suffering from disc compression, some unstable knee problem, and tight hips... and you're running your own company... for the most of the time during the day, you're sitting or you're in the car... for the past two years, your blood pressure has been elevated... But also you started working out... you got kettlebells, you even started eating more steaks, cutting out sugar... And your goal is, as I remember, get back to 90 kilos.' He then checked it: 'That's still the right target for you?' The prospect confirmed every item. That is exactly what the check is for. P1b partial — a light re-frame only ('I've been thinking about what you shared with me yesterday. But before I go anywhere, I just want to make sure I haven't missed anything'), which is appropriate on a continuation. P1c and P1d N/A: the four-part frame agreement and the opening discovery question were both run on the 26 May call and correctly not repeated.

P2.evidence: Baseline was gathered on the 26 May call and is scored there; it is N/A here so the batch does not double-count it. It should be recorded that the rep verified rather than assumed — every baseline item was played back and confirmed at the top of this call. The two gaps left open on 26 May, sleep quality and daily energy, were still not filled, and sleep is now doubly relevant given the hypertension and the self-reported carbohydrate-driven mood swings.

P3.evidence: The best Phase 3 in the batch. P3a hit — the goal was restated and re-confirmed. P3b partial — mobility was established as the foundation and the prospect confirmed the hips are the crux ('everything comes from hips'), but the strength/energy menu was never offered as a choice. P3c hit, and it produced the most valuable material on the call: after the prospect volunteered that he has not run since the knee injury and used to be fast at 17-19, the rep asked the exact check — 'Would you like to get back to it?' P3d hit — the bridge past the physical was run through the identity route rather than the family route: 'when you think about it, actually, what does that version of Marian feel like?' P3e hit, and well followed up: the answer was vague ('I will be too cool') and instead of accepting it the rep pushed — 'Too cool? What does it mean, too cool?' — which produced 'I know myself how I was in that time. So, if I go back to that, that old me.' That is the phase working. P3f partial — the impact on others was still asserted rather than asked: 'you're doing it not only for yourself, but for your family.' P3g hit — the twelve-month future-pace drove all the way through: 'imagine this, like 12 months from now... you're at this 90 kilos, blood pressure is normalizing, you've got energy, you're not stiff, and you can play with your [daughters] whenever they want.' P3h hit, and it is the best reframe in the batch: 'what concerns me, it's not like one specific issue, because to me, all these things — the stress that you have in work, sitting kind of work that you do, the weight, the blood pressure, the back — it all seems connected... These are not like five different problems. It's actually one lifestyle that needs to change.' The prospect bought it outright: 'Yeah, definitely. I'm agree with that.'

P4.evidence: A clean sweep, and the only one in the batch. The rep opened the phase with an unusual and effective move — acknowledging something the prospect had said the day before: 'I also want to acknowledge you for something that you said yesterday and it actually stuck with me. Remember, you said that the change will not come from me, but it will come from you.' That unlocked the entire failure history unprompted. P4a and P4b hit: 'I tried before. So, I tried and I give up. And I tried and I give up and I like giving up. It's not like giving up. It's like finding ways to give up', and the rep named the pattern out loud rather than letting it pass — 'It will be like Monday, and Monday, and Monday. And this Monday never comes.' The Greece story followed later, unprompted: two weeks away and he never returned to the gym. P4c hit — the rep supplied a proper root-cause frame and then tested it: 'even when someone really wants to change, when it starts becoming real, there's another part of them that can show up... We as humans, we are masters of self-sabotage. Our brains are literally wired to keep us safe, comfortable, stay in bed', followed by 'how many times did you set up an alarm to go to the gym and you actually hit the snooze button?' P4d and P4e hit — the prospect named his own blocker without being led: 'I don't want to go to gym because I was last year and I was doing stuff and it doesn't describe me. So I need to do it at home.' That is the gap named, and it maps directly onto the product. P4f hit, and this is the single best-run scripted move in the batch: 'you're an entrepreneur, you run a business, you are successful... you're providing for your family. So you know how to do it. But with health, even the great football players, basketball players, all need coaches. Even though they could be doing themselves, but they need this extra support.' The prospect conceded immediately — 'Yeah, but I need as well. I think that's why I'm here with you.' Compare this with the same rep asking Jared L. to confirm he did not need hand-holding the same week.

P5.evidence: The only Phase 5 that ran in this batch. P5a hit, close to verbatim: 'I'm just curious, like, when things will stay the same, like, if nothing changed over the next few years, like, what concerns you the most?' The rep then did something the script does not require and should: he explained the mechanism, which made the consequence concrete rather than rhetorical — 'when you have an injury in your knee, you're going to walk differently and your body is going to overcompensate in other areas... when you're going to be doing that for one year, two years, or even longer, your body actually changes in the wrong way.' P5b partial — the settling question was a statement, 'if you don't change anything, you know how it can go', though it produced the settling answer anyway: 'I think I'm heading downwards in this game at this point. And I will be more and more weak.' P5c partial — 'why not' was never asked; the prospect supplied it himself, 'But it's not me. I cannot give up... I'm the guy who do things. I cannot sit and wait.' P5d hit, in a variant stronger than the script: instead of the line-in-the-sand phrasing he asked for a mandate — 'Can I have, do I have your permission to hold you accountable to all the things that you said that are important to you?' The answer was 'Yes, you should hold me accountable for that. Because that's what I'm here for.' That is a commitment the rep could have leaned on later, and notably he tried to and it did not survive the deposit request.

P6.evidence: Textbook, and correctly sequenced before any number. P6b was actually run first and verbatim, at 00:14:32: 'If you had a right structure, the right coach, and the right accountability, which is like crucial part over here, is there any reason you wouldn't go all on this?' The answer surfaced only accidents. P6a hit at 00:24:44, after the pillars: 'just to make sure we're on the same page. If you had the right training, simple nutrition, and real accountability from Trevor, all built around your life, do you agree that you would get to your 90 kilo, you would even start running and play with your daughters?' And critically he refused the soft answer — the prospect said 'That would be nice' and the rep came straight back with 'That would be nice? Or are you going to do it?', which forced 'I know it will be.' P6c hit twice over. Before pricing he took a final explicit commitment: 'Are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work to become the too cool version of Marian?' / 'Yes, I am.' / '100%? You need to be 100% on this.' / 'I am 100%.' And when hesitation appeared after the number, he did what the script says and went back rather than forward: 'before we talk about numbers and money, do you actually feel that you can get to your goals with Trevor, and you're 100% sure on this? Is there anything else apart from money that could be stopping you?'

P11.evidence: P11a partial — payment was attempted and not completed. The rep obtained the handshake, named the sequence correctly ('We're going to go through the payment, and then I'm going to onboard you and book you a call with Trevor'), and was blocked pre-payment by the verification demand. He then attempted a $100 refundable deposit as a bridge, which was refused and made things worse. Credit for attempting step 1 immediately; the execution failure is what preceded it, not the ask itself. P11b miss, and it is the recoverable one. The prospect's stated blocker was that he did not know who Trevor was and wanted to check him out. Step 2 of this phase is booking the call with Trevor, and putting the prospect in front of the coach is the direct answer to 'I need to verify Trevor' — it costs nothing, requires no payment, and would have converted an objection into the next step. It was never offered. P11c and P11d N/A: with no payment, the agreement email and the welcome sequence were unreachable.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete money play in the batch, and it worked — it produced a chosen tier, a chosen structure and a handshake. ISOLATE FIRST ran properly and before any negotiation: 'before we talk about numbers and money, do you actually feel that you can get to your goals with Trevor, and you're 100% sure on this? Is there anything else apart from money that could be stopping you?' answered 'It's nothing else that can stop me.' The should-versus-how idea ran in the rep's own words: 'most of the guys pay upfront, but if there's a will, there is a way, we could split it up.' He asked what was coming up. And uniquely in this batch he put real numbers on the table rather than deflecting: half now and half at 30 days, three payments of $2,300, or six of $1,200, with the interest acknowledged. He also created room by stepping down to the six-month tier and adding a the the $500–$1,000 band+ band renewal. Scored hit on execution. Two caveats that belong in the record rather than the score. First, not one of the six financial-picture questions was asked — no cash on hand, monthly surplus, cards, available credit or investments — which was survivable here only because the prospect never claimed he could not pay. Second, two of the three structures he quoted are not sanctioned: the internal onboarding call the previous day defined the plan as payment one today and payment two in 30 days, and said longer splits are 'not generally an option that we offer'. The three- and six-payment plans, and the the the $500–$1,000 band+ band renewal, are all improvisations.

Ran twice, once excellently and once wrongly. The good run was pre-emptive, during Phase 4: the rep inoculated against future resistance with a proper fear frame — 'even when someone really wants to change, when it starts becoming real, there's another part of them that can show up... there is some level of internal resistance. We as humans, we are masters of self-sabotage' — and tested it with the snooze-button question. That is Objection E used before the trigger, which is the strongest possible way to use it. The bad run came at 00:37:29, when the verification demand landed and the rep reached for the same tool: 'isn't that fear creeping in?' It was a misdiagnosis and the prospect corrected it immediately and reasonably — 'I make deals every day. So I'm pretty good to that in my own way... If I don't run a check, I will never do it. Because in these four years, I learned many things about how and why and why not.' When asked directly whether he was looking for a reason not to do it, he answered 'I'm looking for a reason to do it.' Applying a fear play to a competent buyer performing ordinary vendor diligence reads as pressure, and it is the first move in the sequence that ended with 'red flag'.

The delay was real — 'I will come back tomorrow' — and the rep ran the two most useful moves available. He asked for a timeframe ('So what's your time frame on this? When do you want to pick up on this?') and then ran a clean conditional close: 'if I would send you this information today or tomorrow and everything checks out and it's going to be fine, you ready to move forward?' Answer: 'Yeah.' That is good work and it is why a firm next meeting exists rather than a vague follow-up. Partial rather than hit because the rest of the play never ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to [goal]' (already answered, but not reused), no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', and no final 'are you sure? Nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?' once the deposit had been refused.

No partner or third-party consultation objection arose. Recorded because the rep borrowed Objection B's deposit fallback and applied it here — 'we take a small hundred dollar deposit just to make sure it's a token of your commitment... if for some reason tomorrow you will say, look, Andy, I don't want to go with you, fine, we're going to refund it to you.' In Objection B that move exists to give a prospect who genuinely must consult a spouse a way to hold their position. Transplanted onto a trust objection it does the opposite: it asks a man who has just said he does not release money before verifying a vendor to release money before verifying the vendor. The prospect's response was 'it's a red flag for me', and when the rep tested the amount ('If I would ask you for $1,000, would that be a difference?') the answer was 'It doesn't matter so much, if it's $1,000 or $1.' The objection was never about the sum.

SCRIPT GAP, and the one that decided this call — vendor due diligence. 'Before I released money from my account, I need to check some things about you and Trevor. I will not pay before. I don't do that.' He wanted company details, Trevor's background, and independent reviews: 'I think you have also some people who are satisfied or not satisfied with your job... I will check multiple places.' This is an ordinary, competent request from a business owner sending $6,000 abroad to a company he found through social media, and the playbook contains nothing for it. The rep had no collateral ready and had to ask 'What kind of information would you need?', which puts the burden on the prospect and signals that nobody has ever asked before. Two fixes are obvious and neither is in the script: a standard verification pack (entity details, Trevor's credentials, named client references, links to public reviews) that a rep can send inside a minute, and offering the Trevor onboarding call as a pre-payment introduction. Instead the request was reframed as fear and answered with a deposit demand.

SECOND SCRIPT GAP — sales-pace and cultural mismatch. After the deposit request the prospect delivered an explicit instruction on how to sell to him: 'I know the salespeople, I'm also a sales guy, but here in Denmark, we don't do it in this way. We give people time... I know you're from USA... Most salespeople, that's why they [mess] it up, because they want to do it right now, now, now, now.' There is no play for a prospect who identifies urgency itself as the disqualifier, and the entire playbook — same-call close, deposit fallbacks, line in the sand — is built on urgency. Worth building guidance for non-US markets, because the same tactics that close in one market are being read as red flags in another, by a prospect who had already agreed to buy.

THIRD SCRIPT GAP — undifferentiated provider. At 00:32:00 the prospect said he would proceed regardless: 'Either I choose you, and I go with you for a certain amount, even if I find another chance or somebody else... Either with you, either with somebody else.' The rep's entire response was 'That's okay. That's fair enough', and he moved to pricing. A prospect announcing that the vendor is interchangeable, minutes before a close, is a live differentiation problem and there is no move for it. It also compounds the trust gap: with nothing establishing why Trevor specifically, verification became the natural next step.

adherence.notes: This is the reference call for the batch and it should be used as a coaching example on Phases 3 through 6, all four of which scored a hit — the only time that happens here. Specific things worth extracting and teaching: the full recap that opened the call and was confirmed item by item; the single-cause reframe that turned five complaints into one lifestyle problem; the mechanism explanation of how a bad knee reshapes a body over twenty years, which made the consequence concrete instead of rhetorical; the athlete-and-coach analogy that got a self-reliant business owner to concede he needed help; refusing to accept 'that would be nice' as an answer; and taking commitment twice before the number and returning to belief when the number wobbled. The failure is narrow and instructive. Having earned a handshake on six months at $6,000, the rep met an objection the script does not cover — a competent buyer wanting to verify a foreign vendor before wiring money — misclassified it as fear, had no verification material to send, and then asked for a $100 deposit, which the prospect called a red flag before explaining that urgency tactics are precisely what lose his business. Two of the three things needed to recover this were available and unused: the Trevor onboarding call could have been offered as a free introduction, and the prospect's own earlier mandate ('you should hold me accountable') was leverage that got spent on the deposit instead. Escalate separately: the three- and six-payment plans and the the the $500–$1,000 band+ band six-month renewal are all outside the sanctioned structure, and the prospect has verbally agreed to 'the six K' on a monthly schedule that actually totals $7,200 — a $1,200 discrepancy nobody reconciled on the call.

setter.evidence: No setter suffix in the title and no setter named or referenced on the call. Nothing from an application was read back. The lead is inbound from an Instagram advertisement — 'I found one of his ads on Instagram' — and the prospect did not know Trevor's work at all beforehand: asked how well he knew it, he answered 'not at all actually.' Whoever booked the call set no price expectation.

prospect.name: Alexander R.
prospect.location: works outdoors on municipal sports grounds
prospect.occupation: Parks and Recreation grounds manager — manages seven baseball fields and a handful of properties for landscaping. Physically active work: 'On any given day, I could be walking anywhere from five to ten miles.' Also operates spraying machinery. Schedule: up at 3am, out of the door by 5am, works 6am to 2.30pm, then a 30 to 50 minute drive home.
prospect.training_background: Essentially untrained now. Played tennis in high school and used the college gym while studying, then stopped after graduating and never re-established it — partly because the nearest gyms were too far: 'I'm too tired to go to the gym, I don't want to travel that amount of time to get there.' Recently restarted shoulder presses at home with free weights to rebuild shoulder strength after a dislocation. Was given at-home exercises by a physical therapist and has stopped doing them — asked directly whether he still does them, he answered 'Should be, but no.' Also had massage therapy that helped the joints until the therapist moved away, and chiropractic that gave about a day of relief at a time. Gym-averse for social reasons: 'I'm a little too shy to be working out in a gym. And also, the gyms around me, there's a lot of the social media people that are in there trying to get videos, and it's been uncomfortable.' Hobby: archery, used as stress relief.
prospect.medical: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a genetic connective tissue disorder — 'I have what's called EDS or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome' — with recurrent joint instability. Reconstructive elbow surgery in high school. Partially dislocated a shoulder about a month before the call, and partially dislocated it again a few weeks before while catching a swinging door: 'the rotator cuff and all the other stuff in the back here is not as strong or strengthened as it probably should be.' Weak and stiff hip flexors, which he links to lower back pain and knee pain; his kneecap subluxes when he walks more in warmer months — 'my kneecap does this like popping feeling, it's like dislocating a joint' — and it happens daily. Back pain severe enough after two days of spraying twelve acres that he needed ice each evening. Describes his weight as 'technically obese' at 220 lb and 5'11", though he says his primary care physician is not concerned given his activity level. Under chiropractic and physical therapy care. Has ADD and takes medication for it. Drinks alcohol rarely, at most once a month.

signals: Wants a former self back with a specific target and date: 220 lb down to 180-190 lb and a 36-inch waist down to 30 inches, weights he last held in college — 'That would have been 15, maybe even 20 years ago.'

Ground lost across a long hard season rather than one event: a genetic connective tissue disorder progressing, a gym habit abandoned after college, interventions that never stuck, and an accumulating stack of joint problems.

Visible regret and embarrassment, stated plainly: 'Embarrassed of having this gut hanging out front', 'I have to wear a 2XL just to wear a t-shirt when I'd probably, for my frame, be in a large', and 'I feel like I'm probably 10 years older than what I should be, comparative to my friends.'

Expects himself to quit, which is the avatar's characteristic self-doubt — asked what the devil on his shoulder was saying, he answered: 'Nothing demeaning, but just another one of these. Let's see how long this one lasts.'

COUNTER-SIGNAL, and the reason confidence is not higher: the_medically_constrained was seriously considered, since Ehlers-Danlos with recurrent subluxation may well be an injury the programme cannot safely work around. It was rejected because that avatar requires high intent and no price resistance, and here the price resistance is absolute — the under $500 band of cash on hand. On the financial dimension he sits outside every avatar in the taxonomy, which are all drawn from a buying population he is not part of.
