notable.note: Pricing deviation, and the clearest one in this batch. Within roughly 90 seconds of the first price objection — and with no payment plan ever offered — the rep introduced an undisclosed half-price tier: the same six months for $3,000 with Caden doing form checks instead of Trevor. That tier is not in the $6,000/$9,000 offer structure. It reset the anchor mid-call, and the prospect immediately called it 'more palatable', which effectively kills the $6,000 tier for this deal. The rep also garbled the justification — 'That's the reason that that investment is twice as much' — while describing Caden as knowing 'basically everything that Trevor knows', which undermines the premium tier. Separately: the rep never asked what this prospect does for a living, so the primary ICP criterion could not be tested at all. Setter is named as 'Derek', who is not one of the three coded setters; worth checking whether Derek is the person behind the DH code.

quality.notes: Inverted from the first line — 'New Jersey' is labelled Richard when it is the prospect's location, and 'I'm calling all the way across the ocean from a beautiful Europe... calling from Bulgaria' is labelled Jimin when it is plainly the rep. Long stretches merge both speakers into one block, notably 00:07:44-00:09:17 (the nutrition explanation and goal recap), 00:10:02-00:11:07, and 00:15:08-00:16:23 where the prospect's questions about Zoom sessions sit inside rep-labelled text. Role read from content throughout.

P1.evidence: Setter notes used twice and used well — 'I already heard a few things from Derek', then later 'I already heard something from Derek around that sense that you're not 100% happy with [mobility]', which opened the mobility thread. Frame was three-part again — 'where you're at, where you want to go, make sure we really fit in there' — missing what's in the way and what you need. Agreement asked and given ('Sounds good? Sounds good. Yep'), and the standard open question ran.

P2.evidence: The injury probe was the best-run check on the call — the rep asked for severity on a 1-to-10 scale and for duration, and got a precise answer ('For 20 years, back issues were severe probably for like a total of a month'). Diet was properly probed, including pushing on 'for the most part' to get the cheat frequency. Age was asked directly (45); height was never asked and weight was volunteered. Work was never asked at all — the prospect mentioned 'sitting at a desk all day' and the rep did not follow up, so his occupation is unknown, which also means the primary ICP criterion went untested. Health conditions, sleep and energy were all skipped entirely.

P3.evidence: The rep did reach for the bridge, twice — 'What got you to be like, you know what, I'm gonna jump on a meeting with these guys?' and 'What was that switch for you to be like, I'm actually going to take it more serious again now?' — and got nothing back: 'Nothing specific... now is as good a time as'. The failure is what came next. Instead of digging, he ratified the emptiness out loud: 'you're quite straightforward... There's no big reason behind it. You just want to go for it now.' Nobody else was ever brought into the frame, no legacy, identity or longevity thread was pulled, and no reflect-back was attempted. The six-month success question ran but produced only 'physical form should be better, lower body fat, muscular physique. That's it.' The call then priced against a prospect with no stated why, which is the direct cause of the think-about-it.

P4.evidence: Training history was collected but never interrogated as a set of failed attempts. This prospect self-described twenty years of on-and-off training with repeated three-to-four-month lapses — the root-cause question writes itself and was never asked. Worse, the rep supplied the gap himself rather than letting the prospect name it: 'you can keep training on and off the whole time, but eventually those small inconsistencies, they will blow up again.' P4f is the single most relevant check on this call for a capable, self-directed lifter already getting results from free videos, and it was not asked.

P5.evidence: No consequence frame. The closest thing is a rep assertion — 'those small inconsistencies, they will blow up again, they will go away, they will blow up again' — delivered as a statement, not asked as a question, and never landed on the prospect. There is no two-year picture, no willing-to-settle test and no line in the sand anywhere in the transcript. When the price objection arrived the playbook says return to Phase 5; there was no Phase 5 to return to.

P6.evidence: P6b ran cleanly — 'do you feel like when it comes to the training, mobility, nutrition, and that lifelong success part with Trevor, that there would be any reason that you're not going to be able to get to...' answered 'No. I mean, it's pretty straightforward.' But belief in needing the structure was never tested, and P6c failed twice over: the prospect had already flagged cost as the deciding factor six minutes before price ('if money was no object, this would be no question'), and when hesitation duly surfaced the rep did not return to Phase 5 — he cut the price in half instead.

P11.evidence: No agreement on either tier, so payment and onboarding were never reachable. Nothing was sent, nothing was booked, and the rep did not even secure a follow-up call — he accepted 'I'll get back to you within the next two days'.

objection_plays.detail: Trigger at 00:20:56, verbatim 'I need to still think about it'. Two moves ran, and ran well: the isolation, 'Outside of the investment, do you feel like, yes, I do want to do this?', and the value test, 'Do you feel like that is worth 6K to you?' The rest of the play was abandoned — no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here, when do you make a different decision', no closing 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. The prospect's answer to the isolation was diagnostic gold — 'It's not how, it's just a matter of deciding if I should' — which says the blocker is conviction, not money, and the rep responded by discounting.

Trigger at 00:22:52, '6,000 is a lot of money... we're not all millionaires here'. Exactly one financial-picture question ran — 'So what do you feel like you would even have available' — answered 'I don't know yet' and dropped. None of the rest: no 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no credit cards, no available credit, no investments, and critically no 'most clients pay upfront, but for some we break it up' — a payment plan was never offered on this call at all. Instead the rep introduced an undisclosed the the $500–$1,000 band+ band tier with a different coach. Note also that OC was arguably the wrong play: the prospect had just told him it was a should-I question, not a how question, which points to OA and value, not to capacity.

Script gap, and the same one already logged from the Badrane H. call: a cheaper alternative the prospect believes will work. Here it is in-person personal training at his own gym — 'it's a little more accessible when I go to the gym' — plus the free online kettlebell videos that have already produced visible results for him in two weeks. He even handed over the counter-argument himself, 'obviously people are not as much of a kettlebell expert', and the rep never picked it up. There is no scripted play for defending a premium against a functioning low-cost substitute, and this call needed one.
No spouse or partner consult raised; no family situation was ever established.
No timing objection — he volunteered the opposite: 'there's never not a good time to do it'.
No fear or doubt about the programme working. His injury concern is a reason to buy, not a doubt, and the rep used it correctly as such.

adherence.notes: The rep asked the right bridge questions, got nothing, and then told the prospect out loud that there was no big reason behind it — which removed the only leverage the call had. With no why, no root cause and no consequence frame, $6,000 arrived naked and predictably bounced. The coaching priority is what happened next: a half-price tier with a different coach appeared within ninety seconds of the first objection, before a payment plan was ever offered and before the OA play was finished. Discounting to a value objection teaches the prospect the price is negotiable and re-anchors him at $3,000. Finish OA, offer the payment split, and only then consider tier changes — and never before establishing what the prospect actually does for a living.

P3.evidence: The best-run phase. The bridge question landed hard — 'you're 62, it's not like you're in terrible shape... Why do you feel like, no, I'm not happy with it, I want it to be better?' — and produced three minutes of unforced depth about outliving his wife, Medicare, identity and not wanting to retire and sit. 'How would that be for you when you actually do achieve that goal?' pulled out the backpacking trip and the century ride. But 'Who else does that impact?' was never asked, with a wife, four and a half grandchildren and a hiking friend all sitting on the table — the single cheapest miss on the call. P4.evidence: Skipped entirely. Not one past-attempt or root-cause question was asked. The prospect handed the rep the opening unprompted — he has self-programmed since 2005, owns the kettlebells already, and said 'I get on the bike, but it's like, okay, here we are, on the bike, big deal' and 'looking to get a little more of an outside perspective' — and the rep never asked why twenty years of self-direction has not produced the result, or what would be different this time. Because he was volunteered rather than asked, none of it credits.

P5.evidence: The settle question ran cleanly — 'are you willing to settle for a life where you don't get like that longevity because you're not actually doubling down on it?' — and got a firm 'No, life would be a drag.' But the two-year cost-of-inaction picture was never painted, so there was no downside to settle against; the rep worked the upside future instead. 'Why not?' was not asked, the prospect elaborated on his own. The line in the sand was asserted rather than requested: 'it sounds like you're ready for yourself. You have made that commitment to yourself.'

P6.evidence: The go-all-in question ran well: 'do you feel like when we get those all three in place, that there would be any reason for you not to be able to get to the part where you're going to have that longevity...' — answered 'No, I think I can do that.' Sequencing was off, though: the playbook wants a genuine verbal yes before presenting anything, and the full three-pillar presentation ran first, with only a soft assertion of commitment beforehand. Belief in getting there with the right structure and the right person was never directly tested. He correctly did not price until he had a yes.

P11.evidence: Steps 2, 3 and 4 were run properly and in order: Trevor booked for Wednesday 18:15 with the invite confirmed received, the agreement email located on his business address and signed live on the call ('Only have to sign it in one place... Did that'), and the welcome email, Skool link and onboarding questionnaire all confirmed, plus the tracking app. Step 1 is only half done — the first card attempt was declined, $3,000 went through, and the remaining $3,000 was pushed to an unscheduled 'next week' link with the bank limit never confirmed. objection_plays.detail: No hesitation or think-about-it at any point. Price was accepted within seconds.
No spouse-consult trigger. Notable inversion: the wife was raised as an obstacle to training rather than to the purchase, and he treated the decision as entirely his own.
No money objection. 'Fair enough. I can do that.' The later card-limit issue was mechanical, not a value or affordability objection, and correctly was not treated as one.

Card declined and a bank limit below $6,000. No scripted play exists for a willing buyer whose card cannot carry the full amount. The rep improvised well — split to $3,000 and captured it immediately — but then let the balance float to an unscheduled 'next week' and even offered 'next month' as an option. A payment-friction play that fixes a date and sends the second link before hanging up would have closed this properly.

Script gap: an undisclosed-risk medical history in an otherwise ideal buyer. The prospect stated he has had AFib, has a family history of heart issues and blood pressure issues, and has an internist watching him closely — all at 00:04:54 and 00:16:05. The playbook has no screening step and no clearance protocol, so nothing prompted the rep to react, and he did not. This is the same clinical blind spot already flagged from the Tyron G. call, but here it cuts the other way: instead of losing a qualified prospect, the programme sold intense conditioning to a 63-year-old cardiac patient without a single question about it.

adherence.notes: Richard built genuine rapport and ran an excellent Phase 3 — the 'why now, why not settle for it' sequence produced the real motivation and effectively sold the call. But he skipped Phase 4 entirely and half of Phase 2, so he never learned why two decades of competent self-programming has not worked, which is exactly the argument this prospect needed and exactly what he will question in month three. Two concrete coaching points: ask 'who else does that impact' when a prospect has already named grandchildren and a wife, and never let a declined card end the call without a fixed date and a sent link for the balance. Separately, escalate the unaddressed AFib disclosure — that is a process gap above the rep's pay grade.

quality.notes: Sustained inversions. At 00:02:10 and 00:04:48 the rep's questions sit inside prospect-labelled blocks and vice versa; the entire recap at 00:12:32 is labelled Edward but is plainly the rep; at 00:40:12-00:40:17 the prospect's 'training and mobility sounds good to me' is split across both labels; the payment negotiation from 00:54:19 to 00:56:09 attributes several of the prospect's own proposals to the rep. Role read from content throughout.

P1.evidence: Setter notes referenced at the open and used again mid-call on nutrition — 'I heard from Kim, you're not eating like a lot of junk food or anything, you have home-cooked' — which is the check working as intended. Frame remains three-part, missing what's in the way and what you need. Agreement asked and given, and the standard open question ran, then was usefully sharpened when the prospect answered vaguely: 'As in, like, what are you specifically trying to achieve?'

P2.evidence: Work was properly established and mined — the rep named the occupation, confirmed it, and then dug out the single most important operational constraint on the call, that January to April is unworkable and he leaves the house at 7am and gets back at 9-10pm. The injury probe ran well too, establishing the lower back as chronic, currently aches not pain, and self-limiting (he avoids deadlifts). Diet was probed to real specifics, pushing past 'I eat home food' to the daily four-or-five-spoons of sugar and weekend sodas. Against that: age, height and weight were all volunteered in his opening monologue and never asked, so they do not credit. Health conditions were never asked of a 56-year-old, sleep was never mentioned, and energy was never asked.

P3.evidence: The aesthetics question ran cleanly — 'When it comes to getting into better shape for you, what does that mean? Is that just getting a six-pack or describe that for you?' — and the trigger question ran twice and worked, surfacing that his time freed up and that his wife's surgery made him not want to 'stay behind'. The rep also asked the good disqualifying question, 'a lot of people around 50 to 60 say I'll do it later — why is that not you?'. The gap is P3f, and it is expensive: he had already named a 15-years-younger wife, two young children and a circle of run-down friends, and was never asked who else this impacts. Building the wife into the why would have pre-empted the spouse objection that later ended the call. The reflect-back at 00:12:32 listed his goals accurately but never made the 'this isn't really about the weight' turn.

P4.evidence: The strongest phase in the batch so far and the model for how this should run. Past attempts asked and surfaced ('you mentioned you haven't done anything like this before, right?' → CrossFit 2018-19), then interrogated ('CrossFit, why would you just go back into that?' → too energy-driven, not muscle-focused). The blocker question was asked directly — 'what's the reason that you feel like, why don't I just do it with someone one-on-one instead of just trying to figure it out on your own?' — and then the P4f check ran almost verbatim: 'there's always videos online, but what's the reason that you're not going to follow videos online?' The prospect named the gap himself, repeatedly and in his own words: 'a little motivation, it's really probably one of the things', 'have motivation, have the structure, I think it's psychological', 'It's when I don't have anything organized that it's on and off.' Only P4c is soft — the reasons offered were circumstantial (kids, COVID, projects) and the rep accepted them rather than pressing on the pattern.

P5.evidence: The settle question ran close to script — 'Would you be able to settle for not getting to that point for yourself, where you sort of stay the exact same way as it currently is going for the next few years?' — and the rep had already set up a consequence image the prospect supplied himself, his friends being 'run down at this point, and I don't want to get to that point'. He probed it once: 'Do you feel like you would get to that point if you don't really take action on it?' But the prospect deflected ('I don't know if I get to that point, because I'm always doing something') and the rep did not push, then answered his own question with the 70-year-olds contrast instead of asking 'why not'. The line in the sand was asserted, not requested: 'It sounds like you're ready to go. It sounds like you just want to make a decision for yourself and get on with it.'

P6.evidence: P6b ran — 'do you feel like when we get that in place, there would be anything missing to get you to the point where...' — and got 'so far, I don't think so'. But the belief check drew a distinctly soft answer, 'That's what I hope, yeah', which is not a clear yes, and the rep moved to price anyway. P6c then failed a second time: when hesitation surfaced the playbook says return to Phase 5, and instead the rep went into instalment arithmetic.

P11.evidence: No agreement reached, so payment and onboarding were unreachable. Credit where due on the adjacent behaviour: the rep did book a specific follow-up for the next day at 5pm and confirmed the calendar invite arrived live, which is the right move when the close cannot land.

objection_plays.detail: Clear trigger — 'I do have to discuss it with my wife anyway'. One move ran, and ran twice: the personal-commitment isolation, 'do you personally feel like, yeah, I do want to make it work, and I see myself making it work?' and 'just from the top of your head, do you feel like it is something that would be workable, it just comes down to figuring it out with your wife?'. Everything else was skipped — no 'when you talk to her, what obstacles might come up', no 'is there any reason she would not want you stronger and less in pain', no ownership question, no deposit-and-go-talk-to-her fallback. Worse, the rep twice joked about being made to sleep on the couch, which reinforces the wife's veto rather than reframing it. Note the play would need adapting here: she is a fellow accountant who jointly manages the household bills, so the scripted 'this isn't a joint decision like buying a house' line would have been wrong and possibly damaging.

Trigger at 00:59:11, 'the numbers is a little high... The issue for me is the money part, because we're full of bills'. The best move on the call ran: the won't-versus-can't isolation, 'is it more of like, I just don't want to do it all up front, or is it more so I just can't?'. The instalment option was offered, which is the scripted move. But no financial picture was taken at all — no cash on hand, no leftover after bills beyond what he volunteered, no credit cards, no available credit, no investments — and no 'are you comfortable having an open, honest conversation about exactly where you're at financially'. The prospect volunteered his ceiling unprompted (the $1,000–the $2,500–$5,000 band band/month) and the rep responded by quoting $1,200/month, which is the opposite of making it work. The play was also muddied by contradictory instalment terms the prospect had to query.

'I really got to think about it now' at 00:57:31, plus 'I think I need to sleep over on this one'. The rep isolated and secured a next call, which is a legitimate handling, but none of the OA moves proper ran — no 'do you feel what we've gone through can get you to your goal', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in'. Booking tomorrow at 5pm is worth more than a botched OA here, so this is a defensible partial rather than a failure.

Script gap: a proof and credibility objection. 'How do I see something that I could be more assured that this is the program?... it's nothing but a reel and a conversation and going into a $3,000 $6,000 deal almost immediately.' This is not price, timing, spouse, thinking or fear — it is a stranger being asked for thousands 24 hours after first seeing a video, and there is no play for it. The rep isolated it correctly and improvised a screenshare of Instagram testimonials, but had to concede 'there is not much more' to show. A prospect this legitimate deserves a proof asset, and the script should have a route for a same-day-lead trust objection.

Second script gap: an unaddressed contraindication. He stated he must avoid movements that aggravate his lower back and named deadlifts specifically. Kettlebell training is built on the hip hinge. Nobody confirmed the programme can work around it, and the presentation actually promised a mobility routine 'specifically made to you and to of course your lower back' without any qualification. There is no scripted step for checking whether the movement library fits the body in front of you.
No timing objection — the opposite, he volunteered that this is the best window he has had in years and that the three-week holiday starting tomorrow is ideal for building the habit.
No fear or doubt about the programme working; he explicitly ruled it out: 'I don't have any doubts on Trevor and in his program.'

adherence.notes: The discovery here was the best in the batch — Phase 4 ran almost to script and the prospect named his own gap three separate ways, which is exactly the ammunition needed at the close. It was then spent badly. Two fixable errors: nobody was ever brought into the why, so the wife arrived at the end as a pure obstacle rather than as a reason; and the instalment terms were quoted so inconsistently that the prospect had to correct the rep, landing on $1,200/month against a stated $1,000/month ceiling. Coach the numbers cold before the next call, lead the follow-up with the wife as beneficiary rather than approver, and go in with something concrete to show him — he asked for proof and got 'there is not much more'.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete money play in the batch. Isolation ran and got a clean answer — 'outside of the investment, do you feel like, yeah, let's just get started?' / 'I could get started outside of the investment, yes'. Then the financial picture, most of it: leftover each month after bills (the $1,000–$2,500 band), cash set aside ($2,000-2,500 liquid), credit score (self-described poor), number of credit cards (four), debt carried (about the the $500–$1,000 band+ band) and available credit ($300-500/month). The instalment option was offered rather than waited for. Two gaps. The last scripted item — crypto, stocks, investments — was skipped even though the prospect handed it over unprompted, mentioning a Roth account and stock investments he had not recently valued; that is where $6,000 most plausibly lives and it was never opened. And the rep did not use the 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place' reframe, which was available and would have fitted, since the prospect had already conceded he wanted to start.

'I would like to sit down for a day or two and budget everything' at 00:34:51. Several moves ran in substance: the direct feasibility test ('do you feel like $6,000 at the moment is feasible for you?' — answered 'Yeah, I can do that'), the challenge ('is that just a no right now because you really want to look at it, or is it just that uncertainty?'), and a strong pattern-interrupt on what happens after the call ends. Missing the sharpest moves — 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here, when do you make a different decision', and 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now'. That last one was gift-wrapped: the prospect had just quoted Rocky, 'there is no tomorrow', unprompted. The rep echoed the quote twice but never turned it into the decision. Instead he substituted the deposit device.

Timing surfaced in substance — 'that's kind of steep right now with my inconsistent working' and the risk of the assignment ending that night. The rep ran the core OD insight, that waiting becomes never: 'when you go off the meeting, it's like, well, maybe it's not the best time right now. And it gets pushed forward. That is what happens a lot.' None of the harder moves ran — nothing on things never slowing down, nothing on the cost of delay compounding, and notably nothing on the one lever that was sitting there: a doctor has given him six months, so the deadline is external and real. 'The longer you wait the harder this gets' had a literal clinical form on this call and went unused.

The rep probed for it — 'it could be that it's maybe a little bit of uncertainty around making the decision' — and was told directly it was not: 'the uncertainty is just financing the decision.' Correctly did not force the play. He did normalise the discomfort well ('if it wouldn't be somewhat of an uncertain decision, then it probably also wouldn't have been the best decision').
No partner or spouse in the decision; he appears to be deciding alone.

Script gap: genuinely irregular income. This is not the same objection as 'I can't afford it' — he can afford $1,200 in a good month and cannot in a month with no assignment, and he does not know which this is until tonight. OC assumes a stable picture you can total up; there is no play for volatile contract income, no concept of pausing or deferring a payment when work stops, and no scripted way to structure around it. The rep's instinct was right, offering instalments to avoid draining his the $2,500–$5,000 band cushion, but $1,200 a month against a the $1,000–$2,500 band surplus that may vanish is not obviously safe and was never stress-tested.

Second gap: an unpriced commitment device. The rep introduced a refundable $100 deposit as an accountability mechanism rather than as a payment — 'it's not like we need it, it's more so for yourself to actually already make a step'. That is nowhere in the playbook and it was paired with a scarcity claim that was immediately contradicted: 'usually we don't really book in another meeting... unless we actually have a deposit', followed by booking the meeting with no deposit. Either the deposit is a policy and should be scripted, or it is not and should not be implied as one.

Ran: the fit-versus-money isolation ('is this a fit for me, or is that more because of the money aspect?'), the competing-options question ('what other options are you thinking about?'), a strong attack on the open-ended timeline ('if you give yourself another month, why not give yourself another two, another three? Why not actually make that decision?'), and the residual-objection check ('would there still be an objection that's holding you back from making a decision?'). It produced a real commitment to a couple of weeks. Missing: 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal', 'what makes you feel it can', 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', and above all 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now' — which was sitting there fully loaded, since the prospect had just confessed to a lifetime of making excuses for himself in exactly this area.

Trigger is real but soft — 'I don't just go around throwing $6,000 everywhere', plus reallocating against his gym membership and home projects. The isolation ran ('outside of splitting it up or how we specifically would pay it, do you feel like you do see yourself doing it?') and the rep used a decent reframe, that a painless price would produce no commitment. Beyond that, nothing: no financial picture at all, no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no investments, and no actual payment plan ever put on the table despite splitting being mentioned twice as theoretically available. The bigger issue is diagnostic — the prospect signalled clearly this was a value and allocation question rather than a capacity one, so the correct response was to build value against alternatives, not to hint at instalments.

Script gap, and the same one already logged from the Badrane H. call: a cheaper alternative the prospect believes could work. Here it is the free DIY route — 'I could go online and say, hey, show me some kettlebell workouts, tell me what to eat' — reinforced by a trusted friend who trains professional athletes and sends him kettlebell advice for nothing. He also half-defeated it himself, twice, mentioning the sifting through content and the friend being too busy and in another country. Both concessions were available and neither was used. There is no play for defending a premium against a functioning free substitute, and this call needed one more than any other in the batch.

Second gap: an equipment and logistics blocker. He named it unprompted as one of his two main concerns before price was ever discussed — no kettlebells in the hotels and Latin American gyms he lives out of. The response was to suggest most gyms probably have one, admit not knowing, and hand the problem back: 'you're in sales, so you know how to do some problem solving.' The actual answer, that Trevor also programmes calisthenics and maces, emerged half an hour later in an unrelated exchange. The playbook has no step for confirming the prospect can physically execute the programme in their real environment, and for a fully remote product that is a structural omission.

Third gap: a stranger-danger and proof objection from a lead one day old. 'You guys right now, unfortunately, you're a stranger to me' at 00:18:05 went entirely unanswered; the related demand for detail at 00:35:00 was answered well, but only after the prospect pushed twice. This is the second call in this batch (with Edward G.) where a same-day or next-day lead needed evidence before spending thousands and there was no scripted route and nothing to send.
No partner or family in the decision, and none disclosed anywhere in the call.
No timing objection about life being too busy; his travel was raised as an execution constraint, not a reason to delay. The delay here is evaluative, which is OA territory and was handled there.
No fear or doubt about his own ability — he is a lifelong athlete and confident he can do the work. His doubt is about the vendor, not himself.

adherence.notes: This is the call to review with Richard. The prospect matches the stated ICP on every criterion, said outright that money was not the blocker, and still walked. Two causes, both fixable. He gave a price range of '$1,000 to $9,000' before finishing discovery because the prospect asked, then had to explain that the low end buys non-personalised programmes — disclosing a cheap tier and inviting the prospect to anchor there. And he left the two objections that actually mattered untouched: the free DIY alternative, and no kettlebells where this man actually lives. Both were raised by the prospect voluntarily and early. Hold the price until after the commitment check even under pressure, answer the equipment question with calisthenics and maces the moment it is asked, and go into the follow-up with something concrete to send — this buyer told you plainly that he needed to see what he was buying.

objection_plays.detail: Trigger at 00:the under $500 band:07, 'the only thing that's going to stop me is what's going to cost me'. Good moves ran: the isolation, cash available now ('what do you have available now?' — 'nothing, zero'), the leftover-after-bills question ('is it after bills are paid, you seriously have basically zero at the end of the month?'), and a probe on the one credit card with the under 580 band available including whether emergencies actually happen. Missing: the number of cards and total available credit, even though he volunteered 'I have others' with outstanding balances; the 'are you comfortable having an open, honest conversation about exactly where you're at financially' preamble; the 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place' reframe; and above all investments. This man has multiple pensions and a six-figure income and was never asked about savings, retirement accounts or assets. The rep took him at his word that zero meant zero.

A clean not-the-right-time with a specific date attached: 'I'll be willing to do the $1,200 a month, but I have to wait until September', because his Social Security increase lands when he turns 70. The rep resisted once — 'we don't want to wait per se until September' — and then solved it structurally with the self-study bridge, which is a legitimate and arguably better answer than the script. But none of the OD moves ran. 'The longer you wait the harder this gets' had an unusually literal form available here: a 69-year-old diabetic with declining annual strength, whose same-age friend was in intensive care that week. That argument was sitting in the transcript in the prospect's own words and was never made.

The most serious script gap in the batch: an undisclosed-risk chronic condition, volunteered twice and acknowledged zero times. 'I also may be having some issues with my kidneys because I'm diabetic' and 'I've been diabetic for 25 years'. The playbook has no health-screening step and no clearance protocol, so nothing prompted the rep to react, and he did not — he went on to sell a calorie-deficit protocol with restricted eating windows, which for a 25-year diabetic is a medication-timing and glycaemic-control question, not a preference. Same clinical blind spot already logged from the Tyron G. call and repeated here with the Scott H. AFib disclosure in this same batch. The ICP has no clinical criterion and neither does the script.

Second gap: a dated future income event. This is not 'I can't afford it' and not 'now is bad' — it is 'I will have the money on a known date and not before'. OC assumes there is money to find and OD assumes the timing objection is a dodge; neither is true here. The rep improvised well, bridging with a lower tier creditable against the full price, which kept the relationship alive and got a start date. Worth scripting properly, since the same shape will recur with anyone on a pay cycle, a bonus, a tax refund or a pension uplift.
No think-about-it. He gave a specific reason and a specific date rather than a deferral, and volunteered 'I want to do this'.
Widower living alone, and explicit that no one else is involved: 'I'm here by myself, I live peacefully, mind my business, I do what I have to do, and I don't have to explain nothing to nobody.'

The future-pace did work: 'let's say you get back into that old army shape, you look in the mirror, how would that be for you?' produced 'I'm in my prime again', and the rep followed with a genuinely good reframe — 'prime isn't something that was years ago, you can always decide to have a prime right now.' I can do all this, but I just need a routine', and later 'just being accountable... knowing that somebody's better than me is holding me accountable.' But past attempts were never framed as attempts, and P4f was never asked — which matters here more than usual, because this is a man with Army PT training who is currently mimicking free YouTube videos at the gym and already seeing results. P5.evidence: The rep built a reasonable two-year picture and asked the settle question twice, rephrasing when the prospect did not understand it: 'if it stays the exact same because you don't make a change, and six months or a year from now you're still in the same place, do you feel like, yeah, it's whatever, or do you feel like no, I do really want to get to that excellence level?' The answer refused the premise entirely — 'I'm gonna still keep going... if it's six months down the road and I don't see nothing, then it's something on my end' — which is a prospect telling you he will do it with or without you. That is the third call in this batch (with Geoffrey and Richard K.) where the settle question was deflected and the deflection was accepted, and it is the single most repeated coaching theme here.

P6.evidence: The belief check ran early and cleanly — 'Do you believe that you can get back into that old shape?' answered 'A hundred percent' — and the rep supported it well by pointing to older clients: 'if they can do it, why would you not be able to do it?' Perfect' at 00:36:53, then 'Man, $6,000, man. Good gracious' at 00:39:10. Moving to arrange a payment link on a yes that thin is what P6c exists to prevent.

P11.evidence: No agreement on either tier, so payment and onboarding were never reachable. The rep did begin the payment step prematurely, asking where to send the link, before the prospect had registered the price.

objection_plays.detail: Trigger at 00:39:10. Good moves ran: reassurance that this is what the meeting is for, then a clean won't-versus-can't isolation — 'is it absolutely not possible in the years to come, or is it more so like it's just a big chunk?' — which produced the key information, 'It's a big chunk. Like monthly, I can probably pay.' Monthly leftover was then asked and produced the under $500 band, pushed to a possible $200. Savings were asked three times and each time he explained they are ring-fenced family emergency funds. Missing: credit cards, available credit, investments, and any clean 'finances aside, nothing else keeping you from 100%' isolation. The substantive error is what followed. The prospect said he could pay monthly, and the rep never quoted the instalment option on the $6,000 that he had quoted to another prospect the previous day — he jumped straight to the $200 community tier. Even if $1,200 a month was never going to fit a the under $500 band ceiling, the play says explore making it work before changing the product.

Gap: the prospect wants the premium specifically and rejects the substitute. 'I would just want to talk to the man myself. That's just the way I'm wired.' The downsell fails structurally here because direct human contact is the exact thing he values — he had already said the accountability pillar was what would help him most, describing Trevor as a drill sergeant and then as a father figure. Offering him a peer community instead removes the only ingredient he asked for. The rep improvised the best available answer, his own story of starting on the cheap tier because he could not afford one-on-one either, plus the credit-toward-one-on-one promise. There is no scripted route for a prospect who wants the premium, cannot afford it, and correctly identifies that the cheaper tier is not a smaller version of it.

Gap: the price did not land. He answered 'Okay. Perfect' to $6,000 and the rep proceeded to ask where to send the payment link; two minutes later it emerged he had not heard the number at all. There is no scripted confirmation step after quoting — no 'does that number work for you' or read-back — and without one a distracted or poor-connection prospect can be moved to payment on a yes that means nothing. The rep did catch it and asked directly, which is why this is partial rather than a miss.
No think-about-it from the prospect. The deferral at the end was the rep's suggestion, not the prospect's request.

The wife was raised only as a positive — a training partner who pushes him to the gym — never as an approver. He cited having a wife and five children as an affordability fact rather than a consent issue.
No timing objection; he had already started training with kettlebells and was keen to move.

adherence.notes: Good rapport, a well-run belief check, and one excellent question — asking which pillar would help most — that produced the most useful line in the transcript: he wants someone to hold him accountable and will treat that person like a father. Two things went wrong. The price was quoted to someone who did not hear it, and the rep was arranging a payment link before that surfaced; add a confirmation step after quoting. And when he said 'monthly, I can probably pay', the answer was a different product rather than an instalment plan on the one he wanted. P1.evidence: No setter, but the application was genuinely read and fed back twice during the call — 'I saw in your application that you were ripped and quite fit before' and the prospect's own 'one of the things that I put in the application was that I just want to have the mobility to play with my kid' — which is the check doing its job. Frame is the usual three-part version. Agreement asked and given, open question asked verbatim.

P2.evidence: Weight was asked directly ('what are we talking about? Is it like 200, 185?') producing 83.5 kg, with height established and age surfacing in the why question. The injury probe was excellent: the 1-to-10 scale run separately for back and shoulder, duration asked ('How long have you had it for?'), and the functional detail extracted — lateral movements hurt, overhead is restricted, daily life is fine. Training was well covered and the rep caught his own gap mid-presentation: 'I actually didn't ask, but how many steps do you think you're setting a day?' Diet was thoroughly probed and produced keto day eight, the eating window, the smoking-cravings link and his diet history. Against that: health conditions were never asked, sleep was never mentioned, energy was never asked despite being a stated goal, and the eight-to-ten-hour seated workday was volunteered rather than elicited.

P3.evidence: The best-executed goals phase in the batch. The bridge ran twice and produced the age-40 realisation and the scale moment. The future-pace was well framed against his specific doubt — 'imagine in six months your mobility is half as severe as it is at the moment, how would that be for you?' — and produced the deepest answer on the call: 'I'd be proud of myself because I set a goal and I'm keeping my word to myself. I didn't let myself down.' And P3h ran properly, which almost never happens elsewhere in this batch: 'when you would have just had to go off getting ripped, getting a better body, that would have been a nice goal, but then work gets busy and the first thing you'd throw out the window is the training. But when you give that reason that you want to be able to play with your son those four years... that sounds like that's the actual reason.' Only P3f is soft — the son came from the application and was reinforced rather than asked about.

P4.evidence: Past attempts, outcomes and root causes all surfaced with real specificity: the Frank Medrano calisthenics programme that got him shredded and then injured, and the carnivore diet that worked and was abandoned. The prospect named both gaps himself, precisely — on the programme, 'it's not personalized... how could I know if my form was right or wrong if I'm just following a video? And I got hurt'; on the diet, 'I feel great, but I'm not enjoying the process of feeling great'. The need question ran ('what do you feel like you would need in order to actually get to the outcome?') and, pressed again later, produced the sentence the whole sale rests on: 'I just want to feel that there's someone supporting me through this journey.' P4f was never asked as a question, but the reframe ran in an adapted form and landed — 'probably when you began with poker, you had to learn from someone, right? And now you just know what you're doing.'

P5.evidence: The settle question ran almost verbatim — 'do you feel like you're willing to settle for the fact where it only gets worse or sort of stays the same for the next 10, 20 years?' — and got a firm 'No, no. I couldn't settle for that.' But the cost of inaction was built by the prospect, not the rep: 'I'm 40, how can I have back pain? If I'm 50, what's gonna happen?' and 'either I keep living this way and when I'm 50 I'm just gonna be laying down in a bed.' The rep's contribution was one line of amplification, 'it won't get better, I can tell you that'. Why-not was never asked and the line in the sand was asserted rather than requested. The phase worked because this prospect did the work himself.

P6.evidence: Belief was tested and confirmed — 'when we have all that in place, you are going to be able to get to those goals?' answered 'Yeah. Perfect.' The rep then asked an excellent supplementary question that is not in the script and should be: 'is there something specific that stands out to you the most, that's really what we need to double down on?' The answer, 'I just want to feel that there's someone supporting me through this journey', is the single most useful line in the transcript. The go-all-in question was never asked in its 'is there any reason you wouldn't' form, only in the positive. Sequencing was clean — price came only after the yes, and the prospect had already volunteered 'I'm locked in' and 'I'm 100% committed' well before it.

P11.evidence: The weakest close execution in the batch, on the easiest deal in the batch. Step 1: a payment link was sent to the Zoom chat and to WhatsApp and receipt was confirmed, but nothing was collected — the card was at an office fifteen minutes away, the rep floated fetching it ('if it's in the same house, just take a quick walk and get it') and then accepted a two-hour deferral. Step 2: a Trevor slot was proposed for 13:15 the next day and a link sent, but both parties treated the booking as contingent on payment, so it is provisional. Steps 3 and 4 did not happen at all — no agreement email, no signature, no welcome email, no Skool community link, no onboarding questionnaire, none of it mentioned. Contrast the Scott H. call in this same batch, where all four steps ran in order.

objection_plays.detail: A genuine fear-and-doubt trigger, though about capability rather than the offer: 'it's hard for me to believe that I can do this, or grab a kettlebell with the pain that I feel when I do these exercises.' The rep answered it twice and effectively, in substance if not to script — Trevor's own history of shoulder and back injuries, then progressive loading ('we're not going to start with super heavy weights, first of all because of your shoulder'), reinforced with a poker analogy about starting at five-dollar stakes. That is the scripted BRIDGE move — not asking him to see the whole other side, just take the first step — arriving in the prospect's own language. None of the other OE moves ran (certainty, pleasure versus pain, the plane, burned before), and none were needed. The prospect resolved it himself: 'that's why I applied because he said he used to suffer from it.'
No hesitation whatsoever. He had pre-committed before hearing the price.
A girlfriend is mentioned in passing but never as a decision-maker. He decided alone.
Zero money objection. He asked one question about structure — one-time or monthly — accepted the answer and said 'Sounds good.' Correctly treated as logistics rather than resistance.
The opposite: he had already started the diet and stated he would proceed regardless of whether he worked with Trevor.

Gap: a ready buyer without his card to hand. Not an objection and not affordability — the money exists and the decision is made, but the instrument is fifteen minutes away. There is no scripted move for holding a sold buyer through to collection, and the rep improvised weakly: he suggested fetching it, was told two hours, and settled for a second Zoom instead. Two hours is enough time for a poker professional to get distracted, and the whole Phase 11 sequence now depends on a call that may not happen. A scripted line for 'go and get the card, I'll wait' would have closed this on the day.

adherence.notes: Phases 3, 4 and 6 were the strongest of the batch — the reflect-back genuinely ran, the root cause came out in the prospect's own words twice, and the extra question 'what should we double down on?' produced the sentence that sold the deal. Then the close was left half-finished. This buyer had said 'I'm locked in' before the price, accepted $6,000 in one breath, and still walked away without paying, without an agreement, without the community link and without a confirmed onboarding call, because his card was in another building and the rep took two hours as an answer. That is the coaching point: on a zero-resistance close, ask him to go get the card and hold the line. Separately, escalate that a prospect with several years of chronic back pain and a restricted overhead shoulder — who is flying to Dallas in September to see a chiropractor about it, and who named that exact doubt himself — was reassured with the coach's personal injury history rather than any assessment.

setter.evidence: No setter named anywhere. The rep references an inbound application — 'I already saw your application' — and an earlier contact where he learned the prospect's wife had car trouble, but no setter appears in the title or the transcript. Notably no price pre-framing had been done, which is the central fact of this call.

notable.note: A qualification failure, not a selling failure. This prospect arrived expecting a $30-the under $500 band per month membership and was quoted $6,000 — roughly a thirty-fold gap — and there is no setter named anywhere on this call and no evidence of any price pre-framing before it. Compare the Rudolph call the previous day, where Kim had already given the prospect 'an insight from what the costs are going to look like' and price landed calmly. Fifty-three minutes of good discovery were spent on someone who could never buy. Credit where due: once the gap appeared the rep behaved well — he refused to discount, told the prospect plainly that cheaper options exist and that Trevor is at the top of the market, and pointed him to the free YouTube content rather than pushing. Two further notes. He has two shoulder surgeries on his right side, a repaired labrum and rotator cuff, and asked directly whether kettlebells would even help his balance ('I really don't, in all honesty, I don't really know') — neither was ever properly answered. And the rep misnamed him twice, as 'Darren' at 00:00:20 and 'Richie' at 00:44:56, which is the third call in this batch with a name error.

quality.notes: Compounded by both men being called Richard. Attribution inverts repeatedly: at 00:01:57 the prospect's 'I need more sleep' is labelled to the rep; the entire exchange from 00:08:17 to 00:09:44 puts the rep's challenge questions under the prospect's label and vice versa; 00:18:37-00:19:13 splits the rep's rephrased future-pacing question across three blocks attributed to both; and at 00:25:19-00:26:32 the prospect's YMCA weights story runs into rep-labelled text. Role read from content throughout.

P1.evidence: No setter notes to read back — the lead came from an inbound application and no setter is named — though the rep did open on a personal detail from a previous contact, asking whether the wife's car was sorted, which does the same job of making the prospect feel seen. Frame remains three-part. Agreement asked and given. The open question ran and was then improved on: 'Realistic goals or what I really want?' / 'What you want. Be as unrealistic as possible and we'll see if it works' — which unlocked the whole first ten minutes.

P2.evidence: Weight was asked directly ('what do you currently weigh?' — 210) with height and age established in dialogue. The injury probe ran well and produced both shoulder surgeries with timing, the 50-year-old knee injury, the recent fall and the flexibility problem. Current training was fully mapped: 10-20,000 steps a day, kayaking, swimming, YMCA. Results from past attempts were elicited by a good question — 'why didn't you just start that again?' — producing the pre-pandemic drop to 170. Hereditary health came out through the longevity thread. But current day-to-day diet was never actually asked, which is a strange omission on a 50 lb fat-loss goal; what surfaced was a historical protocol plus a gluten intolerance the prospect raised himself. Sleep was volunteered in his opening sentence ('I need more sleep') and never followed up. Energy was never asked. Occupation was never asked at all.

P3.evidence: The strongest goals phase in the batch. The unrealistic-goals invitation produced everything at once — 160 lb, the 135 lb dream, the six-pack as byproduct. The can't-do-now check produced kayaking, swimming a mile, a marathon, archery. The bridge question was well built: 'there are so many 60, 70, 75-year-olds who say it comes with the age and don't take action. Why do you feel like for you, it's so important?' — which produced the three futures (the farm, travelling, and not being fat for 30 years given a family that lives into its 90s). Best of all, the impact question was asked three separate times: the prospect said 'I'm not even sure what you're asking' and the rep rephrased twice rather than moving on, eventually reaching the daughters and the two grandsons. Only the reflect-back is soft — accurate summaries, but no 'this isn't really about the weight' turn.

P4.evidence: Excellent and genuinely challenging. Past attempts surfaced (the pre-pandemic juice cleanse and elimination diet, and the abandoned YMCA weights circuit), what happened surfaced (down to 170; the circuit 'was like working in the fast food industry, there was no joy'), and the rep pressed properly on why it stopped: 'why didn't you just start that again? Why haven't you done it yet?' and then refused the first excuse — 'But you haven't yet' and 'Would it have been absolutely impossible to follow the nutrition already during that time?' and 'What's going to stop you from, in a couple of months, life gets busy again, and you just throw it to the side?' The prospect named the gap in his own words twice: 'I keep finding excuses not to start' and the joy criterion, 'if I'm not finding joy in it, I'm not going to do it.' P4f is partial only because the specific reframe was never made — this man already owns a diet protocol that provably worked and had free access to a nutritionist, and nobody said out loud that the information was never the problem.

P5.evidence: The settle question ran almost verbatim — 'are you willing to settle with it not changing because you haven't actually put in the right efforts?' — and then failed in an interesting way. The prospect answered with a five-minute philosophical monologue about joy, professional musicianship and being told he could not succeed, which never engaged the question at all. The rep summarised it charitably ('sounds like you're not willing to settle for something that you don't like') and moved on. The urgency was never established. The consequence material was there — a man who wants to live past 100, whose family reaches their 90s, who fell over on a walk three weeks ago — and the two-year picture was never drawn. No line in the sand was ever requested.

P6.evidence: The commitment was asserted rather than obtained: 'it sounds like when we begin, you are going to take it serious, right?' answered 'Right', and later 'it sounds like you feel like it's a good fit. I don't know if that's correct?' answered 'Yes.' The go-all-in question was never asked. More importantly, the prospect had left an explicit, unresolved condition on the table twenty minutes earlier — 'I really don't know if this particular activity is going to fulfill me' — and it was never converted into a yes before pricing. Given that joy is the single criterion he told the rep governs everything he sustains, that was the yes that mattered and it was never secured.

P11.evidence: Explicit no on the call. Payment and onboarding were never reachable.

objection_plays.detail: Isolation ran twice and ran well — 'out of the finances, you feel like, yes, I want to do this, or not really?' produced 'If I could afford it, yes, I would do this', which is exactly the answer the play is designed to surface. The budget-range question was then asked twice and produced the decisive number: '30, the under $500 band a month'. Nothing else ran — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments, and no payment plan, even though the prospect raised payment plans himself ('payment plans and things like that, the big number is I don't get the $1,000–the $2,500–$5,000 band band a month'). Scored partial rather than miss because once a $30-the under $500 band/month expectation is on the table, working a financial picture toward $6,000 would have been dishonest rather than diligent. The rep read that correctly.

The strongest instance in the whole batch of the known script gap around a cheaper alternative that genuinely worked — and here the alternative is free and proven. He has a YMCA membership he can use at no cost, an ex-student who is a nutritionist and advises him for nothing, and a dietary protocol he has personally run to a 170 lb result. He stated the conclusion himself: 'there are other ways that I can do things that's not going to cost me $6,000 and I can get healthy.' The rep's reply was a differentiation claim — 'for 50 a month, you're never going to find something that's actually customized to you' — which does not answer why customisation is worth 150 times the alternative to a man whose uncustomised approach already worked. There is no play for this and it decided the call.

A thirty-fold expectation gap, which is a qualification failure rather than an objection. The prospect expected 'any kind of a membership where it's 30, 40 a month' and his wife had pre-framed it as 'you're not going to spend very much'. No setter is named on this call and no price framing had been done. The rep handled the moment with integrity — refused to discount, said plainly 'Trevor is definitely not the cheapest, you're going to be able to find cheaper things', qualified out with 'if you're looking to spend maybe a hundred max, then this is definitely not for you', and directed him to free content. That is the right behaviour and the reason this scores partial rather than miss. The failure sits upstream, in whatever put a $30-a-month buyer on a $6,000 closing call.

'Obviously, I have to run it by her as well', plus the wife having pre-framed the spend downward and separately dismissing his gluten intolerance as psychosomatic. No OB move ran. It was arguably moot by the time it surfaced, since the price gap had already ended the call, but the wife was an active negative influence throughout and was never engaged with — including earlier, when she was raised as doubting his dietary self-knowledge.
No think-about-it. He decided on the call and said so twice.
No timing objection. He volunteered that his hours have dropped and that this is the right moment — 'I really got to get started'.

No fear or doubt about his ability. He did carry an unresolved doubt about whether the programme would be fulfilling — 'I really don't know if this particular activity is going to fulfill me' — but that is a fit question, and it belonged in Phase 6 rather than here.

adherence.notes: Phases 3 and 4 were the best work in this batch — the unrealistic-goals opener, three attempts at the impact question when the prospect did not understand it, and real refusal to accept the first excuse. All of it was spent on someone who arrived expecting to pay $30 a month. The lesson is not for the closer, it is for whoever routed this lead: no setter is attached to this call and no price framing happened, and fifty-three minutes went into a prospect who could never buy. Two coaching points that still stand. When the settle question produced a philosophical monologue instead of an answer, the rep accepted it and lost the urgency; ask it again. And the prospect said outright that he only sustains what brings him joy, then flagged that he did not know whether this would fulfil him — that doubt was never resolved into a yes before the price was quoted, and it was the only yes that mattered.
